method: Built from work/recommendations.jsonl (2,913 mentions): a Python pass grouped mentions by a normalised title key, keying Everything is Everything and The Seen and the Unseen episodes by episode number (resolved from the titles in episodes.jsonl where the mention gave none), and every group was then reviewed by hand for missed merges (subtitles, spellings, author-prefixed titles, unnumbered episode references) and false merges (cover versions, a book versus its film or TV series, show episodes versus the books they share a name with). Titles, creators and types were canonicalised; works mentioned in two or more episodes carry a hand-written synthesis of why the hosts recommend them, and single-episode works copy their mention's reason verbatim.

items.title: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: The show's standing textbook and the frame behind most of Ajay's arguments: when and how the Indian state should act, through market failures, scarce state capability, the marginal cost of public funds, the least-intrusive intervention and dispersed power with checks and balances. It is the book Ajay would send back in time to Nehru, and the second edition pairs every chapter with a reading list.

items.title: The Art of Clear Writing
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's course on writing clearly, plugged in dozens of show notes. It teaches that clear writing is clear thinking, through concrete rules (verbs over adjectives, simple sentences, every sentence earning its place) and constraint-based exercises.

items.title: Life Lessons
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' joint course: a structured on-ramp to the show's way of thinking, covering learning how to learn, frameworks for thinking, writing, productivity, money and relationships, the things they wish someone had taught them at twenty. A community of cohorts, meetups and book clubs has grown around it.

items.title: The India Uncut Newsletter
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's newsletter, the written home between episodes for his columns, essays and recommendations on Indian politics, policy, culture and life, and the place to follow him now that the show has ended.

items.title: Why Freedom Matters (Everything is Everything, episode 10)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The show's foundation stone: freedom is the default, and any state coercion must clear a high bar, told through the hockey stick of world GDP after free markets and India's own story from Nehru's and Indira's controls to 1991 and after. It is companion listening for almost every policy episode, from China and agriculture to women's emancipation through growth.

items.title: The Beauty of Finance (Everything is Everything, episode 21)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's case that finance is not a rich man's casino but the brain of the economy: it allocates capital, bets on many longshots and touches every part of ordinary life. The hosts treat it as the foundation for later episodes on firms, exchange rates, manufacturing and financial crises.

items.title: The LEAP Blog
items.creator: Ajay Shah and colleagues
items.why: Ajay and his colleagues' long-running blog, where the research and policy arguments behind the show, on finance, regulation, measurement and India's strategy in a new globalisation, are written up in full. Ajay holds it up as low-bullshit scientific communication that takes good work straight to readers.

items.title: The Reformers (Everything is Everything, episode 28)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' pitch for a web series on India's silent reformers, Manmohan Singh, Montek Ahluwalia and the economists around them, who worked behind the scenes for decades to build the consensus that 1991 released, and on the Rao-Vajpayee-Manmohan continuity that followed. Amit loves it as proof that long games against the tide can win.

items.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 335)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's long-form masterclass on the Russia-Ukraine war, the harvest of a lifetime of reading on military strategy. It grounds the show's later talk of modern war: mavericks recruited under pressure, Ukraine's 'Uber for artillery', cheap drones and Europe's escape from gas blackmail.

items.title: How to Do Development (Everything is Everything, episode 57)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' case that growth is the only way out of mass poverty, and that development economics went wrong by shrinking its ambitions to RCT-sized problems. Built on Pritchett's finding that per-capita GDP tracks almost every welfare indicator, it is their answer to the show's central question: why is India poor?

items.title: The Seen and the Unseen
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's flagship long-form interview show, the deeper-water sister to EIE: single-guest conversations that often run for hours, which Ajay calls the closest thing India has to an oral economic history, 'conversations with greatness'.

items.title: Understanding the State (Everything is Everything, episode 25)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The foundation of the show's thinking about government: the state as a monopoly on legitimate violence, every act of government as coercion paid for by coerced taxes, and Fukuyama's scope-versus-strength lens that makes India a weak state doing too much. Start here before the episodes on regulation, legitimacy and public policy.

items.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Everything is Everything, episode 41)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts unpack landmark papers, above all Hayek on how prices pool knowledge no planner could gather and Coase on why firms exist. They return to it whenever they argue that society is too complex for top-down planning.

items.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Everything is Everything, episode 33)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The episode Amit says every Indian must watch: the state is not a benevolent beast but people responding to incentives, so government failure is the norm. It explains ribbon-cutting over maintenance, captured subsidy schemes, ever-bigger pension promises and why no one should hold unchecked power.

items.title: The Long Road to Change (Everything is Everything, episode 36)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The show's theory of change: reform travels a 10-20 year pipeline of data, research, debate, expert reports, law and implementation that cannot be skipped, sustained by a lively community of thinkers and critics. It explains why the NPS and inflation targeting took a decade or more, why bankruptcy reform is faltering, and why reforms decay unless someone babysits them.

items.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Amit's pick for the most important essay of the twentieth century: knowledge is scattered across millions of heads, and prices are the system that pools it, which is why no central planner can match a market. Read it slowly; once you see prices as a language between strangers you cannot unsee it, and the case against price controls follows.

items.title: When Should the State Act? (Everything is Everything, episode 26)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The companion to episode 25 and the show's checklist for intervention: start from freedom, find a genuine market failure such as a public good or an externality, and remember that a market failure is necessary but not sufficient, because coercive power, unlike spending, has no budget constraint.

items.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 402)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's 10.5-hour life-and-times conversation with Amit, the long version behind his frameworks: his father, the founding of SEBI and the NSE, the FSLRC and the bankruptcy code, and the 2008 crisis. Amit offers it as a case study of progress built incrementally through feedback, data and many small moves.

items.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Everything is Everything, episode 37)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's account of how Indian firms evolved from regional satraps to top-down 'imperial' firms to adaptive ones with local discretion guided by rules. In a country as varied as India you need a starfish with many thinking heads, not an octopus with one brain, and the lens travels to governments too.

items.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Everything is Everything, episode 48)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's case that internationalisation is how a country grows: firms that compete globally import best practices and lift their standards, while tariffs hide their weaknesses. It underpins the show's arguments on exports, FDI, manufacturing and the road to 8% growth.

items.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Everything is Everything, episode 20)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The source of the show's motto 'people are brains, not stomachs': population density drives prosperity, the 'population problem' is a governance failure in disguise, and coercive sterilisation was among the worst abuses of state power. It also covers India's demographic transition, which shapes later arguments on pensions and migration.

items.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 237)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
items.why: The long-form account, with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay, of what 1991 achieved and what it left undone in factor markets and agriculture, and of how it harvested two decades of upstream work. The hosts send listeners born after 1991 here to understand the licence-raj era and where Indian success came from.

items.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Everything is Everything, episode 24)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' diagnosis of India's broken pipeline from academia to society: disciplines retreated into departments and journal 'clubhouses' that distort incentives, an institutional ladder selects against creative weirdos, and the middle class lacks liberal-arts basics. It is the companion to the education episode on what kind of intellectual ecosystem India needs.

items.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Everything is Everything, episode 34)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A popular episode on how Indian firms mature from autocratic family control to dispersed shareholding and then to boards with professional management, which Amit calls original thinking universities should teach. The hosts reuse it to argue that growth happens through firms, and that even inside firms power must disperse.

items.title: Seeing Like a State
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: The book both hosts cite most on how states fail: bureaucracies impose simplified, legible grids on local realities they cannot see, and 'high modernism' turns that blindness into cruelty. Ajay argued with it on every page and now applies its ideas to firms, migration and India's digital state; as Amit puts it, Scott cured him of 'the fatal disease of seeing like an engineer'.

items.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 355)
items.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
items.why: An eight-and-a-half-hour portrait of a reforming bureaucrat that listeners call the most perfect product for understanding the Indian state. It is the inside story of how inflation targeting and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code got done, and of how Delhi responded when Lehman fell.

items.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 259)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
items.why: Amit's most-listened conversation, with Shrayana Bhattacharya, on the inner lives of Indian women, social conformity and the 'anti-uncle'. It is the show's evidence for why marriage can be a trap for non-elite women and why rising divorce rates deserve celebration.

items.title: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Everything is Everything, episode 18)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The full case that Indian agriculture is crippled by a suppressed price system: MSPs and central planning seeded cereal-heavy diets and diabetes, Punjab's rice and Delhi's smog, and recurring gluts, while politics prefers loan waivers to structural reform.

items.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Everything is Everything, episode 54)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Thirty years of both hosts' thinking on Indian education compressed into an hour, and one of the episodes Amit is proudest of. Piling on inputs like schools and spending without learning outcomes calls for rethinking from first principles, and regimented schooling destroys the curiosity that disruption needs.

items.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Everything is Everything, episode 9)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A personal account of reversing type 2 diabetes by changing what you eat and how you live, with the history of how the sugar lobby and the 1977 US dietary guidelines demonised fat. The hosts use it as a parable against the state as nutrition authority, and for structural over parametric change.

items.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Everything is Everything, episode 46)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on Rob Henderson's 'luxury beliefs': fashionable positions held to signal status by people insulated from their costs, from minimum wages to Western ideas misapplied to India. It also untangles the zero-sum fallacy that confuses fighting inequality with fighting poverty.

items.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Everything is Everything, episode 40)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A master class, in Amit's words, on the economics of solar, wind, batteries and time-of-day pricing, and on why broken Indian electricity quietly kills manufacturing. Ajay rates it among the show's best, and it seeded the follow-up episode making the case for nuclear.

items.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Everything is Everything, episode 56)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' critique of India's celebrated digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI and the rest): calling them 'public goods' hides state-built coercive monopolies that crowd out competition and amass data. Ajay argues the state should delete data by default.

items.title: Economics in One Lesson
items.creator: Henry Hazlitt
items.why: Amit's headline starter book for thinking like an economist. Hazlitt extends Bastiat's seen and unseen across tariffs, price controls and inflation with one lesson: trace a policy's long-run effects on all groups, not just the one it visibly helps.

items.title: I, Pencil
items.creator: Leonard Read
items.why: The parable of spontaneous order: no one on earth knows how to make a pencil, yet millions of strangers across dozens of countries cooperate to make one, coordinated only by prices. Amit treats it as the most accessible cure for hubris about central planning and the first step towards Hayek.

items.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Everything is Everything, episode 68)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The story of how India adopted inflation targeting, a reform Ajay championed for fifteen years and a canonical case of rules over discretion and of ideas creeping into practice. It covers the long, messy history of central banking that makes a 4% bullseye the bedrock of financial planning.

items.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 379)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
items.why: Amit's long conversation with the development economist who argues that growth is necessary and sufficient, since it tracks human-welfare indicators about 99%, and that the RCT turn left the field searching under the lamppost. It seeded the show's thinking on decentralisation and development.

items.title: Poker and Life (Everything is Everything, episode 38)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' poker episode, drawing on Ajay's life as a professional player: in a probabilistic world, judge decisions by process, not outcome; know the difference between game-theory-optimal and exploitative play; and prefer legal, regulated betting to the underworld kind.

items.title: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
items.creator: John Stossel
items.why: The show's shorthand for why voluntary trade is positive-sum: the customer thanks the barista for the coffee and the barista thanks the customer for the money, so both leave better off. A one-page refutation of the zero-sum view of markets.

items.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Paul Graham's map of conformity, used from the show's first episode: the real obstacle to progress is not the passive herd but the 'aggressively conventional-minded' who police the tribe. It explains why heretics from Oppenheimer to medical outlaws were persecuted, and how to spot and route around the enforcers.

items.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Everything is Everything, episode 14)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The EIE-format update on the Russia-Ukraine war, a shorter companion to Ajay's Seen and the Unseen deep dive. It covers Ukrainian innovation under fire such as the 'Uber for artillery', the lessons of combined-arms warfare and the war's toll on Russian demographics.

items.title: XKDR Forum
items.creator: Ajay Shah and colleagues
items.why: Ajay's research organisation and its channel of talks, seminars and papers on Indian law, economics and finance. The hosts present it as the upstream body of policy work that has to exist before the next crisis arrives.

items.title: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 310)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Philips
items.why: Amit's conversation with the 'Liver Doc', a hepatologist who has staked his career on calling out quackery and reads the research literature daily. It is the source of the evidence that flipped Amit on alcohol: even casual drinking does liver damage that outweighs any heart benefit.

items.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Everything is Everything, episode 45)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A diagnostic toolkit for public debate: the zero-sum, top-down and strongman instincts we evolved in small tribes misfire in a complex modern society, which is why Marxism and statism feel intuitive. The same fallacies Hazlitt dissected, in a modern Indian setting.

items.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Everything is Everything, episode 80)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's deep dive on the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: firms must be free to die for an economy to stay dynamic, yet the law's checks and balances were stripped out inside government. It explains why small suppliers don't get paid on time and how financial firms should be allowed to fail.

items.title: India Needs Decentralization (Everything is Everything, episode 47)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case for subsidiarity: push every government function down to the lowest level that can handle it, because a country of a thousand locales cannot be run from one centre. It pairs with Separation of Powers as one of two ways to disperse power, and as a route to legitimacy through local accountability.

items.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's plain-language rebuttal of the 'pro-poor' instinct to cap prices: caps don't lower prices, they make goods disappear, breed shortages and black markets, and hurt the very people they claim to protect, as with stents and Uber.

items.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Everything is Everything, episode 59)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's 20-year blueprint for Indian innovation: gatekeepers such as funders and journal editors reject high-variance bets, so the state should fund research through many industry-neutral grants and contracts rather than pick winners or chase prestige projects.

items.title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Everything is Everything, episode 23)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The first of the show's 'stories that should be films' episodes, with pitches such as a supposedly warrior tribe's non-violent resistance, the fat frogs of World War 2 and a child widow who remakes her world; one story was grand enough to become The Reformers. None has been filmed yet, and Amit invites any would-be producer to get in touch.

items.title: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: The best onboarding text for the seen-and-unseen frame, which names Amit's podcast and inspired Hazlitt: every policy has visible first-order effects and invisible foregone alternatives, and the broken-window parable explained opportunity cost before the term existed. Free online, and the start of economic literacy.

items.title: The Art of Podcasting (Everything is Everything, episode 49)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's account of the craft behind The Seen and the Unseen and EIE: long-form conversation, the new creator economy that makes it viable, why 'short attention spans' is a myth, and a look at his note-taking rig.

items.title: The China Model is Broken (Everything is Everything, episode 16)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' argument that Xi Jinping's recentralisation broke the model Deng built, bringing private-sector disenchantment, FDI flight, overbuilt housing and trapped savings. It is their answer to 'but isn't industrial policy working for China?'

items.title: The End of History?
items.creator: Francis Fukuyama
items.why: Fukuyama's essay asking, question mark included, whether liberal democracy is history's endpoint: the high-water mark of post-Berlin-Wall optimism. The hosts read it as a love letter from a lost era and a reminder, after Trump, Xi, Putin and resurgent nationalism, that progress is not inevitable.

items.title: The Globalisation Episode (Everything is Everything, episode 95)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' foundational case for trade: integration is positive-sum and lets humanity flourish, tariffs redistribute from poor consumers to rich producers, and manufacturing is a global business that protectionism cripples. It anchors their later episodes on tariffs, FTAs and India's strategy.

items.title: The Great Redistribution
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The source of 'Varma's Law': nearly every interference with free markets, tariffs above all, quietly transfers wealth from many poor consumers to a few organised, richer producers, disguised by the rhetoric of protection.

items.title: The Journey of Indian Finance (Everything is Everything, episode 71)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's insider history of building Indian finance after 1991: a 25-year collaboration of the Finance Ministry, SEBI, the NSE and academics that made the equity market a miracle, then petered out once that community dispersed. The companion to The Beauty of Finance and the answer to 'but Indian finance can't do this'.

items.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 285)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
items.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia's own account of his path from St Stephen's and Oxford to the World Bank and a thankless advisory role in Delhi, and of the small group who from the late 1970s patiently built the ideas, including the 1990 'M document', that 1991 released. A model for slow, upstream reform work.

items.title: The Selfish Gene
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: The book that made natural selection Amit's lens on the world: selection works at the level of the gene, and read carefully rather than crudely, 'selfish' genes explain love, family care and altruism. Ajay uses it to show why top-down control fails all the way down.

items.title: The UNIX Episode (Everything is Everything, episode 32)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's one-host deep dive on how an open, hobbyist-and-academic process with many rivals produced the modern computing stack, and why the Soviet Union never could. It grounds his admiration for long, unrewarded devotion and his case for open, self-organising systems in payments and identity.

items.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's provocation that rising divorce rates in India signal progress: women gaining the agency and independence to leave bad marriages. It seeded the show's search for unconventional metrics of empowerment.

items.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Everything is Everything, episode 8)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Why geography is destiny for talent: clusters like Bell Labs' corridors or Huntsville work because bright people feed off each other and the culture tolerates mavericks and failure. It underpins the hosts' case for cities and high-skilled migration.

items.title: The Blank Slate
items.creator: Steven Pinker
items.why: Amit's gateway into evolutionary psychology; he divides his life into before and after reading it. Pinker dismantles left and right resistance to human hardwiring, and his line 'nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them' dissolves the nature-versus-nurture binary.

items.title: Demystifying GDP (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 130)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: Amit's deep dive with Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP is, why it was invented and how India measures it. It is the source of his standing gripe that counting government spending lets a state 'grow' by digging ditches and filling them in, even as he defends GDP as the best single number we have.

items.title: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Everything is Everything, episode 67)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The case that the exchange rate is the most important price in the economy: rigging it is a price control that fakes export competitiveness at the expense of the poor and sets up currency crises, which is why the hosts prefer inflation targeting with a floating rate.

items.title: Fixing Indian Education (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 185)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Amit's deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan, India's leading empirical economist of education: the system is built to sort the already-bright, not to teach them. Amit calls it his best single conversation on Indian schooling.

items.title: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 347)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
items.why: The long-form story, with Ajay and Renuka Sane, of India's move from the old pension scheme to the NPS: a decades-long trip down the policy pipeline, cross-party handovers, and the rollback that followed once the small community behind it dispersed.

items.title: It Is Immoral to Have Children. Here's Why
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's three-premise argument that bringing a non-consenting being into a life of certain pain and death is immoral. He offers it as a hard-to-refute prompt to treat parenthood as a considered choice rather than a default, and notes it drew more hostility than anything else he has written.

items.title: Paul Graham's essays
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Free essays Amit calls a treasure given to mankind: startup wisdom from a founder who is also a deep thinker, and models of plain, elegant prose that Graham workshops for months. Proof that 'thinker' versus 'doer' is a false binary.

items.title: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's essay version of the show's motto, 'people are brains, not stomachs': migration towards density is the dominant story of human history because interaction creates value, so every supposed population problem is a governance failure in disguise.

items.title: The Blind Watchmaker
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: Dawkins's case that complex design such as the eye needs no designer, the biological counterpart to Hayek and I, Pencil. Paired with The Selfish Gene, it rewired Amit's view of how order emerges without a central planner.

items.title: The Evolution of Everything
items.creator: Matt Ridley
items.why: Amit's go-to entry point for spontaneous order: Ridley shows the same bottom-up, designer-free process at work in biology, language, markets, morality and law, extending Hayek's insight about prices to almost everything.

items.title: The Evolution of Everything (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 96)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
items.why: Amit's long conversation with Matt Ridley, the audio companion to his book: a tour of bottom-up emergence through language, biology, prices and culture, recommended for anyone hooked by spontaneous order.

items.title: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Hayek's sharpest statement of why central planning fails: the 'fatal conceit' is believing that one mind or committee can know enough to redesign society from the top down. The hosts use it as a standing rebuke to price controls and national economic planning.

items.title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Everything is Everything, episode 11)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The show's productivity mantra: grind through the unglamorous foundations, week after week, until the magic appears. It also covers the Mueller-Dweck finding that praising effort beats praising intelligence.

items.title: The Hiking Episode (Everything is Everything, episode 35)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's evangelism for hiking and the Indian Himalayas, eloquent enough to get the non-hiker Amit walking, and a way to seed in young people the passion Harish Kapadia's books once seeded in Ajay.

items.title: The Journey of Indian Finance
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's magisterial written history of Indian finance from 1947 through socialism, liberalisation and the derivatives era, by someone who lived three decades of it. The scholarly companion to episode 71 and a roadmap of the unfinished reforms that would cut India's cost of capital.

items.title: The Nature of the Firm
items.creator: Ronald Coase
items.why: Coase's 1937 answer to why firms exist at all: because contracting through markets is costly, a firm's boundary sits where those costs balance. Ajay uses it to show how cheaper coordination, from gig platforms to AI, pushes that boundary outward.

items.title: The Power of Moore's Laws (Everything is Everything, episode 87)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The source of Ajay's Wright's Law argument: every doubling of cumulative output brings roughly a 20% productivity gain, because know-how lives in firms that learn by doing. It is why scale matters in manufacturing and defence, and why he is optimistic about solar, wind and batteries.

items.title: The Practice of Medicine (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 229)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
items.why: Amit's conversation with the pulmonologist Lancelot Pinto, who treated him through COVID and reads research papers every day. It lays out the doctor's dharma: resist patient-driven over-treatment, start with paracetamol and patience, and have the courage to play against the book.

items.title: Understanding India's Pensions Disaster (Everything is Everything, episode 65)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The cautionary tale of India's New Pension System: a great reform built by an intellectual community, then reversed once that community dispersed and its tacit knowledge faded. The lesson is that reforms need permanent guardians.

items.title: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Everything is Everything, episode 104)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Part one of the hosts' manufacturing diagnosis: concrete reasons Indian manufacturing is hobbled, from duties on imported inputs to the long shadow of planning. It recasts manufacturing as high-skill, dense, urban work rather than unskilled assembly.

items.title: A Meditation on Form
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's essay on how moving from short interviews to four-to-eight-hour conversations changed both his show and him: a five-hour conversation is not five one-hour ones but a different activity that teaches you to listen. The seed of his thesis that form shapes content, and what you do shapes who you are.

items.title: Against the Grain
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: Ajay calls it a masterpiece and one of the most perfectly executed non-fiction books he has read. Scott argues that storable grain made taxation, conscription and the state possible, and that the agricultural revolution was a regression for ordinary people, bringing disease, hierarchy and lost diversity.

items.title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Everything is Everything, episode 3)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: An early episode arguing that character is contingent and selfhood less solid than we like to think (Phineas Gage and adjacent stories). The hosts return to it on authenticity, on Semmelweis's decline and on the value of mocking yourself.

items.title: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 296)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
items.why: Amit's conversation with the Dalit thinker whose two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, which grounds Amit's hopeful case that markets and liberalisation have done real work for Dalit emancipation. It includes the reframe that obese, diabetic village elders are a sign of a prosperity their forebears never had.

items.title: Early Indians: The Story of Our Ancestors and Where We Came From
items.creator: Tony Joseph
items.why: Amit's on-ramp to India's genetic history: we are all migrants ('we are all Amits from Africa'), descended from the first Indians, Harappans and later arrivals, and two millennia of caste endogamy split India into thousands of small populations. It brings David Reich's findings to the Indian context.

items.title: Essays
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Amit's model of clear, morally serious prose and his cure for writer's block: read two or three Orwell essays at random. They are also a chronological window into a great mind at work, written fast, three or four columns a week.

items.title: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
items.creator: Akshaya Mukul
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece: the history of the publishing house that cultivated Hindu nationalism from below while westernised elites imposed a secular 'idea of India' from above. It is his evidence that India's Hindu-Muslim fault lines are homegrown.

items.title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Everything is Everything, episode 19)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's strategic and economic take on cricket, from work he has done since 2008: front-loading innings, dot balls versus wickets, why selectors are the root cause, and how cricket journalism shifted from information to perspective.

items.title: India's Problem Is Poverty, Not Inequality
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's essay untangling two problems that need opposite policies: in a positive-sum world, liberalisation lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty even as inequality rose. Ask yourself whether you would rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh.

items.title: Is Globalization Doomed? (Everything is Everything, episode 96)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The second half of the hosts' globalisation pair: how the world reached Trump's tariffs, taking Robert Lighthizer's arguments seriously, and whether the trading order can survive, ending on Ajay's cautiously hopeful reading that later trade deals seemed to vindicate.

items.title: Is the Singularity Near? (Everything is Everything, episode 2)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' early debate on AI and a model of two friends disagreeing strongly in good faith. Amit's case: don't judge AI's future by its present, any more than you would have judged computing by IBM's room-sized machines of the 1950s.

items.title: Life Lessons From Chess in 2024 (Everything is Everything, episode 81)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit draws life lessons from a big year in chess: mastery is not enough without renewal, early success can rot character, chess peaks come early because it is a finite pattern-recognition game, and great teams hire the best people from anywhere.

items.title: Metrics of Empowerment (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 88)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
items.why: A Seen and the Unseen conversation on unconventional measures of women's empowerment, such as who orders the household groceries, including Amit's own: rising divorce rates. The hosts use it to show how odd proxies reveal social truths that GDP-style data misses.

items.title: Milton Friedman on the Minimum Wage
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: The seven-minute clip that changed Amit's mind on the minimum wage: a legal minimum does not raise the pay of workers whose labour is worth less than it, it pushes their wage to zero. A lucid short version of Hazlitt's chapter on the subject.

items.title: On Exactitude in Science
items.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
items.why: Borges's parable of a perfectly accurate map, which would have to be as large as the territory and would be obsolete the moment it was finished. Amit uses it on the limits of any representation, from Caro's total biographies to cartography and language.

items.title: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 253)
items.creator: Amit Varma with M. R. Madhavan
items.why: Amit's conversation with M. R. Madhavan, whom both hosts admire, on how the anti-defection law killed legislators' independence. It is the source of Amit's framework that electoral politics, governance and policy are separate games whose skills do not transfer.

items.title: Perfect Days
items.creator: Wim Wenders
items.why: Wim Wenders's film about a quiet, devoted working life, which Amit says could only have been made by an old man. Recommended by Amit and by Nomsita, who says it changed how she sees work, ambition, silence and solitude.

items.title: Private Truths, Public Lies
items.creator: Timur Kuran
items.why: Kuran's theory of preference falsification: when people publicly profess what is safe while privately disagreeing, societies look stable but are brittle, and one crack can trigger a cascade, as with the fall of the USSR. Amit also uses it to explain how social media surfaces and amplifies hidden views.

items.title: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 326)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pushpesh Pant
items.why: Amit's feast of a conversation with the food historian: his pet peeves (the tyranny of the tandoor, the myth of the Mughlai), India mapped by souring agents rather than borders, and the Columbian Exchange origins of 'Indian' staples like potato and chilli.

items.title: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 360)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rahul Matthan
items.why: Amit's conversation with the technology lawyer: how architecture created privacy and the interior life, how big-data signals now predict creditworthiness, and the strongest insider case for Aadhaar's design, which the hosts argue against.

items.title: The 1991 Project
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan's trove of primary documents, interviews and analysis on India's 1991 reforms, including Montek's pre-crisis 'M document'. It shows the reforms were fifteen years of unglamorous intellectual work, not just a response to crisis.

items.title: The Clash of Economic Ideas
items.creator: Lawrence H. White
items.why: Lawrence White's history of the twentieth century's battles of economic ideas, from Fabian socialism and Soviet planning to Keynesianism and market liberalism. Amit's recommended way to learn what Keynes, Hayek and Friedman really argued, and how ideas travel from lonely researchers to policy.

items.title: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek (Everything is Everything, episode 6)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' long-form introduction to two of their intellectual heroes: Bastiat's seen and unseen, and Hayek's prices as the coordinator of millions of independent decisions. It spells out why tariffs redistribute from poor consumers to concentrated interests and why meddling with food prices backfires.

items.title: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 387)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: Amit's near-ten-hour history of the Indian economy with Rajeswari Sengupta and his most popular episode of that year: how India ended up so poor per head, and what its growth episodes looked like up close. It is also his proof that very long audio finds an audience.

items.title: The Logic of Collective Action
items.creator: Mancur Olson
items.why: Olson's key text on why small, organised interests with concentrated benefits beat large publics with diffuse costs, the mechanism behind regulatory capture and sticky subsidies. The hosts also use it for the roving-versus-stationary bandit lens on Naxals and state legitimacy.

items.title: The Moral Animal
items.creator: Robert Wright
items.why: Robert Wright on what natural selection implies for human moral life: morality as hardwired reciprocal altruism rather than a gift of religion, and monogamy and polygamy as different stable equilibria of the same drives. A core text in Amit's evolutionary reading after The Blank Slate.

items.title: The Mystery of Capital
items.creator: Hernando de Soto
items.why: De Soto's idea of 'dead capital': without clear, tradeable property rights, slum homes, farmland and rent-controlled flats are worth a fraction of their value because they cannot work as capital. It opened Amit's eyes to how much of India is locked up this way.

items.title: The Populist Playbook (Everything is Everything, episode 42)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' anatomy of populism: not 'what is popular' but a specific, dangerous package of beliefs and tactics, including insular nationalism and hostility to foreign capital, that is on the rise worldwide.

items.title: The Power Broker: Robert Moses and the Fall of New York
items.creator: Robert Caro
items.why: Amit's masterpiece pick: Caro's biography of Robert Moses is at once the story of a man, of a city reshaped by top-down high modernism, and of how power corrupts. Read it for the clash between Moses and Jane Jacobs's bottom-up city.

items.title: The Wealth of Nations
items.creator: Adam Smith
items.why: The starting point of economics: Amit calls Smith the Charles Darwin of the field and finds him eerily relevant today. The hosts quote him on traders' conspiracies against the public, and on how little a state needs to prosper: 'peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice'.

items.title: The World in 2050 (Everything is Everything, episode 106)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' futurism episode on what the world might look like in 25 years, from drone-swarm terrorism to the unbundling of marriage, and a reminder that even 25-year horizons sound like science fiction.

items.title: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: The Story of India through Its Languages
items.creator: Peggy Mohan
items.why: Peggy Mohan reads India's history of migration in its languages, as Tony Joseph reads it in DNA: male migrants plus local women produce a creole, and Sanskrit itself picked up its retroflex sounds from the languages already here.

items.title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Everything is Everything, episode 55)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts question the modern Indian belief that every new road and airport is an unalloyed good: infrastructure has diminishing returns, roads to nowhere are real, and it is not the binding constraint on manufacturing.

items.title: Who We Are and How We Got Here
items.creator: David Reich
items.why: David Reich's account of how ancient DNA overturned older views of human history, including the finding that India is not one large population but thousands of small ones, the genetic signature of caste endogamy.

items.title: You're Missing
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: The Springsteen song that gave the show its name: grief rendered through ordinary household objects, with 'everything is everything' gesturing at the world's wonders around one absence. Amit teaches it to writing students as proof that plain, literal words move us more than ornament.

items.title: Is Manufacturing the Answer? (Everything is Everything, episode 105)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Part two of the hosts' manufacturing pair: why factories live in cities and agglomeration matters, and how structural transformation and the demographic transition fit into India's growth story.

items.title: 1,000 True Fans
items.creator: Kevin Kelly
items.why: Kevin Kelly's charter for independent creators: you don't need a million casual fans, only a thousand who care enough to pay you, and once geography stops mattering they can be found anywhere. Utopian when written, Amit notes, and everyday reality on Substack now.

items.title: A Scientist in the Kitchen (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 204)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok
items.why: Amit's conversation with Krish Ashok on the science behind Indian cooking, the food-science foundation for their later episode. It also gave Amit his favourite example of the brain's plasticity: a visually impaired colleague who listens to podcasts at 6x.

items.title: A Trade Deficit With a Babysitter
items.creator: Tim Harford
items.why: Tim Harford's one-paragraph demolition of trade-deficit panic: he pays his babysitter constantly, she buys nothing from him, and both are better off. Amit's go-to debunking of the idea that a deficit is a loss.

items.title: Atomic Habits
items.creator: James Clear
items.why: The best book on productivity Amit has read: habits, not goals, are the compound interest of self-improvement, so focus on daily processes over heroic sprints and use small rewards to cement routines.

items.title: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah Will Not Wear a Blue Tie to Work (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 389)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
items.why: Amit's conversation with one of the drafters of India's bankruptcy code: the history of bankruptcy, the human story behind the IBC, and her thinking on financial regulation, which Ajay credits as scaffolding for the KYC episode.

items.title: Biju Rao Won't Bow to Conventional Wisdom (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 392)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Biju Rao
items.why: One of Amit's favourite conversations, with the World Bank economist who argues you cannot understand or govern people from a distance: fieldwork beats reading data in Washington. It gave Amit the phrase 'cognitive empathy' and the paper behind the episode on what economics can learn.

items.title: Blade Runner 2049
items.creator: Denis Villeneuve
items.why: One of Amit's favourite films, which he rates above the masterpiece original: science fiction at the level of literature, taking on the biggest questions about the nature of being, and proof that Hollywood can still give great filmmakers room.

items.title: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
items.creator: Bruce Yandle
items.why: Bruce Yandle's durable frame for how regulation gets made: moral campaigners (the Baptists) supply the legitimacy and rent-seekers (the bootleggers) supply the money, both wanting the same ban for opposite reasons. It is the spine of the hosts' case against prohibition.

items.title: Climate Change and Our Power Sector (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 278)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: The long-form conversation with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay on India's electricity grid: intermittency, prices and a dysfunctional grid that squeezes manufacturers and shapes how new technologies like small reactors will scale.

items.title: Constitutional Amendments Through the Decades
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan's talk on how every government from Nehru onwards has amended the Constitution to make the unconstitutional constitutional: the wider context for the First Amendment's curbs on speech, and the source of the hosts' joke that the parliament bookshop stocks no periodicals.

items.title: Consumer Pyramids Household Survey
items.creator: Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE)
items.why: CMIE's vast household survey of around 190,000 households, three times a year, which Ajay uses to see India's heterogeneity, with incomes five times apart across its roughly 100 homogeneous regions. Independent enough of the government to serve as a check on official data.

items.title: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 305)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Coomi Kapoor
items.why: The companion conversation to The Emergency: A Personal History: a journalist's inside view of how the Emergency unfolded, and how it was reported and suppressed.

items.title: Deepak VS and the Man Behind His Face (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 373)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Deepak VS
items.why: Amit's conversation with the coaching-class entrepreneur that produced the IIT swimming-race thought experiment, the case that coaching classes are a rational market response, and the ethic 'how you do the small things is how you do the big things'.

items.title: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
items.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper on the staggering scale of money moved across borders through fake invoices: when legal cross-border activity is too painful, firms route around capital controls. The hosts' answer to whether a state can really choke off such flows.

items.title: Doing better than a competitive exam
items.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
items.why: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah's case against India's monolithic exam regime of UPSC, JEE and board exams, which paints numbers on children's foreheads, and for a lottery: a conceptual test for the top lakh, then random allocation of IIT seats. The seed of a planned book.

items.title: Don't Mess With the Price System (Everything is Everything, episode 66)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on prices as the economy's coordination system: price controls invariably produce shortages, and a tariff sets off many small adjustments rather than one big collapse. Pair it with the exchange-rate episode, which extends the same logic.

items.title: Don't Run a Country Like a Company (Everything is Everything, episode 60)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' warning against importing corporate intuitions into government: no amount of business brilliance maps onto state reform, and acquiring the levers of power is a skill that does not transfer. Recommended, Amit says, for Elon Musk himself.

items.title: Early Indians (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 112)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Tony Joseph
items.why: Tony Joseph's audio companion to his book: a walk through the four waves of migration into India, the science of ancient DNA and the lock-in of caste endogamy.

items.title: Economic Facts and Fallacies
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Sowell, one of Amit's intellectual heroes, on 'generative' fallacies that spawn many other errors: a working manual for spotting bad economic reasoning that leaves you, Amit says, a clearer thinker than when you started.

items.title: Economic Growth Is Enough and Only Economic Growth Is Enough
items.creator: Lant Pritchett and Addison Lewis
items.why: Pritchett's empirical case that around 99% of the variation in human-welfare indicators tracks per-capita GDP, leaving about 1% for redistribution and welfare programmes. The hosts' hardest evidence for putting growth first.

items.title: Education in India (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 77)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Amit Chandra
items.why: An early Seen and the Unseen conversation with Amit Chandra on the structural failures of Indian education, part of Amit's twenty years of writing on the subject.

items.title: Five Epic Stories That Must Be Films (Everything is Everything, episode 29)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The second instalment of the hosts' 'stories that should be films' series: the hardest decision of World War 2, a couple who drift apart because they hear the world differently, air raids on Japan, the making of a nation and a man who refused to flee.

items.title: Glimpses of World History
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: Nehru's history of the world written as letters to his daughter from prison, with no library to consult: an extraordinary feat of memory and a monument to what careful letter-writing can become. Ajay read it as a child and felt a father telling stories.

items.title: Gods, Guns and Missionaries: The Making of the Modern Hindu Identity
items.creator: Manu Pillai
items.why: Manu Pillai's history of how a pan-Hindu identity emerged late, first against Islam and then against colonial rule, after centuries in which Vaishnavites fought Shaivites more than Muslims. Its opening essay on Hinduism as an open-source religion is the best synthesis Amit has read.

items.title: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
items.creator: Jonathan Rauch
items.why: Jonathan Rauch's mind-blowing account of how interest groups multiply, regulation grows and reform becomes structurally impossible in Washington. Amit reads it as a warning of where India heads if rent-seeking deepens.

items.title: Hardcore History
items.creator: Dan Carlin
items.why: Dan Carlin's history podcast, which Amit calls perhaps the greatest of all time and his way into long-form audio: one man talking, no production, riveting for the 25-odd hours of the World War I series Blueprint for Armageddon.

items.title: History of European Morals
items.creator: W. E. H. Lecky
items.why: Lecky's original statement of the 'expanding circle': moral concern widens over history from family to tribe to nation to humanity, long before Peter Singer popularised the idea. Amit's anchor for the worry that nationalism is shrinking the circle again.

items.title: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
items.creator: Robin Dunbar
items.why: Robin Dunbar on the finite budget of human relationships: about 150 meaningful connections, with much of our emotional energy spent on five people and most of the rest on the next fifteen. Ajay uses it to argue that friendship deserves deliberate effort.

items.title: India Moving
items.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: Chinmay Tumbe's history of Indian migration, which Amit calls one of the great books of the last decade. Its most striking fact: India's largest internal migration is women moving to their husbands' homes at marriage, leaving their former lives behind.

items.title: India's Greatest Civil Servant (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 167)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Narayani Basu
items.why: Amit's conversation with Narayani Basu on V. P. Menon, the boy who burned down his school and grew into the executor of India's integration, and on how Patel and Menon put the country together in two and a half years through coercion and broken promises. Amit pitches it as a story that should be a film.

items.title: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 321)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Josh Felman
items.why: Amit's conversation with one of the most thoughtful observers of the global economy, which surfaced things even Felman's friends of fifteen years had never heard, and the source of the BMW-off-a-cliff metaphor for American college costs.

items.title: Kashi Ka Assi
items.creator: Kashinath Singh
items.why: Kashinath Singh's novel, source of the hosts' line 'Bharme Jaye Duniya, Hum Bajayein Harmonia' (let the world go to hell, I'll play my harmonium). Ajay turns it into a social-media philosophy (block the noise, curate the finest minds), then argues against the temptation to opt out entirely.

items.title: Larry White and the First Principles of Money (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 397)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Larry White
items.why: Amit's masterclass on free banking with its leading expert: history shows that banks issuing their own currencies often worked without chaos, which breaks the assumption that money must come from a single central bank and leads into the case for cryptocurrency.

items.title: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on why reading matters, prompted by Narendra Modi as an experience-only thinker who doesn't read: one life gives you a finite set of dots, books multiply them and let you inhabit other minds, and the deepest truths, like spontaneous order, can be reached only through books.

items.title: Luck Is All Around
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on the staggering odds against any of us existing, and his thesis that 98-99% of what happens to us is luck. The lesson: don't let good luck make you arrogant or bad luck defeatist; sweat what you can control.

items.title: Malini Goyal Is the Curious One (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 377)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Malini Goyal
items.why: Amit's conversation with the co-author of Unboxing Bengaluru about the city's predicament, and the source of striking findings on Bangalore's dating-app culture, where abundant choice makes stability harder.

items.title: Narendra Modi Takes a Great Leap Backwards
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column calling demonetisation the largest assault on property rights in history, born of the same delusion as Mao's Great Leap Forward: that a leader can redesign society by decree. His test case for when insiders must speak out.

items.title: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 250)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Narendra Shenoy
items.why: Amit's witty conversation with his friend Naren Shenoy: the origin of the show's t-shirt, their first riff on how caste and class shape cuisine, and a charming arranged-marriage anecdote.

items.title: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Everything is Everything, episode 7)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: An early episode tracing the intellectual scaffolding behind Newton and Gandhi: disruptive figures don't appear from nowhere, and free thinking often comes bundled with eccentricity or worse.

items.title: Om Namah Volume
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on putting in the volume: a small edge becomes reliable returns only through sample size, the insight linking poker, cricket strategy and why young online-trained chess players rise so fast.

items.title: Order Without Design
items.creator: Alain Bertaud
items.why: Alain Bertaud's masterpiece, and Amit's desert-island book, on what happens when sound economics meets urban planning: it exposes the follies of high-modernist planning and respects how cities and streets actually work.

items.title: Our Unlucky Children
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column arguing that education is the great market failure of our age: we get forty flavours of chips because markets respect individual difference, but in education, where it really counts, markets are not allowed to work.

items.title: Praise for Intelligence Can Undermine Children's Motivation and Performance
items.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
items.why: The Mueller-Dweck study behind the show's growth-mindset advice: children praised for being smart tried less and cheated more, while those praised for effort kept improving. Praise effort, not ability, or as Amit puts it, verbs over adjectives.

items.title: Profit = Philanthropy
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's argument that in a world of voluntary exchange the only way to profit is to make someone else better off, which makes profit, properly understood, the greatest form of philanthropy.

items.title: Public Choice: A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: Amit's gateway to public choice theory, readable in under an hour: politicians and bureaucrats are self-interested actors, not benevolent stewards, which is why government failure is so common. The best entry point before the dense Buchanan and Tullock originals.

items.title: Public finance research at XKDR Forum
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: Ajay's research programme on doing government contracting better, which he sees as the missing frontier of Indian state capability, and the base of his collaboration with R. A. Mashelkar on science policy.

items.title: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's film review arguing that Raees gets the economics of bootlegging backwards: the bootlegger and the prohibitionist politician are allies whose incentives align, not enemies. A pop-culture entry into Bootleggers and Baptists.

items.title: Range Rover (Amit Varma's Economic Times poker column)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The archive of Amit's year-long Economic Times poker column, a pun on poker 'ranges', applying poker reasoning about probability, sample size and decisions to everyday life.

items.title: Rules, Not Discretion (Everything is Everything, episode 92)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's episode on why predictable rules beat discretionary power, built on a paper he loved as a young PhD student. It feeds the show's ideas on procedural fairness as a path to legitimacy and on preferring rule-bound democracies to mercurial strongmen.

items.title: Songs of Surrender
items.creator: U2
items.why: U2 reimagining their own classic songs decades later: the hosts' example of artists refusing to be frozen at their hit moment, as Picasso refused when he repainted Las Meninas. Ajay suggests discovering U2 backwards, starting here.

items.title: Stage.in
items.creator: Vinay Singhal
items.why: A streaming service for content in dialects like Haryanvi and Bhojpuri, which Amit cites as proof that markets first homogenise to chase scale and then re-diversify, letting technology save the long tail from broadcast Hindi.

items.title: State Building
items.creator: Francis Fukuyama
items.why: Fukuyama's frame of the state as two dials, scope (how much it tries to do) and strength (how well it does it). The hosts' diagnosis: India is a weak state with too broad a scope, and should do a few things well, beginning with the rule of law.

items.title: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
items.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
items.why: A masterful primer on thinking in probabilities: good forecasters are not confident TV experts but people who break problems down, hold ranges and keep updating their beliefs. Amit felt it already said everything poker had taught him.

items.title: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 323)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Mohit Satyanand
items.why: Amit's conversation with Ajay and Mohit Satyanand after Silicon Valley Bank collapsed: why bank failures are part of a healthy financial system, and how electronic payments make weekend bank runs possible.

items.title: Swapna Liddle and the Many Shades of Delhi (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 367)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Swapna Liddle
items.why: Amit's conversation with the historian whose work recovers 19th-century Delhi: Delhi College, poetry-filled newspapers and mushairas, and how British education shaped Indians' view of their own history.

items.title: The Adda at the End of the Universe (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 309)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
items.why: A free-wheeling Seen and the Unseen adda with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas: the 120-year-life provocation, FU money versus FO money, and how Bollywood's shallow culture can corrupt talent as well as elevate it.

items.title: The Age of Hybrid Warfare (Everything is Everything, episode 84)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' toolkit for conflict below the thresholds of detection and attribution, from cyberattacks to drone terror, where a state may not even know whether it is at war or who is attacking it.

items.title: The Ascent of Man
items.creator: Jacob Bronowski
items.why: Bronowski's sweeping tour of human ideas and science, which Ajay says every literate adult should read. It gave Ajay his stock of stories about intellectual outlaws such as Wegener and Boltzmann, and Amit his frame that the glory is the human journey, not lines on a map.

items.title: The Bankable Wisdom of Harsh Vardhan (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 352)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Harsh Vardhan
items.why: Amit's conversation with a deep thinker on banking about why banks blow up every 20-30 years. Harsh Vardhan argues India must build a great banking sector even if regulation is weak, a disagreement Ajay calls heartbreaking.

items.title: The Broken Script
items.creator: Swapna Liddle
items.why: Swapna Liddle's history of 19th-century Delhi and the best quasi-Mughal history Amit has come across: Delhi College, the shift between languages, and a city whose newspapers routinely printed poetry.

items.title: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Everything is Everything, episode 72)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' argument that form determines content: the dominant forms of songs, albums, books and films arose from constraints that no longer apply, and today niches multiply as the mainstream shrinks.

items.title: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
items.creator: Mohandas K. Gandhi
items.why: A hundred volumes, free online, that Amit reads as the daily blog of a man's evolution: Gandhi engaging with the world, admitting when he was wrong and thinking by writing. A priceless way to trace a life of ideas.

items.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
items.creator: Jane Jacobs
items.why: Jane Jacobs, one of Amit's intellectual heroes, on why cities are about people rather than buildings and must grow organically from the bottom up, the 'ballet of the streets'. The antidote to Robert Moses and to Indian yearning for top-down planning.

items.title: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 223)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: A master class with Ajay on healthcare versus public health, vaccine production and distribution, and the state's role in a pandemic, including the Serum Institute's partnership with global science and Ajay's case for shifting health spending towards prevention.

items.title: The Emergency: A Personal History
items.creator: Coomi Kapoor
items.why: Coomi Kapoor's remarkable insider history of the Emergency and the best source on its lived horrors, from jailed journalists to forced-sterilisation quotas. Amit reads it as a reminder that democracy is not a given and as a portrait of the Indian state's oppressive power.

items.title: The Expanding Circle: Ethics, Evolution, and Moral Progress
items.creator: Peter Singer
items.why: Singer's restatement of Lecky: as moral reasoning matures, the circle of concern keeps widening, beyond nation to all of humanity and, for Singer, to other sentient creatures. It prompts Amit's thought that eating animals may one day look like slaveholding, and his rueful note that nationalism has not yet let the circle include all humans.

items.title: The First Assault on Our Constitution (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 194)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh
items.why: Amit's conversation with Tripurdaman Singh, behind Sixteen Stormy Days, on how the 1951 First Amendment gutted the Constitution's free-speech protections: Indian free speech hobbled almost at birth.

items.title: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 283)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Amit's conversation with Vinay Sitapati, companion to Half-Lion, on the polyglot, COBOL-coding prime minister who staked his political capital on 1991, whose political instincts complemented Manmohan Singh's economics, and whom his own party abandoned at his funeral.

items.title: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
items.creator: Amity Shlaes
items.why: Amity Shlaes's market-oriented retelling of the Great Depression: the 1929 crash did not cause the slump, and government interventions and the New Deal deepened it. A counter to the textbook story of stimulus to the rescue.

items.title: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 139)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
items.why: The conversational companion to Akshaya Mukul's book on how nationalist religious narratives were embedded in Indian society long before politics caught up, and Amit's evidence that India's communal tensions are homegrown.

items.title: The Heart of Disruption (Everything is Everything, episode 86)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on disruption: Netflix bet on streaming before bandwidth was ready, the honourable counter-example to the Kodaks of the world, alongside Amit's first startup failure and how firms can write rules that enable adaptation.

items.title: The Importance of Finance (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 125)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: The long-form Seen and the Unseen primer on why finance drives the modern economy, and why a working credit market, and so a working bankruptcy code, is not optional.

items.title: The Incredible Curiosities of Mukulika Banerjee (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 276)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mukulika Banerjee
items.why: Amit's conversation with the anthropologist on her decade-long ethnography of the Khudai Khidmatgars, the non-violent Pathan movement behind The Pathan Unarmed, and her quest to find surviving members in Pakistan.

items.title: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 349)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Timur Kuran
items.why: Amit's conversation with the economist of preference falsification: why seemingly stable autocracies collapse in cascades, how institutions like waqfs ossify when their purpose is locked in, and the Middle East's long divergence.

items.title: The Law
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's short, clear masterpiece on the limits of the state: it distinguishes property earned by applying one's faculties from plunder, and argues that most government interventions are a subtle form of plunder. Amit says you must read it to understand the modern state.

items.title: The Life and Times of Chess (Everything is Everything, episode 52)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A synthesis episode in which Amit explains chess from passion and structure: the world champions through Ding Liren and the rise of computer-driven preparation, and the prequel to their 2024 chess episode.

items.title: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 314)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jerry Pinto
items.why: Perhaps Amit's most memorable oral history, in which host and guest both cried talking about their mothers: his example of how vulnerability begets vulnerability, and of unrepeatable human moments no LLM could produce. It also gave the show the Kaator Re Bhaaji story.

items.title: The Lost Decade
items.creator: Puja Mehra
items.why: Puja Mehra's account of what went wrong after India's golden run from 1991 to 2011: after 26/11 moved Chidambaram to Home, a wave of bad calls, retrospective taxation among them, ended an era of reform. The hosts' diagnostic frame for the slowdown.

items.title: The Outlaws (Everything is Everything, episode 61)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on heretics who turned out right, such as Semmelweis, Mendel and Darwin, figures who would not have survived modern peer review. It grounds their argument that authoritarian regimes and conformist institutions crush the mavericks who drive breakthroughs.

items.title: The Pathan Unarmed
items.creator: Mukulika Banerjee
items.why: Mukulika Banerjee's answer to a historical puzzle: how Pashtun peasants led the subcontinent's largest non-violent movement. She shows its non-violence grew from Pathan society's own values, not from Gandhi: a book about how cultures contain their own quiet correctives.

items.title: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 291)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Singhal
items.why: The story of a Haryanvi-speaking village kid who built Stage.in, a 'Netflix of Bharat' for dialect content: reverse migration from Bollywood, and the case that dialect media is a market opportunity, not charity.

items.title: The Soul of a New Machine
items.creator: Tracy Kidder
items.why: Tracy Kidder's account of a computer-engineering team, which gave Ajay his first glimpse of building something with all your heart and soul. A non-fiction quest, with a link to Data General, the company Narayana Murthy spent months chasing import licences for.

items.title: The Story of Art
items.creator: E. H. Gombrich
items.why: Gombrich's history of art told through the stories and contexts behind individual works, which both hosts recommend for anyone who finds art arcane. Read a page a day and you absorb the whole arc.

items.title: The Tamilian Gentleman Who Took on the World
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column putting Viswanathan Anand's achievement in context: he won world titles without the Soviet pedagogical machine, a Maruti 800 in a Formula 1 race, and seeded an Indian chess ecosystem rather than being a lone Ramanujan-style genius.

items.title: The Three Globalizations (Everything is Everything, episode 17)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's framework of three globalisations, the latest of which makes access to the core advanced economies conditional on good military and foreign-policy behaviour. It explains sanctions and supply-chain integration as alternatives to war, today's tech wars, and how recent passports and capital controls are.

items.title: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 211)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: The political-economy story of how a sound liberalising farm reform was lost to politics, and why agriculture stays untouchable even when reform is needed.

items.title: Understanding India Through Its Languages (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 232)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Peggy Mohan
items.why: Peggy Mohan's audio companion to Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: language as a forensic tool for reconstructing history, the role of mothers in passing tongues on, and how Hindustani and Urdu emerged.

items.title: Unlikely Is Inevitable
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on the law of large numbers: given a big enough sample, every freakishly unlikely sequence will happen, so losing five 80%-favourite hands in a row is not 'rigged'. A guard against the gambler's fallacy and a route to equanimity.

items.title: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 342)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vitalik Buterin
items.why: A three-way conversation with Ajay and Vitalik Buterin on politics, identity and voting, including why bribery is the core weakness of voting systems and Ajay's case for cash: anonymity, universal acceptance and freedom from surveillance.

items.title: Wanting
items.creator: Luke Burgis
items.why: Luke Burgis's primer on mimetic desire, the idea that we want things because others want them, which Amit applies to life choices like marriage and children. Its frame of thin versus thick desires explains who puts in the hard reps.

items.title: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Everything is Everything, episode 27)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The third episode in the show's trilogy on the state, prompted by COVID: India failed to procure vaccines on time for want of contracting capacity, and vaccine makers captured only a tiny fraction of the value they created, which weakens incentives for pandemic preparedness.

items.title: Wet Streets Cause Rain (the Gell-Mann Amnesia passage)
items.creator: Michael Crichton
items.why: Michael Crichton's passage on Gell-Mann Amnesia: you spot the media's errors on subjects you know well, then trust it on everything else. Amit calls it the single most important idea for media literacy.

items.title: What Bruce Springsteen Means to Us (Everything is Everything, episode 13)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The show's least-watched episode and a labour of love: why Springsteen matters to the hosts, including his lines on a child as 'another shot', a moment of optimism.

items.title: What Just Happened Between India & Pakistan? (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 418)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan
items.why: A topical Seen and the Unseen episode on the recent India-Pakistan clash, showing both armies using advanced equipment and raising a concrete near-term worry: drones used for terror rather than war.

items.title: Where Indian Regulation Went Wrong (Everything is Everything, episode 99)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's diagnosis of Indian regulators: too much discretion and too little rule of law, producing more rules than anyone can check, and no reason to expect regulators to be the smartest people in the room. The basis of his regulatory-reform agenda.

items.title: Why We Sleep
items.creator: Matthew Walker
items.why: Matthew Walker's case that sleep is badly underrated: sleep-deprived driving causes more accidents than drunk driving, poor sleep means living at a 20% discount, and chronotypes are real, so night owls are not lazy.

items.title: Understanding Gandhi (The Seen and the Unseen, episodes 104-105)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ramachandra Guha
items.why: Amit's two-part conversation with Ramachandra Guha, for which he read some thirty books on Gandhi, with Guha's verdict that Gandhi was right about the one thing he knew from personal experience, satyagraha, and wrong about much else.

items.title: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister
items.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
