items.why: The British satire of bureaucracy and power ('We must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this'): a treasure-house on how the levers of power fail to respond to the people pulling them.

items.title: 100 True Fans
items.creator: Li Jin
items.why: Li Jin's update to Kevin Kelly: fewer fans who pay more, through courses, communities and premium products, can sustain a creative career.

items.title: A Billion Wicked Thoughts
items.creator: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam
items.why: Amit calls it the most comprehensive picture of what people actually want sexually: revealed preferences from internet searches at scale, confirming the arguments of Symons, Buss, Miller and Pinker. It launched the show's episode on human sexuality.

items.title: A Deep Dive Into the Indian Military (Everything is Everything, episode 31)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's foundation for understanding India's force posture, from someone who lectures rooms full of generals. The first item on the military-reform agenda is fixing the pension problem that crowds out a modern force.

items.title: A new dawn for nuclear energy?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's earlier case that nuclear weapons and nuclear energy are separate stories, and that India should buy commercially competitive reactors from private Western firms.

items.title: A Passion for Cycling (Everything is Everything, episode 53)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' love letter to cycling: how a pursuit stays culturally vital after its practical purpose is displaced, and how a peloton combines apparent high-modernist order with spontaneous chaos.

items.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
items.why: Wollstonecraft's polemic, close to Amit's heart, asking the question the men of her age refused to ask: if rights come from self-ownership, why are women excluded? Read it for its original audience and its radicalism is unmistakable.

items.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (The Book Club on Storytel, episode 2)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's short Storytel audio appreciation of Wollstonecraft's book: a quick on-ramp into its argument and the world it was written in.

items.title: Accelerating India's Development
items.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Karthik Muralidharan's systematic synthesis of what works in Indian governance and schooling, with startling comparisons of scale (the average Indian district is bigger than 85 countries) and evidence that spending more on buildings, 'better' teachers or student inputs alone does nothing for learning.

items.title: Administrative Procedure Act (1946)
items.creator: U.S. Congress
items.why: The 1946 US law Ajay calls a blueprint for checks and balances inside government agencies: one horizontal law setting basic principles of hygiene and transparency for every regulator, something India never had.

items.title: Adolescence
items.creator: Jack Thorne and Stephen Graham
items.why: The Netflix series that left Amit weeping by episode four: a new pinnacle of filmmaking craft, each episode shot in a single take, and a small-window dramatisation of how manosphere grievances reach a teenage boy.

items.title: Anatomy of a Fall
items.creator: Justine Triet
items.why: A masterpiece, says Amit, about the tension between the urge to tell a simple story and honest acknowledgement of complexity, one of the films in his one-film-a-month deal with Ajay.

items.title: Atomic State: Big Science in Twentieth-Century India
items.creator: Jahnavi Phalkey
items.why: Jahnavi Phalkey's history of India's early nuclear pioneers, Bhabha, Sarabhai and Saha, and the politics of building Indian big science: the Indian parallel to the Oppenheimer story.

items.title: Backstage
items.creator: Montek Singh Ahluwalia
items.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia's memoir, the best inside-the-room account of the road to 1991, from the M document to the import-licence regime that crippled Indian industry.

items.title: Basic Economics
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: With Hazlitt, Amit's pick for a single fundamental book on economics: Sowell explains the basic concepts in simple language. Amit urges reading all of Sowell.

items.title: Being Muslim in India (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 216)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ghazala Wahab
items.why: Amit's conversation with Ghazala Wahab, which he uses to demonstrate his Roam note-taking workflow: chapter-by-chapter notes linked into themes like double victimisation.

items.title: Beware of Industrial Policy (Everything is Everything, episode 89)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' case against the state picking winners, grounded in limited state capability and public choice. Ajay uses it to critique narrow economists' enthusiasm for industrial policy in developing countries.

items.title: Biophilia
items.creator: Edward O. Wilson
items.why: E. O. Wilson's frame for wonder at living things: every leaf and fungus is a statistically improbable collection of atoms, and we are one more branch of the tree of life. Ajay's scientific case for why hiking and nature matter.

items.title: Blue
items.creator: Joni Mitchell
items.why: Amit's standing album recommendation: Joni Mitchell, a pioneer admired across folk, rock and jazz, whose singular guitar approach, born of childhood polio, is most audible here.

items.title: Blueprint for Armageddon
items.creator: Dan Carlin
items.why: Dan Carlin's World War I series, the work that convinced Amit long-form solo audio can be a primary art form: when Carlin read soldiers' farewell letters, Amit wept on a run.

items.title: Brave New World
items.creator: Vasant Dhar
items.why: Vasant Dhar's podcast of long-form conversations on technology and society, which Amit produces.

items.title: But Clouds Got in My Way: Bias and Bias-Correction of VIIRS Nighttime Lights Data in the Presence of Clouds
items.creator: Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal and Susan Thomas
items.why: Ajay's team's paper correcting the cloud bias in NASA's nighttime-lights data: proof that India can measure its economy from satellites, independently of official statistics. It underpins their Russia paper.

items.title: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
items.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
items.why: Subhashish Bhadra's source for one of Amit's favourite frames: constitutions are products of their moment. America's, born of religious refugees, protects people from the state; India's, born of fragmentation, centralises power.

items.title: Capital Ideas
items.creator: Peter L. Bernstein
items.why: Peter Bernstein's narrative of how the academic ideas of modern finance came into being and fed back into real markets: a bit dated, says Ajay, but still the best way to see why finance is the brain of the economy.

items.title: Capitalism and Freedom
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Ajay's pick from the liberal canon: not introductory, but each chapter 'like an earthquake' that shakes how you think about the world.

items.title: Caste & the Census (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 417)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A topical Seen and the Unseen episode arguing that classifying castes in the census itself ossifies them, relevant to the debate over a new caste census.

items.title: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
items.why: An early conversation with Pranay Kotasthane on how Delhi-designed schemes ignore the states' different needs and quietly extend central control over state subjects: a working case for subsidiarity.

items.title: Civilisation
items.creator: Kenneth Clark
items.why: Kenneth Clark's sweeping history of Western culture, originally a BBC series, which Ajay grew up on and pairs with The Story of Art as a broad, integrating antidote to narrow specialisation.

items.title: Dawn of the Third Globalisation?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's print formulation of his third-globalisation framework: globalisation has not ended but acquired conditions, as sanctions, SWIFT cutoffs and export controls exclude rogue states from the core.

items.title: Declutter (Everything is Everything, episode 30)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on decluttering, where the open-ended fallacy first surfaced: as time shrinks with age, prioritising means saying no even to things you love.

items.title: Dekalog
items.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
items.why: Kieslowski's ten films for Polish television, each loosely inspired by a commandment, which Amit calls the pinnacle of cinematic storytelling: a web series before the web that set the template for The Wire and Adolescence.

items.title: Demonetisation, with Suyash Rai (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
items.why: A Seen and the Unseen episode with Suyash Rai, source of the principle that cost-benefit arguments collapse when the costs fall on one group and the benefits on another, which Amit uses against demonetisation and bailouts.

items.title: Designing the Monetary Policy Committee
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's technical design for India's Monetary Policy Committee, written as it was being built: adding four independent economists alongside a governor who is a government employee guards monetary policy against political capture.

items.title: Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh
items.creator: Shrayana Bhattacharya
items.why: Shrayana Bhattacharya's book that 'contains multitudes', economics, sociology and beautiful writing, and is really about the loneliness of the Indian woman, the title Amit gave their episode. She also coined Amit's favourite compliment, 'anti-uncle'.

items.title: Devangshu Datta Traded His Corduroy Pants (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 348)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devangshu Datta
items.why: Amit's conversation with the writer Devangshu Datta, full of cinematic family nuggets, like a great-grandfather who did river piracy in a dhoti, and first-hand reflection on the Brahmo Samaj's fade into irrelevance.

items.title: Don't Get Fooled by Success
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on survivorship bias, built on the cricket-tipster scam: five- or six-year track records of funds can be pure selection, so be wary of lionising winners.

items.title: Don't Insult Pasta
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's Pastafarian satire and an early entry in two decades of writing on free speech: if you don't want me to offend your god, don't offend mine.

items.title: Don't Punish Victimless Crimes (Everything is Everything, episode 73)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' case that bans don't make demand disappear but create black markets and bootleggers, and that an 'icky' reaction is not the same as an ethical argument.

items.title: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches
items.creator: B. R. Ambedkar
items.why: Sixty-plus volumes, free online. Read in sequence, they show Ambedkar's thinking evolving, more pro-market by the 1950s as markets changed Dalit lives, and a first generation of leaders who thought by writing.

items.title: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 345)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand
items.why: Amit's conversation with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand on semi-urban Bihar: streets of idle young men as a demographic dividend turning into disaster, and stories of stolen bridges and ponds that reveal latent entrepreneurial energy.

items.title: Economical Writing: Thirty-Five Rules for Clear and Concise Prose
items.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
items.why: Deirdre McCloskey's rules for clear, concise prose, which Amit gives students who arrive full of insider jargon: written for economists but useful for any technical subject, and a lesson in respecting readers.

items.title: Economics in One Lesson (Everything is Everything, episode 109)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on Hazlitt's book and the broken-window fallacy: what is unseen is what would have been built without a tariff or a bailout, so 'tariffs cause adjustments' must not be misread as 'tariffs aren't bad'.

items.title: EconTalk
items.creator: Russ Roberts
items.why: Russ Roberts's long-running podcast and one of Amit's favourites: relaxed, deep conversations about ideas without a rigid structure, in the same school as his own.

items.title: Elite Imitation in Public Policy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 180)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: Amit's conversation with Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok on their paper: Indian elites copy the form of Western institutions without the substance that made them work.

items.title: Emergent Ventures
items.creator: Tyler Cowen (Mercatus Center)
items.why: Tyler Cowen's grants programme for high-variance, often very young thinkers, without target-driven contracts: the hosts' model for funding weirdos directly instead of through the credentialed pipeline.

items.title: Essays on Nationalism
items.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
items.why: Tagore's beautifully written attack on the nation-state as a force that crushes the individual and human brotherhood, Ajay's main recommendation and the source of the hosts' most-quoted lines against nationalism.

items.title: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
items.creator: Tom Robbins
items.why: Tom Robbins's novel, source of two lines the hosts live by: 'There are no strangers, there are just friends you don't have yet', and that the only people on routine flights are those who think they are.

items.title: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's moral frame for thinking about the state: government action is funded by coerced taxes, so whatever your ideology you must justify that coercion. Every ideology is really an argument about when it is acceptable.

items.title: Every Grain of Sand
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: A Dylan song whose lines about 'the ancient footsteps like the motion of the sea' Amit reaches for when wonder at the world, and at the information carried in every human being, needs words.

items.title: Ex Machina
items.creator: Alex Garland
items.why: Alex Garland's film, Amit's anchor for the case that science fiction grapples with questions philosophers haven't begun to answer: if we create something approaching consciousness, what do we owe it, and it us?

items.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
items.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
items.why: Hirschman's framework for the choices people face when an institution declines: leave, speak up or stay loyal. Ajay notes that Indians mostly use loyalty and a little voice, and sees migration as the underused exit lever.

items.title: Export Versus FDI in Services
items.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper on India's internationalisation in services, which finds an inversion: in Indian software, firms that set up abroad are weaker than the pure exporters, a rare exception to the textbook ladder.

items.title: Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek
items.creator: John Papola and Russ Roberts (EconStories)
items.why: EconStories' viral rap battle staging the Keynes-Hayek debate: fun, rigorously accurate and a useful entry point if the original papers feel daunting.

items.title: Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek Round Two
items.creator: John Papola and Russ Roberts (EconStories)
items.why: The second round of the EconStories Keynes-Hayek rap battle, equally accessible for newcomers to the price-system view.

items.title: Frankenstein
items.creator: Mary Shelley
items.why: Mary Shelley's pioneering novel, read for its three nested narrators and as a live AI-ethics text about what a creator owes its creation. Paired with her mother Wollstonecraft's Vindication, it spans two generations of pioneering thought.

items.title: Frankenstein (The Book Club on Storytel, episode 3)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's Storytel audio episode on Frankenstein, designed to be heard back-to-back with his Wollstonecraft episode as a mother-daughter story.

items.title: Free to Choose
items.creator: Milton and Rose Friedman
items.why: The Friedmans' popular, first-principles introduction to free markets, more accessible than Capitalism and Freedom, tying capitalism to consent and separating markets from cronyism. It accompanies the TV series of the same name.

items.title: Free to Choose (TV series)
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Milton Friedman's TV series making the case for free markets, easy to watch on YouTube as a vivid introduction to the book's arguments. Amit's example of 'stock': lasting work that others build on, as against the constant flow of tweets, columns and episodes.

items.title: Freedom House country scores
items.creator: Freedom House
items.why: Freedom House's democracy ratings, which the hosts use to measure how far populists have hollowed out democracies, and which Ajay proposes as the yardstick for how much state legibility is safe.

items.title: Friedrich Hayek: The Ideas and Influence of the Libertarian Economist
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: Eamonn Butler's friendly distillation of Hayek's core ideas for newcomers, since Hayek's own books can be heavy going.

items.title: GNU Emacs
items.creator: Richard Stallman
items.why: Ajay's editor and his example of old, weathered tooling: decades of survival have given it an elegant, bulletproof design, and a hundred lines of Lisp let you build your own productivity world on top of it.

items.title: Google Earth (desktop version)
items.creator: Google
items.why: Ajay's 'greatest joy in the world' for planning hikes: on a big screen in terrain mode, the desktop version lets you check every elevation, fly over routes and circle peaks like Nanda Devi.

items.title: Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals
items.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper behind the episode of the same name: firms from developing countries graduate to global operation step by step, through exports, imports and inward and outward FDI. The first study of Indian firms going multinational.

items.title: Great Books of the Western World
items.creator: Mortimer Adler (ed.), Encyclopaedia Britannica
items.why: The set Amit kept from his father's house purely out of sentiment, recommended for its Synopticon volumes, which show what synoptical reading looks like in practice.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal Examines Human Nature (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 331)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Amit's long conversation with a sharp psychologist of internet behaviour, known for Twitter mega-threads of original synthesis, and the source of the 'looking-glass self' framing Amit uses.

items.title: Half-Lion: How P.V. Narasimha Rao Transformed India
items.creator: Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Vinay Sitapati's biography restoring Narasimha Rao to his place: a polyglot who taught himself programming in his sixties, played Machiavellian power games and believed in reform. Its view of 1991 as a re-liberalisation after the Nehruvian break shapes Ajay's revisionist history.

items.title: His Dark Materials
items.creator: Philip Pullman
items.why: Philip Pullman's trilogy, which Amit calls masterpieces that still make him smile or tear up in bed. Trust him and read it; its daemons give shape to the AI companions he imagines in our future.

items.title: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
items.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
items.why: Yuen Yuen Ang's account of what actually happened in China, with her parable of two inadequate development gurus. It keeps Amit from a cartoon good-versus-evil view of China.

items.title: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books
items.creator: Josh Jones
items.why: The story of the novelist editing scientific manuscripts, which Ajay recommends to every academic: watch a master of language clean up research prose and see what good writing does.

items.title: How Music Works
items.creator: David Byrne
items.why: David Byrne's book, which Amit gifts to everyone: the space shapes the music, from cathedral acoustics producing long-note modal music to cramped clubs producing punk. It feeds Amit's obsession with how form shapes the world.

items.title: I Play to Play
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's essay naming his philosophy of play: chess for the joy and the dopamine, without ego, because the point of rolling the rock up the hill is the rolling, not the summit.

items.title: If You Are a Creator, This Is Your Time
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's case that this is the creator's moment: cheap means of production, no gatekeepers, no constraints of form, and direct reach to and payment from audiences, so niches no one knew existed can find their people.

items.title: In a Silent Way (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 316)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gaurav Chintamani
items.why: Amit's conversation with the musician Gaurav Chintamani on how a big hit can freeze an artist in time, and his working artist's scepticism about whether true originality exists.

items.title: In Defense of Globalization
items.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
items.why: Bhagwati's definitive case that globalisation has been history's greatest engine of poverty reduction, that protectionism hurts the people it claims to protect, and where its critics go wrong.

items.title: In Praise of Floods
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: James C. Scott on how homogenisation impoverishes the world, with a dozen plant varieties dominating our food, and on how suppressing every small flood or fire stores up catastrophe, Amit's analogy for bailouts and moral hazard.

items.title: India Awakes
items.creator: Johan Norberg
items.why: Johan Norberg's documentary, including Barun Mitra's story of using historical Google Earth images to win tribal land rights in Gujarat, after which people built pakka houses and toilets: proof of what property rights unlock.

items.title: India's Agriculture Crisis (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 140)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand
items.why: Amit's conversation with Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand on agriculture as a price-system failure, including the finding that of 24 commodities promised MSPs, only six actually get them.

items.title: India's Lost Decade (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 116)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Puja Mehra
items.why: Amit's conversation with Puja Mehra, companion to her book, on how India's golden run from 1991 to 2011 was derailed from 2008-09 by personnel changes and bad calls.

items.title: India's Supply Chain Vulnerability With Chinese APIs
items.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade and Ajay Shah
items.why: A multi-author paper, Ajay among them, on India's dependence on Chinese pharmaceutical ingredients: it asks when protectionism becomes defensible (very narrowly) and sets out a minimal, sophisticated design for state intervention.

items.title: India: An Agricultural Trade Powerhouse
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's case that free trade in agriculture serves India: let farmers sell to the world and import freely when short, against the old assumption that agriculture is untouchable.

items.title: Indian Colours
items.creator: Indian Colours (indiancolours.com)
items.why: The brand behind Ajay's on-camera shirts, whose business model makes art affordable for buyers and pays artists ongoing royalties.

items.title: Instant Cross-Border Payments vs. Current Account Inconvertibility
items.creator: Ajay Shah and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
items.why: Ajay and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah show that India's claimed current-account convertibility is largely a delusion: money moves globally in milliseconds while Indian rules still treat every cross-border transaction as suspect.

items.title: Is India a Flailing State?
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Pritchett's diagnosis of an Indian state whose head cannot control its limbs, the 'severed nerves' image Ajay extends to old Indian firms and to cynical civil servants who quietly route around edicts.

items.title: Jahnavi and the Cyclotron (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 319)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jahnavi Phalkey
items.why: Amit's delightful conversation with Jahnavi Phalkey on the Indian counterpart to the Oppenheimer story, three scientists contesting how to build Indian physics, with detours into Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe.

items.title: Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat's Burden (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 375)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Part of Amit's series with Karthik Muralidharan, rich in data on Indian state capacity: India spends 3% of its budget at the local level against China's 50%, and 250 PhDs applied for 368 peon jobs.

items.title: Knowingless
items.creator: Aella
items.why: Aella's newsletter, one of the few Amit pays for: rigorous data work on young people, sex and gender relations by an unusual data scientist.

items.title: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's long-standing written argument that banning prostitution, betting and alcohol hands the trade to the underworld and worsens every problem the law claims to solve.

items.title: Madame George
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: Amit's all-time favourite song, Van Morrison at his most haunting, best triangulated through the cover versions by Marianne Faithfull and Luka Bloom.

items.title: Magic Fruit: A Poetic Trip
items.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
items.why: A remarkable hour-long musical play written by Vaishnav Vyas, the show's cinematographer, which Amit praises for its creativity and ambition.

items.title: Maps Are Magic (Everything is Everything, episode 44)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on maps, including OpenStreetMap as a genuine digital public good, the yardstick against which they judge claims made for UPI and Aadhaar, and Ajay's love of paper maps.

items.title: Marching For Salt
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column pointing out that independent India ended up taxing salt more heavily than the British Raj did: evidence that the freedom struggle, by its own measure, is unfinished.

items.title: Math Is Better Than the Brigadier's Girlfriend (Everything is Everything, episode 15)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: An early EIE episode on mathematics, born of face-to-face conversation (Amit's evidence for in-person creative work), in which Ajay first recommended The Soul of a New Machine.

items.title: Memories and Things (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 195)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Aanchal Malhotra
items.why: Amit's conversation with the oral historian Aanchal Malhotra on Partition memories and the reconstructive nature of memory, including a Lahore story of prejudice collapsing on contact with an actual Indian.

items.title: Metrics for Intervention (Everything is Everything, episode 101)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's four metrics of how hard a state intervention is: discretion, number of transactions, stakes and opacity. They explain where bureaucracies fail to see correctly, and why finance is among the hardest fields to regulate.

items.title: Midnight in Chernobyl
items.creator: Adam Higginbotham
items.why: Adam Higginbotham's reportage, which Amit rates above the good HBO series: Chernobyl as a story of political economy rather than nuclear physics, in which operators kept making bad calls because dissent meant Siberia.

items.title: My Friend Sancho
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's own novel, self-deprecatingly recommended, with the bittersweet story of Govind Nihalani's attempt to film it and Bollywood's indifference even to the maker of Ardh Satya.

items.title: Natasha Badhwar Lives the Examined Life (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 301)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Natasha Badhwar
items.why: The episode in which Amit feels he balanced biography, work and ideas perfectly, with the writer and homeschooler Natasha Badhwar, full of practical and philosophical thinking on raising children.

items.title: National Highway 420 (and the EV of Aggressive Batting)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column applying expected-value thinking to cricket: in T20, aggressive batting pays, and captains set par scores too low because they are stuck in the ODI rhythm.

items.title: Naushad Forbes Wants to Fix India (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 282)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Naushad Forbes
items.why: Amit's conversation with the industrialist, source of the story of Manmohan Singh whispering 'tell the world everything you said today inside here': a glimpse of how isolated the reformers were, and of reform by stealth.

items.title: Nehru's Debates (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 262)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
items.why: The conversation behind Nehru: The Debates that Defined India, showing that the founding generation's own debates contained the seeds of opposition to the speech restrictions Nehru imposed.

items.title: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
items.creator: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
items.why: The founding generation's great debates with Nehru, including from his allies over the early curbs on speech. Amit prizes the manner of disagreement more than who was right: great minds arguing in good faith, an ethic lost in public life today.

items.title: Not What They Had in Mind
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: Arnold Kling's structured case that misaligned incentives and government distortions, not unfettered markets, produced the 2008 financial crisis.

items.title: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
items.creator: Joshua S. Goldstein, Staffan A. Qvist and Steven Pinker
items.why: The op-ed that compresses the safety, climate and cost case for nuclear power: sixty years of nuclear power have caused fewer deaths than a single month of coal, and it is the source of most of Amit's nuclear statistics.

items.title: Objects From Our Past (Everything is Everything, episode 77)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A favourite Amit-conceived episode on objects the hosts have kept, such as Ajay's old mixtapes, and what assembling a mixtape in 1985 says about today's post-scarcity world of bits.

items.title: Paris, Texas
items.creator: Wim Wenders
items.why: Amit's favourite Wim Wenders film, a masterpiece of storytelling and cinematography, and his reminder that great films come from young directors too.

items.title: Poker and Stock Markets (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 47)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mohit Satyanand
items.why: Amit's early long conversation with Mohit Satyanand on expected value, randomness and the cognitive biases, such as loss aversion and hindsight bias, shared by the poker table and the trading desk.

items.title: Politics and the English Language
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: The Orwell essay Amit gave every young writer he edited: clear thinking produces clear writing, and forcing yourself to write clearly forces you to think clearly. Unreadable prose usually hides muddled thought.

items.title: Politics as a Vocation
items.creator: Max Weber
items.why: Weber's lecture, which Ajay calls one of the great works everyone should read: the state as a monopoly on legitimate violence, the classical sources of legitimacy, and politics as 'a strong and slow boring of hard boards' that needs both passion and perspective.

items.title: Premature Imitation and India's Flailing State
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok's paper on isomorphic mimicry: Indian institutions that look like central banks or regulators from the outside but lack the capabilities inside, which is why imported policies fail.

items.title: Prices, Fast and Slow
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's paper extending Hayek's view of prices as society's information system: when prices are allowed to move, and the politics of letting them.

items.title: Public Choice Theory (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 121)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's solo audio primer on public choice theory: politicians and bureaucrats act in their own interest, the mirror image of market failure.

items.title: Public Opinion
items.creator: Walter Lippmann
items.why: Lippmann's foundational account of how mediated information forms the 'pictures in our heads' of a world we cannot see, with his parable of islanders who stayed friends for six weeks while their nations were at war.

items.title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
items.creator: Edmund Burke
items.why: Burke's founding text of considered conservatism, the kind the hosts share: change the world humbly, one step at a time, because it is too complex for grand schemes pursued through violent, hubristic means.

items.title: Remnants of a Separation
items.creator: Aanchal Malhotra
items.why: Aanchal Malhotra's history of Partition told through the objects survivors carried across the border, a model of humanising a political tragedy through concrete things. Researching his episode with her taught Amit that memory is a remembering of the last remembering, 'Chinese whispers all the way down'.

items.title: Rent Control (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 14)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
items.why: An early Seen and the Unseen primer with Alex Tabarrok on how rent control destroys housing supply, with rent-controlled New York looking like a 'bombed out city'.

items.title: Restaurant Regulations in India (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 18)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Madhu Menon
items.why: Amit's conversation with the restaurateur Madhu Menon on contradictory rules, with the fire department demanding many doors and the excise department one, that turn honest businesses into permanent bribe-payers.

items.title: Roam Research
items.creator: Conor White-Sullivan
items.why: Amit's daily driver for analytical reading and show prep: nested notes (chapter, point, quote) and two-way links let every quote live both in its source and in his themes.

items.title: Rohini Nilekani Pays It Forward (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 317)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rohini Nilekani
items.why: Amit's conversation with the philanthropist, source of the 'state, society, market' framing he argues against: markets are not a third pillar but the way people in society meet each other's needs.

items.title: Romantic Outlaws
items.creator: Charlotte Gordon
items.why: Charlotte Gordon's joint biography of Mary Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley, two lives lived against the grain, to read alongside Vindication and Frankenstein.

items.title: Russia, Ukraine, Foreign Policy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 268)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai
items.why: Recorded just after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai warned that Europe's dependence on Russian gas was about to become blackmail. Amit cites it as the receipt for a prediction that came true.

items.title: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 255)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sara Rai
items.why: Amit's conversation with the writer Sara Rai, whose vivid, novelistic memory of a childhood without constant stimulation becomes his evidence that boredom made earlier generations notice the world.

items.title: Sell the Tiger to Save It
items.creator: Barun Mitra
items.why: Barun Mitra's counterintuitive case for using the price system in conservation: if tigers could legally be bred and sold, the incentives that keep cows and chickens abundant would keep tigers abundant too.

items.title: Separation of Powers (Everything is Everything, episode 91)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on why legislative, executive and judicial power must not be fused, one of two grand ways, with decentralisation, to disperse power, applied to Indian regulators that combine all three.

items.title: Servant of the People
items.creator: Volodymyr Zelensky
items.why: The Ukrainian sitcom in which Zelensky played a teacher who becomes president and faces a Russian invasion, before he did it for real: comedy, and the cultural artefact Putin underestimated.

items.title: Seven Bridges Road
items.creator: Steve Young
items.why: A song Ajay loves in both Steve Young's original and the Eagles' cover, for its beauty and for the pleasure of hearing a song evolve from one version to the next.

items.title: Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War
items.creator: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
items.why: Ajay's team's paper using nighttime lights to measure the Russian wartime economy: aggregate radiance in January 2025 roughly matched January 2019, with damage concentrated near the borders. A worked example of satellites giving independent observers leverage over official statistics.

items.title: Shephali Bhatt Is Searching for the Incredible (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 391)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shephali Bhatt
items.why: Amit's conversation with the journalist behind the finding that over 1,12,000 Indian creators earn Rs 1-10 lakh a month, proof that the creator economy's middle is real, and a candid account of her early years in a financial newsroom.

items.title: Six More Stories That Should Be Films (Everything is Everything, episode 43)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The third of the hosts' 'stories that should be films' episodes: Amit's fiction about IIT aspirants and vloggers and a story of 1800s Delhi, and Ajay's missing plutonium on Nanda Devi, a navy that was 'delivered' and a package parachuting into Africa, stories whose arcs map onto Booker's seven basic plots.

items.title: Sixteen Stormy Days
items.creator: Tripurdaman Singh
items.why: Tripurdaman Singh's definitive account of the First Amendment of 1951: where America's First Amendment protected speech, India's damaged it, as Nehru amended the Constitution to get past court rulings and curb his rivals.

items.title: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
items.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
items.why: Pritchett and Woolcock's paper that first asked whether a state intervention is an easy or a hard problem, measured by transaction volume and frontline discretion. Ajay builds his four metrics of intervention on it.

items.title: South India Would Like to Have a Word (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 320)
items.creator: Amit Varma with RS Nilakantan
items.why: Amit's conversation with R. S. Nilakantan showing with data how centrally driven policy misreads South India, where the problem is diabetes rather than stunting: a concrete case for subsidiarity.

items.title: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 380)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sowmya Dhanaraj
items.why: One of Amit's ten favourite episodes: a researcher who questions received wisdom from lived working-class experience, an antidote to imported jargon in thinking about Indian poverty.

items.title: Startup Archive
items.creator: Startup Archive
items.why: The curated trove of founder advice, from Zuckerberg, Thiel, Chesky, Khosla and others, from which most of the hosts' startup-gyan episodes were harvested. Amit treats it as required reading.

items.title: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 333)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Subhashish Bhadra
items.why: The long conversation behind Caged Tiger: how India's constitution borrowed the colonial state's design, and the lived costs of an over-broad state.

items.title: Suyash Rai Embraces India's Complexity (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 307)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
items.why: Amit's conversation with the policy researcher who originated several of the show's themes, the dharma framing and the state as neither necessary nor sufficient among them, and who nudged Amit towards MacIntyre's After Virtue.

items.title: Ten Years Gone
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: Ajay's pick for the greatest Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known, a perfect fit for the arena-rock form. Worth really sitting with.

items.title: The Age of Pandemics
items.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: Chinmay Tumbe's history of pandemics, with the cholera story that parallels Semmelweis's, and the claim that pathogens have tended to evolve towards lower virulence rather than be eliminated.

items.title: The Anti-Defection Law (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 13)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
items.why: An early Seen and the Unseen conversation with Barun Mitra on how the well-intentioned anti-defection law ended genuine debate in Parliament, turning MPs into party-bloc votes: you can now 'run Parliament from an Excel sheet'.

items.title: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 154)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's deep-dive conversation with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah on the toolkit of their book In Service of the Republic: market failure, state capability and implementation constraints.

items.title: The Baptist, the Bootlegger and the Dead Man Walking
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's long-form telling of the Lal Bihari saga, a life that could be a film, and of how moralisers and rent-seekers walk arm in arm into regulation.

items.title: The Bookshop Romeo
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on an expected-value calculation in a bookshop: when the upside is high and the downside near zero, always make the approach. A small, portable framework from his poker-and-life writing.

items.title: The Calculus of Consent
items.creator: James M. Buchanan and Gordon Tullock
items.why: Buchanan and Tullock's masterpiece, regarded by many as the start of public choice: how collective decisions get made by self-interested actors, and why constitutional rules matter more than day-to-day politics. Not an easy read, but foundational.

items.title: The Candlemakers' Petition
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's satire showing how protectionist logic, taken seriously, leads straight to absurdity: one of the greatest pieces of satire ever written, and every protectionist argument since is a candlemakers' petition in fancier clothes.

items.title: The Case for Nuclear Electricity (Everything is Everything, episode 78)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' case that nuclear power is the obvious answer to climate change (France runs at 71% nuclear and emits a tenth of the world average per kWh), the nuclear half of Amit's optimism about the energy transition.

items.title: The Case for Trade Barriers Against Chinese Imports
items.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah's case for limits on free trade with revisionist powers, on four grounds: military conflict, economic statecraft, scale-economy gaming and macroeconomic spillovers. Amit disagrees with its broader stance.

items.title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
items.creator: Eric S. Raymond
items.why: Eric Raymond's essay on why open, teeming 'bazaar' development beats top-down 'cathedral' building, which Ajay calls critical reading for every advocate of state-built technology monopolies.

items.title: The Constitution of Liberty
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Part of the Hayek triptych behind the hosts' freedom arguments, and bedrock first-principles reading on why capital controls and the rest of the architecture of unfreedom are illegitimate.

items.title: The Design of Everyday Things
items.creator: Don Norman
items.why: Don Norman's masterpiece on why everything around us looks and works the way it does; it turns the world into an exercise in noticing. Ajay's lesson from it: everything beautiful is also beautifully functional.

items.title: The Discovery of India
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: The book, Ajay says, that invented the idea of India: a concept grounded in Indian history yet free of hatred, setting the stage for a modern, scientific nation. Read it as an adult, not at twelve.

items.title: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: Keynes's 1919 warning that impossible reparations would push Germany to print money into hyperinflation, which also helped seed the demand for something like GDP, with its famous passage on the integrated pre-1914 world economy.

items.title: The Elements of Style
items.creator: William Strunk Jr. and E. B. White
items.why: Strunk and White's guide to brevity, precision and clarity, which Ajay calls universal knowledge for researchers and the model for The Elements of Programming Style.

items.title: The Elusive Quest for Growth
items.creator: William Easterly
items.why: Easterly's first cut at clearing away the rubbish of development fads, showing how top-down expert interventions have failed. Essential, say the hosts, for seeing where development economics goes wrong.

items.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
items.creator: Robert Axelrod
items.why: Axelrod uses game theory to show why cooperation evolves even when the maths seems to favour selfishness, and how to respond to misbehaviour: strike back once, but don't bear a grudge forever.

items.title: The Evolution of Human Sexuality
items.creator: Donald Symons
items.why: Donald Symons's founding work applying natural-selection logic to human sexual behaviour, Amit's second great milestone in evolutionary reading after Dawkins, whose arguments A Billion Wicked Thoughts later confirmed with data.

items.title: The Ferment of Our Founders (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 272)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
items.why: Amit's conversation with the historian Shruti Kapila, source of the line 'Hindutva is a theory of violence in search of a history', which the hosts use to show how nationalisms invent or rewrite the past.

items.title: The Free Press
items.creator: Bari Weiss
items.why: Bari Weiss's publication, which began as a single newsletter and grew into a serious, hundred-million-dollar media operation: proof that creator-led journalism works at scale.

items.title: The Functions of the Executive
items.creator: Chester Barnard
items.why: Chester Barnard's study of how organisations really work from the inside, which Lant Pritchett paired with Seeing Like a State as books that would change how Ajay thought about firms and governments.

items.title: The Game
items.creator: Neil Strauss
items.why: Neil Strauss's bestseller on pickup artistry, read by Amit as anthropology of the manosphere: beneath the manipulation lies a sharp folk understanding of human nature and of how validation markets work.

items.title: The God Delusion
items.creator: Richard Dawkins
items.why: A central text of New Atheism, which Amit recommends taking seriously for its critique of organised religion, along with the line that everyone is already an atheist about thousands of gods and just stops one short.

items.title: The Good Boatman
items.creator: Rajmohan Gandhi
items.why: Rajmohan Gandhi's book of ideas on Gandhi's contradictions, recommended to Amit by Ramachandra Guha, and an exemplar of synoptical writing that synthesises a whole corpus by theme.

items.title: The History of the Planning Commission (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 306)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Menon
items.why: Amit's conversation with Nikhil Menon on the Planning Commission and the Mahalanobis vision that framed Indian economic and manufacturing policy for decades.

items.title: The Hobbit
items.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
items.why: Tolkien's tale, the cleanest example of the voyage-and-return plot (a finite mission, then home, but never the same), and like Glimpses of World History a story first written for one's own children.

items.title: The Indian Armed Forces (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 175)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Lt Gen Prakash Menon
items.why: Amit's conversation with Lt Gen Prakash Menon, an inside-the-institution view of Kashmir and Indian military strategy that tested Amit's own framing.

items.title: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's condensed written case that the state's coercive role in agriculture, not farmers' lack of skill, is the source of their misery.

items.title: The Indianness of Indian Food (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 95)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Doctor
items.why: Amit's conversation with Vikram Doctor on how Indian cuisine is a layered import: the Columbian Exchange, idli's Indonesian roots, marigolds from Mexico and how fuel shaped cooking.

items.title: The Innovator's Dilemma
items.creator: Clayton Christensen
items.why: Christensen's puzzle of why successful firms fail to disrupt themselves (Kodak had the know-how for digital photography), which Ajay counters with Sun, Google and Amazon as big firms that did.

items.title: The Lesson From This IPL: Front-Load Your Innings
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's original T20 front-loading argument: don't hoard wickets for the death overs but attack from ball one, because the ratio of resources to constraints demands it, a lesson teams took years to learn.

items.title: The Liberal Nationalism of Nitin Pai (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 318)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Nitin Pai
items.why: Amit's long argument with Nitin Pai over whether liberalism and nationalism can coexist, including on Kashmir and national security. Listen and decide whether Pai's reconciliation lands for you.

items.title: The Life and Times of Gurcharan Das (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 425)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gurcharan Das
items.why: Amit's conversation with Gurcharan Das: his letter to Manmohan Singh asking why reforms were being done by stealth, corporate stories from his career, and a reading of Sisyphus as doing your dharma that Amit counts as an ancestor of 'I play to play'.

items.title: The Life and Times of Mrinal Pande (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 263)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mrinal Pande
items.why: Amit's conversation with Mrinal Pande, whose first answer ran an hour and five minutes through nearly thirty years of her life (his case for never interrupting), with her memory of her mother Shivani writing amid family dinners.

items.title: The Lives of Others
items.creator: Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck
items.why: One of the finest debut films Amit has seen, up there with Pather Panchali and Court: a meditation on surveillance that makes you feel the Berlin Wall as a daily psychic crushing rather than a line on a map.

items.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Man (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 303)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Taneja
items.why: The second-most-popular Seen and the Unseen episode, with Nikhil Taneja, and the companion to The Loneliness of the Indian Woman. Together they show how half of India struggles to talk to the other half.

items.title: The Looking-Glass Self
items.creator: Charles Cooley
items.why: Charles Cooley's idea that we shape ourselves by how we believe others see us, so the real choice is not 'who am I' but whose mirrors we choose to stand before.

items.title: The Lowest Hanging Fruit On The Coconut Tree: India's Climate Transition Through The Price System In The Power Sector
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah's blueprint for India's climate transition through prices in the power sector: enable rather than pick technologies, so exporters can get clean, reliable electricity at competitive prices.

items.title: The Mahatma and the Poet: Letters and Debates between Gandhi and Tagore
items.creator: Sabyasachi Bhattacharya (ed.)
items.why: The letters and debates of Gandhi and Tagore on nationalism, industrialisation and modernity: two great minds disagreeing respectfully, with Tagore, in the hosts' view, right that nationalism is simply toxic.

items.title: The Matunga Racket
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column on how outlawing a victimless act lets the police turn the law into an extortion racket against the very people it claims to protect, the case study behind the hosts' arguments on homosexuality and victimless crimes.

items.title: The Narrow Corridor
items.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
items.why: Acemoglu and Robinson's frame: freedom and prosperity live in a narrow corridor where a capable state and an empowered society hold each other in check. Ajay's lens for worrying about India's mass surveillance.

items.title: The Nighttime Lights of Russia (Everything is Everything, episode 116)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on measuring Russia's wartime economy from space, part of their argument that new measurement opens up phenomena previously hidden from us.

items.title: The Notebook Trilogy
items.creator: Agota Kristof
items.why: Agota Kristof's novels, set on the border of an unnamed country during an unnamed war and written in a language she acquired, stripped of every ornament: Amit's benchmark for prose in which every word does a job.

items.title: The Open Society and Its Enemies
items.creator: Karl Popper
items.why: Popper's case against utopian schemes that assume knowledge we don't have, and for piecemeal, reversible change, with his diagnosis of nationalism's appeal to tribal instinct. The philosophical backbone of the hosts' incrementalism.

items.title: The Paper Menagerie and Other Stories
items.creator: Ken Liu
items.why: Ken Liu's collection, whose title story Amit calls a masterpiece of decluttered language that always makes him cry. He uses it to teach that simple prose can be music.

items.title: The Policy Posture as an Incomplete Contract
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's argument that no law is permanent: a reform endures only when a persistent community of owners guards it and public communication 'pours concrete of credibility' on it.

items.title: The Pune Public Policy Festival
items.creator: Pune Public Policy Festival
items.why: A festival trying to revive Pune, once 'the Oxford of the East', as a decentralised hub of Indian policy debate after intellectual gravity shifted to Delhi.

items.title: The Push Man and Other Stories
items.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
items.why: Yoshihiro Tatsumi's bleak, powerful stories that stare into the depths of the human soul, which Amit places in the dark-realist line that runs from Goya.

items.title: The Road
items.creator: Cormac McCarthy
items.why: Cormac McCarthy's novel, one of Ajay's father-son picks: stripped to the bare conditions of love and survival, it takes you deep inside what it means to be a father and a son.

items.title: The Road to Serfdom
items.creator: Friedrich Hayek
items.why: Hayek's original case that the road to economic control is the road to serfdom: the book Margaret Thatcher slammed down at her first cabinet meeting, and the one Amit wishes Deng Xiaoping had carried.

items.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Friedman's 1968 presidential address, a turning point that moved macroeconomics from Keynesian discretion towards rules. Ajay draws from it the insight that high inflation scrambles firms' ability to tell real price signals from monetary noise.

items.title: The Rooted Cosmopolitanism of Sugata Srinivasaraju (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 277)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sugata Srinivasaraju
items.why: Amit's conversation on the milieu Sugata Srinivasaraju grew up in and Bangalore's transformation, and the source of 'rooted cosmopolitanism': being at home in your own soil and a citizen of the world. Amit admits he has only the second half.

items.title: The Royal Game (Chess Story)
items.creator: Stefan Zweig
items.why: Stefan Zweig's moving story of chess as a prisoner's only company in solitary confinement, and a quiet warning that even isolated genius hits a ceiling without conversation.

items.title: The Skeptical Environmentalist
items.creator: Bjørn Lomborg
items.why: Lomborg's tracing of how London and other Western cities grew heavily polluted on the way up and cleaned up as they got rich: Amit's evidence that growth and sustainability go together.

items.title: The State of Our Farmers (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 86)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gunvant Patil
items.why: A Hindi-language Seen and the Unseen conversation in which farmer-leaders articulate Hayekian ideas from lived experience rather than books: a 'masterpiece of illumination', says Amit.

items.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
items.creator: Adam Smith
items.why: Adam Smith's philosophical masterpiece and the source of the 'Man of System' passage, a critique of central planning, chessboard metaphor and all, written 150 years before central planning existed.

items.title: The Three Languages of Politics
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: Arnold Kling's insight that progressives, conservatives and libertarians each argue along a different axis (oppressor versus oppressed, civilisation versus barbarism, liberty versus coercion), so arguments across tribes fail before they begin. Amit's key to talking across those lines.

items.title: The Vintage Book of Indian Writing 1947-1997
items.creator: Salman Rushdie and Elizabeth West (eds.)
items.why: Rushdie and West's anthology, which opens with Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny', the hosts' example of a leader who could articulate complex ideas so they lasted, read among other great Indian prose.

items.title: The White Man's Burden
items.creator: William Easterly
items.why: Easterly's clear-headed account of why decades of foreign aid have not moved national development, and how the aid industry's incentives favour attributable results over impact. The companion to The Elusive Quest for Growth.

items.title: The Wire
items.creator: David Simon
items.why: Amit's favourite TV show, which brought a novelistic ethic to the screen: fifteen-plus major characters, no manipulative score, things unfolding organically. Proof of what long-form storytelling can do.

items.title: This Be The Verse
items.creator: Philip Larkin
items.why: Larkin's poem, whose image of misery deepening 'like a coastal shelf' Amit turns benign: knowledge also accretes in layers across generations, and books and durable work add to the shelf.

items.title: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Everything is Everything, episode 22)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The foundation of the hosts' episodes on firms: three companies that surprised them by how boldly they changed, with firms as the central productive units of modern society.

items.title: Three Hundred Ramayanas: Five Examples and Three Thoughts on Translation
items.creator: A. K. Ramanujan
items.why: A. K. Ramanujan's essay showing that the Ramayana is not one book but a river of regional versions, each a fork that picks up local additions: the foundational text for treating India's epics as open source.

items.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
items.creator: Harper Lee
items.why: Harper Lee's novel, which Ajay grew up reading as a masterpiece of parent and child facing a darkness that now looks less vanished than he thought. Amit draws from it the premise that most people are good once known.

items.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
items.creator: Ludwig Wittgenstein
items.why: Wittgenstein's treatise, which Amit invokes for the inadequacy of language, the setup for why plain storytelling, as in Springsteen, can still be beautiful.

items.title: Traffic
items.creator: Tom Vanderbilt
items.why: Tom Vanderbilt's book on driving, source of the finding that many accidents happen close to home because the brain switches off on familiar ground: the 'almost done' failure mode the hosts see in hiking and chess.

items.title: Triumph of the City
items.creator: Edward Glaeser
items.why: Edward Glaeser's case that urban density, many clever people in close proximity, is the heart of modernity, and that cities are the most important units of modern political economy.

items.title: Two Great Investment Strategies
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's piece on selection in investing: throw 10,000 darts and ten will look brilliant by accident, which is why the show will never celebrate 'great fund managers'.

items.title: Unboxing Bengaluru
items.creator: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash
items.why: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash's book on Bangalore, source of the line 'the software is 5G but the hardware is 2G', and of dating-app data showing romance moving in months in Delhi, weeks in Mumbai and days in Bangalore.

items.title: Underrated, Overrated, Complicated (Everything is Everything, episode 85)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' game of rating things underrated, overrated or complicated, including their debate on whether social media is a force for bad, and the setup for Amit's lessons from his own startup failure.

items.title: Varun Grover Is in the House (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 292)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Varun Grover
items.why: Amit's conversation with the writer Varun Grover on language, culture and home as the vibe, books and people around you: the portable home of the cloud era.

items.title: Watching the Wheels
items.creator: John Lennon
items.why: John Lennon's song, one of the two finalists for the show's name before 'Everything is Everything' won.

items.title: We Are All Gamblers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column arguing that every romantic, financial and career choice is a bet on probabilities, so stigmatising or banning games of chance is incoherent.

items.title: What Cricket Can Learn From Poker
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's piece on expected value: why a 51-49 bet is right regardless of any single result, and how cricket could use granular probabilities the way football already does.

items.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
items.creator: Thomas Nagel
items.why: Nagel's essay on why we can never directly inhabit another consciousness, the setup for Amit's case that novels are the closest we get.

items.title: What Is Libertarianism? (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 117)
items.creator: Amit Varma with David Boaz
items.why: Amit's conversation with the late David Boaz, the audio companion to The Libertarian Mind, recommended as a tribute and a chance to hear Boaz work through the ideas himself.

items.title: What Is Populism?
items.creator: Jan-Werner Müller
items.why: Jan-Werner Müller's definitive frame: populism is not 'what is popular' but an anti-pluralist moral claim that only some of the people are the real people, and only the populist speaks for them.

items.title: What Is the Cost of One-Rank-One-Pension?
items.creator: Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
items.why: Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah's costing of One Rank One Pension, showing military pensions rising from 12% to 23% of the defence budget and crowding out modernisation, and Ajay's model of transparent analysis with open code and visible assumptions.

items.title: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us (Everything is Everything, episode 117)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' episode on what new data, from genomes to phones, reveals, so rich in findings that the material on men and women became an episode of its own.

items.title: What Really Happened?
items.creator: Lawrence H. White
items.why: Lawrence White's case that the 2008 crisis was a crisis of the state, not of capitalism, driven by distorted incentives from US housing policy, monetary policy and bailouts.

items.title: When Ideas Have Sex
items.creator: Matt Ridley
items.why: Matt Ridley's metaphor for progress: ideas generate progress only when they can collide and recombine freely, which Amit applies to contracting out research and to free speech.

items.title: Where Has All the Education Gone?
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: One of the most important papers in development economics, in which Pritchett demolished the post-1945 consensus that more schooling causes growth. When inputs pile up and outputs don't follow, the hosts' lesson is scepticism.

items.title: Where Have All the Leaders Gone?
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column arguing that incentives explain the calibre gap: the freedom struggle attracted people of principle because power was not the prize, while a centralised state full of rents attracts a different kind.

items.title: Wherever I Lay My Hat (That's My Home)
items.creator: Marvin Gaye
items.why: Marvin Gaye's masterpiece, the lyric behind Amit's answer to 'where is home?': wherever you are, and whatever you keep around you.

items.title: Who Lends to the Indian State?
items.creator: Aneesha Chitgupi, Ajay Shah, Manish K. Singh, Susan Thomas and Harsh Vardhan
items.why: Ajay's co-authored paper putting a number on financial repression: about 95% of the Indian state's borrowing is coerced out of the financial system, which is why India's debt looks deceptively benign.

items.title: Why Both Modi and Trump Are Textbook Populists
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Amit's column applying Müller's checklist to live politics on two continents: populism trades in emotionally potent, simplistic narratives such as foreigners taking your jobs.

items.title: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist (Everything is Everything, episode 88)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit's case for free speech, including Nehru's First Amendment and the claim that the Indian Constitution barely protects speech at all, and why legitimacy is impossible without a real marketplace of ideas.

items.title: Yuganta
items.creator: Irawati Karve
items.why: Irawati Karve's masterpiece of literary criticism on the Mahabharata's characters as fully human, misogyny and all, which doubles as an analysis of Indian society: what she wrote about the epic is, distressingly, still about us.

items.title: Zelensky playing the piano with his penis
items.creator: Volodymyr Zelensky
items.why: The clip from Zelensky's comedy career that the hosts allude to, for Ajay's serious point: 'It takes courage to fight Russians on a battlefield, but it also takes courage to make a fool of yourself on stage night after night.'

items.title: Independence Day
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Ajay's lead recommendation in the closing father-son cluster. He says the small-town despair, the conflict with family, the decision to leave and the loss of social network in the song are the universal Indian small-town story too — anyone moving from a mofussil to a metro can hear their own life inside it.

items.title: $800,000 to Zero: The Fascinating History of DaVinci Resolve
items.creator: YouTube documentary
items.why: The full story of how the most expensive piece of post-production software in the world became a free download — a parable of the democratisation of creative tools.

items.title: 100BeatlesX30
items.creator: The Pocket Gods
items.why: Companion piece to Sleepify. Same arbitrage, different jokes. Together they make the abstract argument visceral: form is whatever the algorithm pays for.

items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Amit calls it 'the future written in the past' — a masterpiece on the manipulation of truth, language, and history by authoritarian regimes that becomes more relevant as the technology of control improves.

items.title: 2,374 IAF Crashes. 1,305 Pilots Killed
items.creator: Ajai Shukla and Devesh Kapur
items.why: The numerical backbone of Ajay's argument that forced self-reliance has a body count. Worth reading to confront the human cost of bad procurement.

items.title: A Bridge Too Far
items.creator: Cornelius Ryan
items.why: Ajay invokes it as the cautionary case in his potted history of paratrooper warfare: a brilliant invasion plan that failed because the main force never reached the bridgehead.

items.title: A Brief History of Globalization
items.creator: Peter Vanham
items.why: Amit reads from this piece on the post-Columbian-Exchange transformation of the global diet ('Imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes...'). Useful as a one-page tour of the four phases.

items.title: A Business History of India
items.creator: Tirthankar Roy
items.why: Ajay's book pick of the week. The takeaway that struck him: how little has fundamentally changed in Indian business over a hundred and fifty years. Reading it left him with a new respect for entrepreneurs of a century ago. A book Ajay urges even people who 'have never read a book before' to read for the larger strategic sense.

items.title: A Christmas Carol
items.creator: Charles Dickens
items.why: If DDLJ's Amrish Puri is the modern Babuji-as-Scrooge, this is the original. Read it to see where the form lives in its purest form.

items.title: A Commentary on the UNIX Operating System
items.creator: John Lions
items.why: How Unix actually spread — universities all over the world received the source and a teacher who would walk students through it. The 'lingua franca' of operating-systems education for a generation.

items.title: A Conflict of Visions
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Foundational reading on why political disagreements aren't just about facts but about competing intuitions of what humans are. Amit recommends Sowell's work generally and is half-afraid to invite the man on his show out of reverence.

items.title: A Deregulatory Moment
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The longer-form companion to Ajay's argument in the episode — why this is the moment to move on the regulatory-theory agenda, what to demand, and how to think about sequencing.

items.title: A Dominant Character
items.creator: Samanth Subramanian
items.why: A beautifully written biography of a wild, eccentric genius who loved India enough to take Indian citizenship and refuse to wear socks. Captures both the spirit of mid-century scientific inquiry and the political radicalism of the man.

items.title: A Few Thoughts on Limericks
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: For readers wanting the technical case: a limerick isn't just A-A-B-B-A rhyming, it's a 9-9-6-6-9 syllable count. Form is what gives compression its punch — and why ChatGPT, which can't count, can't write them.

items.title: A First Course in Probability
items.creator: Sheldon Ross
items.why: Mentioned by Ajay as the rigorous companion to the cricket-and-poker conversation. For the reader willing to do the math under the intuitions discussed in the episode.

items.title: A Godless Congregation
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: An earlier articulation of Amit's position on atheism as absence-of-belief and the misunderstandings that surround the term.

items.title: A History of Global Health: Interventions into the Lives of Other Peoples
items.creator: Randall M. Packard
items.why: Public health is a field practically absent in India — what we have is health care and doctors trying to do health policy without having read this book. Packard's history is what gives you the long-run perspective on how interventions actually shape the lives of populations.

items.title: A History of Hinduism (Everything is Everything, episode 76)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Builds on Manu Pillai's framing of Hinduism as something far more open and assimilative than the Brahminical narrative the British inherited — context for why caste and religion in India had different historical paths.

items.title: A Life in Indian Politics (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 149)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
items.why: Source of the story that JP almost got proportional representation through the UPA government in the early 2000s — and that Sonia Gandhi vetoed it because she believed Congress would be in power forever under first-past-the-post.

items.title: A Moveable Feast
items.creator: Ernest Hemingway
items.why: Source of the Hemingway dictum Amit invokes at the end — that a good writing day is one on which you write one true sentence. Ajay reads 'true' as authentic to the moment, not factual.

items.title: A petty money dispute holds market to ransom
items.creator: Jayanth R. Varma
items.why: The contemporaneous account of the moment that re-taught Ajay Percy Mistry's lesson — that a financial centre can never have a payment failure, regardless of who is right and who is wrong.

items.title: A Poetry Handbook
items.creator: Mary Oliver
items.why: Amit's mid-episode recommendation on poetry. Not just the mechanics of poems, but the mechanics of language. 'You will fall in love with language all over again once you read this book.'

items.title: A Prehistory of Hinduism
items.creator: Manu Devadevan
items.why: Source of the line 'just as wearing cotton clothes, residing in a thatched hut or making love never produced identities like cotton wearer, thatched hut dweller, or love maker, so also the worshipping of Shiva or Vishnu did not confer identities' — central to the argument that pre-modern devotional practice wasn't an identity marker.

items.title: A Short Film About Killing
items.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
items.why: The other feature-length expansion from the Decalogue cycle. Recommended alongside *A Short Film About Love* as the second self-contained masterpiece spun out of the larger ten-film work.

items.title: A Short Film About Love
items.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
items.why: Contains the bicycle-in-the-courtyard scene that Amit uses to teach 'show don't tell' in his writing classes — a single shot that conveys, without dialogue, everything about a young man's first attempt at love. A masterclass in cinematic compression.

items.title: A Small-Sized Mystery
items.creator: Jane Hirshfield
items.why: Recommended in the spirit of the show — a quiet poem about the small mysteries of the world being one of the works that lives the 'everything is everything' frame.

items.title: A song from Pink Floyd's The Final Cut
items.creator: Roger Waters / Pink Floyd
items.why: The lines surfaced for Ajay while Amit was reading the Bourdain procrastination quote: 'There's a guy who had a big hallucination making love to girls in magazines. He wonders if you're sleeping with your newfound faith. Does anybody love you, or is it just a crazy dream?' Offered as a counterweight to the comfortable adult narrative — that the younger self had a different, hungrier dream.

items.title: A sustainable and scalable approach in Indian pension reform
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: A core paper from the period when the pension reforms community was still active, articulating the design and rationale of the NPS.

items.title: A Tale Of Two Bandits: Naxals And The Indian State
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Argues that in many Naxal-affected areas, both the state and the Naxalites have behaved as roving bandits — and in some pockets it was the Naxals who tried to settle in, tax sustainably, and provide services. Reframes the conflict from a law-and-order problem into a legitimacy problem.

items.title: A Venture Capitalist Looks at the World (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 213)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sajith Pai
items.why: Amit's source for the 'India is actually a small market' frame — Pai's argument that the real first-world Indian market is only 20-30 lakh people, the middle-income segment is about 10 crore, and the rest is sub-Saharan-Africa-poor.

items.title: Aadha Gaon
items.creator: Rahi Masoom Raza
items.why: Source of the 'Where is your Gangali?' question — a Muslim villager rejects the call to migrate to Pakistan because his idea of home is the village, not the religion. A masterclass in rooted, complicated, lived identity.

items.title: Abandon the Old in Tokyo
items.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
items.why: Includes 'My Beloved Monkey,' the story of a man whose pet monkey he releases into a zoo enclosure 'natural habitat' after losing his arm — and is forced to watch the other monkeys tear his pet to shreds. Brutal, unforgettable, ends in a way you have to read for yourself.

items.title: Accidental Politicians (Everything is Everything, episode 108)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Where Ajay laid out his love for Nehru as a 'great artist' even while believing his economic art was bad — the model for how to separate the man from the policy in evaluating high-modernist leaders.

items.title: Action produces information
items.creator: Brian Armstrong (reel)
items.why: Armstrong's three-word doctrine — 'action produces information' — and his metaphor of the foggy mountain: if you wait at the bottom for the fog to clear, you'll be at the bottom forever.

items.title: Activism and Wonkery Are the Yin and Yang
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Argues that activism — going to the streets, shouting, demanding change — is necessary but useless without 'wonkery,' the patient theoretical and conceptual work of building coherent policy. Social media has multiplied activists without multiplying wonks.

items.title: Adam Smith — A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: Smith is more than the invisible hand; the primer recovers the moral philosopher behind the economist.

items.title: Adaptive Political Economy: Toward a New Paradigm
items.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
items.why: Independent convergence on the same diagnosis — that development economics is searching where the light is rather than where the keys are. Ang will eventually be on The Seen and the Unseen after she finishes her current book.

items.title: Adriaan de Groot's chess study
items.creator: Adriaan de Groot
items.why: The famous result: they look the same number of moves ahead — what separates them is pattern recognition. Sets up Amit's contrast between Mr. B's calculation and Sultan Khan's positional sense.

items.title: Aella on Twitter
items.creator: Aella
items.why: A live counter-image to the standard Indian script for prostitution: agency, intellect and sex work can coexist openly. Amit cites her surveys as 'incredible' on data about gender relations.

items.title: Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: Cited as the rigorous test of whether affirmative-action policies actually help the people they were designed to help. Amit invokes it as the empirical counter to lazy assumptions on either side.

items.title: After the Gold Rush
items.creator: Neil Young
items.why: Listed in the show's resources as one of the musical references woven through the episode.

items.title: After Virtue
items.creator: Alasdair MacIntyre
items.why: The book that ambushed Amit on a tired night and made him jump out of bed the next morning to keep reading. Used here as the proof-of-concept story that real reading is fueled by joy and curiosity, not duty.

items.title: Ahimsa: 100 Reflections on the Harappan Civilization
items.creator: Devdutt Pattanaik
