items.why: Source of the reading of Harappan urban design as prioritising traders over raiders, and ahimsa as voluntary transaction between consenting adults — a framing Amit finds resonant with classical liberalism.

items.title: Ajay Shah on state capacity, governance and institutions (Episode 18 of Jack of All Knowledge)
items.creator: Ajay Shah on Jack of All Knowledge
items.why: The episode where the host's surprise question elicited Ajay's confession about turning down Kirit Parikh's apprenticeship offer — the seed of this episode's most personal anecdote.

items.title: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72, Brave New World)
items.creator: Ajay Shah on Vasant Dhar's Brave New World
items.why: A direct application of the public-goods definition: what India is selling as digital public goods are usually rival and excludable — i.e., not public goods at all. Ajay's case for technical rigour in language.

items.title: Ajay Shah's constitutional-law paper on why the Indian FRBM failed
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's test case for his rule on whether to bother writing a paper at all: if a prompt can produce it, publish the prompt instead. He could not get prompt-engineered LLMs to write this one, so it was worth writing.

items.title: Ajay Shah's conversation with Rahul Ahluwalia
items.creator: Rahul Ahluwalia with Ajay Shah
items.why: The longer companion conversation to this episode. Amit endorses Rahul as 'a great guy' and asks viewers to support his channel as a free thinker.

items.title: Ajay Shah's Mass Media Writings
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Another part of Ajay's deliberately built body of public work — referenced as fulfilling his 'responsibility' so he can decline lower-leverage outreach.

items.title: Ajay speaks out against Hydroponics
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Background to the conceptual bridge Ajay draws here: feeding chemical fertilizer to plants makes them mean to their root microbiome; feeding simple carbs to ourselves makes us mean to our gut microbiome.

items.title: Alan Turing's Life and Work
items.creator: various biographers
items.why: Engaging with Turing's story should 'reshape your moral calculus' — both the daily indignity of bad law and the exceptional lives it cuts short become viscerally legible.

items.title: Ali Abdaal's '1 Million Subscribers' video
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: The chart that crystallises why exponential growth feels like failure for a long time. Required viewing for any creator about to give up at video twelve.

items.title: Ali Abdaal's advice on the two-year rule
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: The source of Amit's pact with Ajay at the start of EIE: do this for two years without looking at the numbers. The reasoning that chasing validation early forces creators to dumb themselves down before they have found their voice.

items.title: Ali Abdaal's YouTube channel
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: Abdaal is living his own advice — he ground through 50 videos and 26 weeks before hitting 1,000 subscribers — which gives his advice on tools, mental models and frameworks unusual credibility. His parable of patience for creators is the heart of this episode.

items.title: Alice Evans Studies the Great Gender Divergence (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 297)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Alice Evans
items.why: Connects caste endogamy to the control of female sexuality — once you must police lineage, you must police women.

items.title: Alice in Wonderland
items.creator: Lewis Carroll
items.why: Alice goes to a strange world, returns transformed. Foundational Voyage-and-Return.

items.title: Alice Munro
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: Amit has talked about Munro's stories on the show before. Here he revisits her in light of the news about her daughter's abuse — saying he will continue to love the work and withhold judgment on the person, because the world is too complex.

items.title: AliExpress
items.creator: Alibaba Group
items.why: 'Gentle reader, if you have not used AliExpress, you should.' Recommended in the context of Ajay's argument that India's recent arrival of cheap manufactured plenty is what made decluttering a problem here in the first place — but also that the bounty enables consumer-surplus experimentation.

items.title: Alone in the City
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The piece that connects the loneliness of urban life to the housing policies that make cities harder to enter. A more humane way into a topic usually argued in graphs.

items.title: AlphaDev Discovers Faster Sorting Algorithms
items.creator: DeepMind
items.why: The companion piece to the matrix-multiplication result: a second proof of concept that gamification + RL can find improvements in algorithms so fundamental that humans had stopped looking for them.

items.title: Amitava Kumar Finds the Breath of Life (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 265)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Amitava Kumar
items.why: Source of the Aadha Gaon anecdote about the village of Gangali — the seed of Amit's recurring 'Where is your Gangali?' question to his guests.

items.title: Amused to Death
items.creator: Roger Waters
items.why: A musical meditation on the same diagnosis: that mass entertainment is hollowing out the capacity for serious public attention. The pairing of book and album is the recommendation.

items.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death
items.creator: Neil Postman
items.why: Prophetic about what TV news became and predicts the trajectory of every screen-mediated public square. Roger Waters reportedly read this book and wrote the album Amused to Death directly in response.

items.title: An Act of War: Inside America's Silicon Blockade Against China
items.creator: Alex W. Palmer
items.why: The clearest exposition of how extreme US export controls have become — Amit reads from it to show that even items 'made and shipped outside the United States' with no US components can be classified as American and blocked.

items.title: An Adman Reflects on Society & the Self (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 199)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ambi Parameswaran
items.why: Source of the killer line that online advertising is 'pray and spray' — and that what's happening online as advertisers is 'a scandal.' Indispensable counter to the assumption that digital ad spend is rational.

items.title: An American Tail
items.creator: Don Bluth
items.why: Source of the joke 'there are no cats in America and the streets are paved with cheese' — used to mock the myth of a lost golden age. The streets were never paved with cheese.

items.title: An Annotated Reading List on Indian Bankruptcy
items.creator: The Leap Journal
items.why: A self-guided syllabus for serious readers who want to do the work rather than just talk about it.

items.title: An Area of Darkness
items.creator: V.S. Naipaul
items.why: Cited as the source of Naipaul's famous line that Gandhi was 'the least Indian of the Indian leaders' — anchoring Amit's case that Gandhi's influences (Tolstoy, Ruskin, the London Vegetarian Society) were random and atypical, unlike the Mill-Bentham-Smith reading of Naoroji, Gokhale, Agarkar, and Pherozeshah Mehta.

items.title: An Economic Theory of Democracy
items.creator: Anthony Downs
items.why: The book that introduced Amit to the concept of rational ignorance — why voters logically choose to remain uninformed when their individual vote has near-zero probability of being decisive.

items.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
items.creator: Thomas Robert Malthus
items.why: The seminal mistake. Amit notes Malthus actually wrote that 'instead of recommending cleanliness to the poor, we should encourage contrary habits and court the return of the plague' — because for Malthus the plague would be 'deliverance.' Read it to understand where the rot started.

items.title: An important change of course by policy in Indian Covid-19 vaccination
items.creator: Amrita Agarwal and Ajay Shah
items.why: Walks through what India got right and wrong in opening up vaccine procurement, and the moment the policy stance changed for the better.

items.title: An Interview with Mike Kofman
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: The interview where Kofman articulated the key reframing — that the invasion succeeding (not just the occupation) was the surprise; everyone expected occupation to fail, but no one expected invasion to fail. Source of one of the conceptual moves at the heart of this episode.

items.title: An Ode to Perun (and Orry)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The longer-form version of Amit's enthusiasm for Perun — and the contrast with the prevailing celebrity-shallow culture of social media.

items.title: Anais Nin tweet — 'We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.'
items.creator: Anais Nin (shared by Nella, @GG_dreamer)
items.why: The opening provocation of the episode — used to argue that perception is necessarily filtered through who we are, even when objective reality is shared.

items.title: Analysing India's KYC Framework through the Privacy Lens
items.creator: Vrinda Bhandari, Rishab Bailey and Trishee Goyal
items.why: First entry on Ajay's reading list — the foundational scholarly text for anyone wanting to understand how Indian KYC reads against the Putaswamy ruling and the constitutional right to privacy.

items.title: Analysing India's KYC Framework: Can We Do Things Better?
items.creator: Rishab Bailey, Trishee Goyal, Renuka Sane and Ridhi Varma
items.why: The companion piece on Ajay's list — for the constructive question of what a saner Indian KYC architecture might look like.

items.title: Anatomy of a Folly
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The longer write-up behind his recommendation. Linked from the show notes as the place to read his argument about editing, simplification, and complexity in cinema.

items.title: Andaz Apna Apna
items.why: Confusion and mistaken identities resolved into joy — a Bollywood instance of the Booker comedy structure.

items.title: Andrew Doyle's tweet on Kemi Badenoch's grilling
items.creator: Andrew Doyle
items.why: Source of Amit's anecdote about cultural shows being weaponised politically. Doyle is described by Amit as 'a great free speech thinker' — the tweet itself is the entry-point for the longer point about the absurdity of treating Netflix as a political litmus test.

items.title: Animal Farm
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: A brilliant satire of how revolutions are betrayed and how power corrupts — the dynamics of political decay rendered with cruel clarity.

items.title: Anora
items.creator: Sean Baker
items.why: Amit cites it as further evidence we are in 'a golden age of cinema.' The last 20-25 minutes are 'just so masterful, so masterful. Just brilliant.' Two decades ago the Oscar often went to mainstream pap; now genuinely great films are winning.

items.title: Answering Machine
items.creator: The Replacements
items.why: A poignant museum-piece of a lyric: the kind of pathos available only when the answering machine still existed as a felt object — and a line whose pathos is now lost on a generation that has never seen one.

items.title: Anthony Bourdain on procrastination
items.creator: Anthony Bourdain
items.why: The most honest description Amit has read of his own daily fight. The guy in your head dwarfs you; your life is the strategy by which you are not him.

items.title: Anupam Manur's piece on the Bangalore water crisis
items.creator: Anupam Manur
items.why: The counterintuitive case for water pricing as a pro-poor reform: the rich currently capture far more than their share of underpriced water; pricing it would reallocate it away from waste and end the shortages.

items.title: Applied Economics
items.creator: Thomas Sowell
items.why: The natural follow-up to Basic Economics for readers who want to see how the same intuitions explain real-world outcomes.

items.title: Arati Kumar-Rao Took a One-Way Ticket (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 383)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Arati Kumar-Rao
items.why: The conversation that surfaced the desert-dwellers'-maps-of-bird-flight image and the broader argument that abstract cartography buries lived, ecological geographies.

items.title: Aravind Srinivas speaks of Larry Page
items.creator: Aravind Srinivas
items.why: The customer-as-always-right story that snapped Srinivas out of correcting his own mother's search grammar — and the same lesson Amit asks every founder to absorb.

items.title: Ardh Satya
items.creator: Govind Nihalani
items.why: Cited as proof of Nihalani's stature — the kind of director one assumes any industry would back, and yet he could not get funding for an independent project in 2010.

items.title: Are all calories created equal? Your gut microbes don't think so.
items.creator: Anahad O'Connor, The Washington Post
items.why: Accessible journalistic version of the gut-microbiome calorimetry findings.

items.title: Army and Nation
items.creator: Steven I. Wilkinson
items.why: Amit discovered this while preparing his Prakash Menon episode and praises it as a nuanced history that explains why India's military has remained apolitical when so many post-colonial militaries did not.

items.title: Arrival
items.creator: Denis Villeneuve
items.why: An example of what Amit calls a golden age of mainstream cinema — a director keeping his identity and bringing intellectual concepts onto the big-budget screen. The film that hooked Amit on Villeneuve.

items.title: Arshia Sattar and the Complex Search for Dharma (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 315)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Arshia Sattar
items.why: Companion reading to the discussion of the epics as 'open-source' rivers rather than fixed scriptures.

items.title: As You Like It
items.creator: William Shakespeare
items.why: If you want a clean Booker comedy: confusion, mistaken identities, dispelled shadows, joyful reunion.

items.title: ASER Reports
items.creator: ASER Centre
items.why: The single most important data infrastructure in Indian education. Ajay calls the philanthropic capital that funded ASER the most effective use of philanthropic money he has ever seen — it changed how thinking people frame the problem.

items.title: Ash Joglekar (Curious Wave Function) tweet on solitary hobbies
items.creator: Ashutosh Joglekar
items.why: Catalysed the episode's discussion on the importance of being alone with oneself — and the modern problem that even when alone, we are consumed in some black screen.

items.title: Ask Me ANYTHING! (Everything is Everything, episode 50)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The natural companion piece to this one — the halfway-point AMA, a fifty-episode-earlier version of the same exercise.

items.title: Aspects of the Novel
items.creator: E. M. Forster
items.why: A great novelist's window into how novels actually work — tools for reading novels more deeply.

items.title: Astral Weeks
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: The result is an absolute masterpiece — deeply moving songs whose final form Morrison did not control and initially resented, but came to recognise as a masterpiece. Decades later, when he toured with Davis again, Davis (a jazz musician) refused to replay it identically — proof that the original was a one-time miracle of improvisation.

items.title: Atlantic City
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit notes Springsteen had originally intended to record it with the full E Street Band; a note to Landau even said 'get the band, rock-and-roll sound.' They tried, it didn't work, and what was released was the stripped demo. The whole Nebraska story, Amit argues, is the story of accepting that a polished version can lose what a rough one had.

items.title: Atomic Chess and Fog of War
items.why: Variants strip away your trained heuristics and pattern recognition, forcing you to work out a correct way to play from first principles. The intellectual thrill of a beginner, recovered. Amit was briefly world #1 on chess.com in a couple of these formats.

items.title: Aubrey
items.creator: Bread
items.why: Ajay's reach for an underrated 70s gem from a band most listeners have written off — recommended specifically because Bread has been culturally erased.

items.title: Autumn Passage to the Himalaya
items.creator: Harish Kapadia
items.why: Ajay calls it one of the lovely books and essential reading for anyone interested in the Himalayas — a continuation of the spell that Trek The Sahyadris cast on him decades earlier.

items.title: Back to the Future
items.why: Marty travels, has the trip, returns — the classic form in a sci-fi wrapper.

items.title: Backstreets
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit tells the story of Springsteen, after learning the editing discipline from Landau, almost cutting Bittan's piano interludes and Landau saving him from himself. He quotes Greil Marcus's review describing the opening as 'so stately, so heartbreaking, that it might be the prelude to a rock and roll version of the Iliad,' and says it captures the song's intimate-yet-epic quality.

items.title: Bad
items.creator: U2
items.why: Part of Ajay's pair from a 1984 U2 album he loves — a continuation of his ongoing campaign to convince younger listeners to dig past Joshua Tree into the earlier, more atmospheric U2.

items.title: Bad Science
items.creator: Ben Goldacre
items.why: The book Amit reaches for to teach the discipline of double-blind randomised controlled trials — why a medicine must beat placebo, not just nothing.

items.title: Basic facts about the map (NYT visual explainer on Robotyne)
items.creator: The New York Times
items.why: If the Bakhmut/Zaporizhia/Crimea geography in this episode is hard to picture, this is the cleanest visual primer.

items.title: Beat a Drum
items.creator: R.E.M.
items.why: The source of the show's central metaphor — 'halfway from coal, halfway to diamond' — for the human condition as a work in progress.

items.title: Beautiful Boy
items.creator: John Lennon
items.why: Amit reaches for the line to capture the limits of agency — that we should not exaggerate our capacity to curate our circumstances. The show notes also point to a Paul McCartney video listening to the song and remembering John, recommended as a tender artefact.

items.title: Beauty and the Beast (1991 film)
items.creator: Walt Disney Animation
items.why: The cultural anchor for the joke about people who need pictures in their books — and a sly reminder that engaging with the world via imagination versus literal-mindedness is a choice with consequences.

items.title: Beauty and the Beast (fairy tale)
items.why: The Beast's transformation through love is the canonical fairy-tale rebirth.

items.title: Behave
items.creator: Robert Sapolsky
items.why: Recommended alongside the lectures as a long-form companion to the Sapolsky course.

items.title: Ben Wolff's X thread on Ritz-Carlton
items.creator: Ben Wolff
items.why: The original source where Amit first encountered the chain of incidents — the laptop flown to Hawaii, the wedding ring on the Cancun beach, Thomas the Tank Engine's spa treatment — that illustrate empowered customer service.

items.title: Beowulf
items.why: If you want to see how ancient the monster-slaying story is, go to its source. Booker draws a direct comparison between Beowulf and Jaws.

items.title: Beta Tumse Na Ho Payega
items.creator: Anurag Kashyap (Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2)
items.why: Amit invokes the line as a Bollywood capture of the disconnect between a strategising big brain at HQ and a local manager 'who really kind of doesn't get it.'

items.title: Beware of Quacks. Alternative Medicine Is Injurious to Health
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: His own argument for being deeply sceptical (but never dismissive) of tradition — including the mechanisms of reversion to the mean, confirmation bias and placebo that keep quackery alive.

items.title: Bezos interviewed by Lex Fridman
items.creator: Lex Fridman with Jeff Bezos
items.why: Where the 'disagree but commit' practice is laid out at length — argue freely, but once a decision is made, commit fully and never throw 'I told you so' at it later.

items.title: Bezos on Akio Morita
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Source of the 'mission bigger than yourself' framing — Morita's 'make Japan known for quality again' as the template for non-trivial company purpose.

items.title: Bezos on business plans
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: The plan is worthless; the act of writing 30 pages is priceless. It clarifies the thinking, surfaces unknowns, forces the long-term frame.

items.title: Bezos on professional pride
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Most of what you do is never seen by a customer — so the only honest motivator for excellence in those moments is pride. 'How you do the small things is how you do the big things.'

items.title: Bezos on truth-telling
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Humans evolved to get along, not to tell the truth — so an organisation has to actively build mechanisms (disagree-and-commit, etc.) that override the social instinct.

items.title: Bezos on Work-Life Harmony
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Work and life shouldn't be in zero-sum tension; you go where the energy is, and energy in one feeds the other. Reframes 'balance' as a category mistake.

items.title: Bhagavad Gita — duty without attachment to fruits
items.creator: Vyasa (traditional)
items.why: Ajay invokes it to marry purpose with happiness — you are obliged to try, but you don't control external outcomes; distancing from the fruit is what saves a purposeful life from being a miserable one.

items.title: Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah and Ajay Shah on capital-account convertibility
items.creator: Bhargavi Zaveri and Ajay Shah
items.why: The myth-busting reading for anyone who believed the 1993 announcement that India had achieved current-account convertibility. Reading the actual rules destroys the press-release version of the story.

items.title: Bhatiali Dhun
items.creator: Jaya Bose and Himangshu Biswas
items.why: Ajay had assumed his love for it was nostalgia, then on returning to it years later concluded it is genuinely great music, not mere sentiment — a useful filter for distinguishing nostalgia from quality.

items.title: Bill Gates and David Letterman on the internet
items.creator: David Letterman (interview)
items.why: Letterman's incredulous skepticism — treating the internet as a curiosity — is the perfect period artefact for the way mainstream commentary misreads transformative technology in real time.

items.title: Bill Gates and Warren Buffett on the best advice they got
items.creator: Gates and Buffett (interview)
items.why: Both Gates and Buffett, asked separately, name 'focus' as the most important quality they share. Source of the Buffett 'empty calendar' anecdote.

items.title: Bill Joy biography (Britannica)
items.creator: Encyclopedia Britannica
items.why: A quick way in for listeners to understand the kind of magnetic engineering presence that gave Sun the confidence and recruiting power to attempt the SPARC leap. Amit's aside: 'What a great name, Bill Joy — who can not like a guy with a name like that?'

items.title: Bimal Patel's forthcoming book on town planning
items.creator: Bimal Patel
items.why: Ajay reveals the secret that Bimal Patel is working on a book. When it comes out, run, not walk. Patel gets town planning in a way that essentially nobody else in India does.

items.title: Birds Aren't Real? How a Conspiracy Takes Flight
items.creator: Peter McIndoe
items.why: The full account of the most elegant reductio of how a conspiracy theory propagates — and why it's harder than ever to tell satire from sincerity in the post-truth landscape.

items.title: Blade Runner
items.creator: Ridley Scott
items.why: Acknowledged as a masterpiece, and Scott himself was one of Christopher Nolan's inspirations — closing the loop between the auteurs Amit admires in mainstream cinema.

items.title: Blankets
items.creator: Craig Thompson
items.why: Listed as one of the graphic novels Amit deeply loves and uses as evidence that the form belongs alongside the best of literature.

items.title: Bollywood Masala and a French Art Film
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Linked in the show notes alongside this episode's themes — Amit's larger framing of world cinema versus mass-market spectacle.

items.title: Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna
items.creator: Ludwig Boltzmann
items.why: Ajay's 'oddball' recommendation of the episode: visit it. The tombstone vindicates a man who hanged himself in 1906 and was proven right within years — a physical monument to the cost and the eventual victory of the scientific outlaw.

items.title: Bonnie and Clyde
items.why: Two protagonists, lured into criminality, falling toward death — the modern American tragedy.

items.title: Born a Muslim
items.creator: Ghazala Wahab
items.why: Used as the live demo for Amit's Roam workflow, showing how he extracts and links chapter-level notes. The 'shelling pine nuts' image of her grandfather is held up as a gold-standard example of show-don't-tell writing.

items.title: Born in the U.S.A.
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit's example of how surface and content can be at odds — a protest song about a damaged veteran that conservatives heard as a flag-waving anthem. He uses it to introduce Springsteen's habit of writing convincingly inside lives that aren't his.

items.title: Born to Run (memoir)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit's main recommendation of the episode. He treats it as literature in its own right — Springsteen analysing his own depression, his father, his craft, his band — with the same lyric power as the songs. The chapters on the rented childhood guitar, on first seeing the cover of Meet the Beatles, and on his decision to be 'an ancestor' rather than a ghost, are mined throughout the conversation.

items.title: Born to Run (song and album)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Discussed at length as Springsteen's signal of artistic intent. Ajay says the album version didn't reach him at first; the stripped-down acoustic live version, just Springsteen with guitar and harmonica, was what cracked it open. He also notes the album's deliberate architecture — Born to Run opens side A, Thunder Road closes it, Jungleland anchors side B.

items.title: Botany of Desire
items.creator: Michael Pollan
items.why: Source of the unforgettable account of Pollan's son Isaac's first taste of sugar at his birthday cake — an 'ecstasy in the literal sense' that he was 'beside himself with the pleasure of, no longer here with me in space and time.'

items.title: Both Sides Now
items.creator: Joni Mitchell
items.why: The source of the title 'But Clouds Got in My Way' (paraphrasing the lyric 'But now they only block the sun / They rain and snow on everyone'). Ajay calls out to Joni Mitchell fans to listen.

items.title: Brave New World — Jonathan Haidt episode
items.creator: Vasant Dhar with Jonathan Haidt
items.why: Recommended for Haidt's research on the link between social media and teenage depression, especially among girls — a key empirical leg of Amit's complicated verdict on social media.

items.title: Breaking Out
items.creator: Padma Desai
items.why: The autobiography of an economist who studied the Soviet Union for years, co-authored a seminal 1968 critique of the Indian state with Jagdish Bhagwati, and converted to Christianity to escape an abusive marriage and marry the love of her life. Doubly remarkable for being a woman in that era.

items.title: Breaking Through
items.creator: Isher Judge Ahluwalia
items.why: The story of a Hindi-medium girl from a Marwari school in Calcutta becoming one of India's finest economists. Amit calls it lovely; he regrets that he kept it on the shelf and never invited her on the show before she passed away.

items.title: Brian Chesky on co-founder relationships
items.creator: Brian Chesky
items.why: Source of Amit's favourite line: 'winning the argument is not as important as preserving the relationship.' The structural reason ego-driven founders break apart.

items.title: Brian Chesky on Graham's advice
items.creator: Brian Chesky (clip)
items.why: Source of the Chesky-with-the-camera anecdote — concrete proof that the love of a hundred customers is more valuable than the indifference of a million.

items.title: Brighter Than a Thousand Suns
items.creator: Robert Jungk
items.why: The book that planted Oppenheimer in Ajay's imagination as a child and that he returned to many times. Foundational for any reader who wants to understand the Manhattan Project from the biographical side, before Rhodes existed.

items.title: Brilliant Disguise
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit reads it as a textbook lesson in turning the gaze. The song asks whether the lover is really there, then by the last verse asks whether the singer himself is — a study in the masks we wear and the trust we cannot find even in ourselves.

items.title: Brown Eyed Girl
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: Recommended as the source of the lovely linguistic artefact 'transistor' as shorthand for portable radio — a fossil of a vanished era when the transistor was synonymous with miniaturised modernity. Amit calls the song itself a bit cheesy but worth knowing for the cultural fragment.

items.title: Bruce Springsteen: All the Songs
items.creator: Philippe Margotin and Jean-Michel Guesdon
items.why: Amit's other top recommendation of the episode and a gift he had given Ajay. Its value is that it tells the story behind every single song — useful precisely because Springsteen's catalogue is so deep that even devoted fans have only scratched the surface.

items.title: Building a Second Brain
items.creator: Tiago Forte
items.why: Names the central problem of modern reading: 'all day we are taking in learnings that we do not retain.' Forte's framework gives you a way to externalise and reuse what would otherwise wash through you.

items.title: Building State Capability
items.creator: Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
items.why: Source of the striking finding that during India's great growth episode (1991-2011) state capability actually got worse, even as GDP soared — demonstrating that growth and state quality can run in opposite directions.

items.title: Building the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
items.creator: MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain
items.why: Ajay's exhibit for how Indian institutions should be built. Reading it shows that the knowledge exists; the challenge is using it instead of notifying laws and wishing five people into a working agency overnight.

items.title: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid
items.creator: George Roy Hill
items.why: An offhand recommendation closing an episode about the death of firms — a film about the romance and finality of running out of road.

items.title: Caesar and Cleopatra
items.creator: George Bernard Shaw
items.why: The line — 'a barbarian is one who thinks the customs of his own tribe are the laws of nature' — anchors the episode's warning against ethnocentrism.

items.title: Can Economics Become More Reflexive?
items.creator: Vijayendra Rao
items.why: One of the two papers the episode is built around. The four lessons (cognitive empathy, taking words seriously, paying attention to process, treating subjects as participants) are the spine of the conversation, and the paper itself is a compressed and rich illustration of the everything-is-everything thesis.

items.title: Can Men and Women Be Just Friends?
items.creator: The Economist
items.why: Where the 'WIMSY' framing is laid out — including India's surprisingly high score of 0.35.

items.title: Capital Account Openness in India and a Comparison with China: Then versus Now
items.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: Important comparative work showing how the two large Asian economies diverge in their openness to foreign capital, and what India can learn — even after China's recent retreat under Xi.

items.title: Carnage and Culture
items.creator: Victor Davis Hanson
items.why: Ajay calls it 'a very disturbing book' that he doesn't agree with entirely, but believes everybody should read — the rare combination of provocation and depth that forces clarification of one's own views.

items.title: Cathedral
items.creator: Raymond Carver
items.why: Amit calls it a masterpiece — minimalist, elegant, and a gateway to Carver's full body of work. He frames the digression as 'payments for the soul, Ajesha, these are payments for the soul.'

items.title: CDC Adult Immunization Schedule
items.creator: U.S. CDC
items.why: Ajay's actionable recommendation — the show's argument is not abstract; go look up the schedule and get the vaccines. Approval by the US FDA is a high bar (Ajay thinks too high) but that makes it a global public good — the rest of the world should ride on the testing they have already done.

items.title: Chandrahas Choudhury's Country of Literature (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 288)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Chandrahas Choudhury
items.why: The show's living example that letter-style correspondence is still possible in 2024, and that an email can rise to the standard of long-form writing if you choose.

items.title: Chapter 1 of Rising to the China Challenge
items.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade and Ajay Shah
items.why: A no-cost on-ramp for readers who want the framing of the China problem before committing to the full book.

items.title: Chariots of the Gods
items.creator: Erich von Daniken
items.why: Cited (anti-recommended) by Ajay as a perfect example of the unfalsifiable end of the spectrum — fanciful claims that produce no testable propositions, the opposite of evolutionary biology's rich predictive content.

items.title: Charlie Munger
items.creator: Charlie Munger
items.why: Munger's lattice-of-mental-models approach is itself the canonical entry point. Worth reading whichever of his speeches and compilations you can find.

items.title: Charter 77
items.creator: Václav Havel and co-signatories
items.why: Worth reading directly, both for its content and as the document where Havel told a hesitant signatory: 'You have already taken a side, just not the one you think you have.'

items.title: Chernobyl
items.creator: HBO
items.why: Recommended by Amit as a powerful audiovisual companion to the historical record. The series is, in Ajay's framing, a 'textbook delineation of how a big oppressive state inevitably fails' — the lesson is about Soviet authoritarianism's distortion of decision-making, not about nuclear power itself.

items.title: Chess Base India
items.creator: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal
items.why: A pure labor of love: Sagar would go to obscure tournaments, talk to players, analyse games to almost no audience. During COVID it exploded (helped by comedian Samay Raina collaborating). The 90-minute deep-dive interview with Gukesh after he won the candidates is exemplary. 'Every chess fan in India really appreciates' what Sagar and Amruta do for the ecosystem.

items.title: ChessBase India report on Gukesh's win, with Game 14 analysis by Rafael Leitao
items.why: If you want to actually see the position drift Amit describes — the bishop ending on a8, the king moving two squares — this is the reference.

items.title: chickenhappyhour
items.creator: Instagram account
items.why: Used as a comic example of the shallow distraction Kindle apps must out-compete. Amit insists the videos are genuinely 'mind-blowing' and asks for them to be linked in the show notes.

items.title: Child Labor in the Global Economy
items.creator: Eric V. Edmonds and Nina Pavcnik
items.why: A third complementary study cited by Amit, reinforcing the empirical case that growth — not bans — is what reduces child labour.

items.title: Chimes of Freedom (Springsteen cover)
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Cited as evidence that Dylan's songs are rich enough for great covers, but also that the originals are sometimes irreplaceable.

items.title: China's Future
items.creator: David Shambaugh
items.why: Ajay's single-book recommendation on China. In 2016 it ran against the prevailing China-as-rising-superpower consensus; the seven years since have been extraordinarily kind to its diagnosis. It effectively predicts everything that happened from 2016 to 2023.

items.title: China's Gilded Age
items.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
items.why: The darker complement to How China Escaped the Poverty Trap — examines the role of corruption and the evolving political economy that shaped the Chinese miracle, completing a more honest picture of what happened.

items.title: Chintaman and I
items.creator: Durgabai Deshmukh
items.why: Out of print on Kindle and hard to find anywhere; Amit located a free copy on the internet and links it from the show notes. A first-person window into a remarkable woman who walked out of a child marriage at fourteen and later married one of independent India's most cultured public servants.

items.title: Chip War
items.creator: Chris Miller
items.why: The definitive book for understanding the origins and current stakes of the global tech competition — the intricate supply chains, the strategic importance of chips, and the historical arc that led to today's export controls.

items.title: Chocolate by Manam
items.creator: Manam Chocolate (Hyderabad)
items.why: Pure indulgence pick. Ajay clarifies it is unsponsored — 'Manam chocolate is awesome.'

items.title: Chris Horner Cycling (YouTube channel)
items.creator: Chris Horner
items.why: After every major race Horner records his post-stage take, calling out tactical errors with his trademark 'knuckleheads' framing. He doesn't just call the action — he teaches you how to think about it, which makes the whole sport richer to watch.

items.title: Cicada
items.creator: Shaun Tan
items.why: A marvellous, haunting book about alienation, the corporate/bureaucratic grind, and the possibility of transcendence. Amit normally doesn't recommend many books, but this one — borrowed from his editor Nomsita — is one he just says: look, trust me, read it.

items.title: Citizens Jain
items.creator: Ken Auletta
items.why: The piece in which Vineet Jain famously says 'we are not in the news business, we are in the advertising business.' The single most efficient way to understand what India's largest newspaper actually optimizes for.

items.title: Classical Liberalism — A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: Amit's argument: most of the ideas we absorb by osmosis when young are wrong but feel virtuous (the soft socialism of 'social justice' that quietly relies on state coercion). Butler's primers are an antidote — short, free, and crystal-clear introductions to the ideas Amit has spent his career writing about. 'These books are an education, and it is a miracle that they are free.'

items.title: Climate Change for Practical People
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The longer version of the climate-and-land-markets argument — why a liquid land market is climate adaptation.

items.title: Code 2.0
items.creator: Lawrence Lessig
items.why: Picks up the episode's central image — that we live 'in the shadow of the law' — and shows how every word of a statute, every line of code, is doing work to constrain or enable human action. Every word in a bankruptcy code matters.

items.title: Collected Poems
items.creator: Mark Strand
items.why: Strand's last book, Almost Invisible, is a masterpiece — little prose poems, almost a paragraph each — and it is included in the collected hardback. Amit means it personally: 'sometimes I feel that you know you read that book, you'll feel like you know a part of me.'

items.title: Common Sense
items.creator: Thomas Paine
items.why: Origin of the phrase that captures the 'great liberal paradox' — for our rights to have meaning we must surrender some of them to a state that will protect them, while always remembering that the state does this through coerced taxation and a monopoly on violence.

items.title: Communism
items.creator: Richard Pipes
items.why: A slim entry point into the actual horrors of communism in practice — connecting the journey from idea to action to consequences. A useful corrective for anyone tempted by the theory.

items.title: Concerns About Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI): An Indian Perspective
items.creator: University of Navarra and XKDR Forum
items.why: Ajay points to it as a wake-up call: Indians read about hybrid warfare in the Baltic Sea and Australia, but don't realise foreign actors are heavily active in India too. The paper assembles the evidence.

items.title: Conflict
items.creator: David Petraeus and Andrew Roberts
items.why: Amit's pick — a book he had originally hoped to anchor a 'history of war' episode around. He calls the authors 'a great historian and a general and very fine thinker' and the book a strong base for understanding how war has evolved into the world Ajay describes.

items.title: Conflict in Ukraine: A timeline (2014 – present)
items.creator: Nigel Walker (House of Commons Library)
items.why: A clean, sourced timeline for anyone who wants to grasp the arc from the 2014 Crimea grab through to today.

items.title: Consciousness Explained
items.creator: Daniel Dennett
items.why: Part of the popular-science canon through which Amit, the literature-and-arts person, came to natural selection as a master frame for understanding human nature.

items.title: Conversation and Society (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 182)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Russ Roberts
items.why: Ajay's pointer for listeners who want to dive into Smith's moral philosophy via Roberts.

items.title: Conversations with Tyler
items.creator: Tyler Cowen
items.why: The polar-opposite school to Amit's, and a great podcast precisely for that reason. Cowen produces questions Amit says someone like him is not even capable of formulating, then moves crisply through them — a different kind of intellectual seriousness, also worth studying.

items.title: Cooking the world's oldest known curry
items.creator: Soity Banerjee
items.why: Sets up the punchline that the only ingredient recognisable in a 4,000-year-old Indus Valley meal is brinjal — almost everything else came later from somewhere else.

items.title: Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice
items.creator: David Galula
items.why: The foundational text. Source of the fly-and-lion metaphor and the five-step framework: concentrate force to push insurgents out, hold the area, make contact with the people and earn their trust, destroy the insurgent political organisation and replace it with a legitimate one, mop up the remnants. Every later counterinsurgency thinker is in conversation with Galula.

items.title: Court
items.creator: Chaitanya Tamhane
items.why: The third in Amit's pantheon of all-time-great debut films alongside Pather Panchali and The Lives of Others — bracketed with these to underscore how much he rates The Lives of Others.

items.title: Covid-19 in the tropics: How will high heat and humidity shape the outcomes?
items.creator: Suja Thomas
items.why: Ajay's exemplar of work that nobody outside India will do: how COVID transmits in Indian homes, with their cross-ventilation, fans, heat and humidity. The kind of question that demonstrates why a country needs its own research capability even in a free-riding age.

items.title: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
items.creator: Ila Patnaik
items.why: Ajay's go-to text for the argument that job loss in a creatively destructive market economy is mostly not a crisis: India's millions of displaced STD-booth workers found other work, and the country is the better for it.

items.title: Crime Victimisation in India
items.creator: Ajay Shah and co-editors
items.why: Context for the survey question Ajay cites — what time parents say their teenage daughter is allowed home — as a measure of female empowerment and perceived public-space safety.

items.title: Cross-Border Activities in India Need More Freedom, Not Less
items.creator: Pratik Datta and Ajay Shah
items.why: Direct prescription for the policy person in this episode: the Indian state's instinct that 'foreign engagement is suspicious' is a major drag on firm productivity, and the solution is liberalisation, not more compliance theatre.

items.title: Crowds and Power
items.creator: Elias Canetti
items.why: Ajay's recommended companion to thinking about why simplistic economic narratives win — they mobilise crowds. Connects the seen-and-unseen problem to the political economy of rage.

items.title: CRRao.jl
items.creator: Sourish Das, XKDR Forum, Chennai Mathematical Institute
items.why: Named after C.R. Rao as a commitment device to do the work right. Ajay believes a uniform Bayesian-first calling convention is what serious data science needs, and that Julia is the right substrate for it.

items.title: Cycling monument (Wikipedia)
items.why: A clean reference for anyone wanting to pin down what Amit means by 'cycling monuments' and why those particular five matter.

items.title: Dancing in the Dark
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Discussed as the perfect demonstration of upbeat synth-pop carrying lyrics about creative exhaustion and self-loathing. Amit calls it Springsteen's defiant retort to the demand for a hit: 'fuck it, you want a hit, I'll write you a hit' — and the resulting song is also a confession of the very depression that produced it.

items.title: Daniel Hannan's Tweet on the Left and Compassion
items.creator: Daniel Hannan
items.why: Hannan's framing: the defining characteristic of the left is not compassion but the conviction that compassion is unique to its side, leading to a grotesque misunderstanding of what the other side thinks.

items.title: Danish Husain and the Multiverse of Culture (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 359)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Danish Husain
items.why: The episode where Suvinder Vicky's earlier work in Milestone was discussed — establishing him in Amit's mind as the perfect actor for Montek in the proposed series.

items.title: Darkness at Noon
items.creator: Arthur Koestler
items.why: A book that 'changed the world' — its electrifying portrait of Soviet show trials helped tip France's 1946 elections away from communism. Ajay calls it part of the mid-20th-century battle of ideas alongside Orwell, Camus, Friedman, Hayek and Stigler. He recommends reading both Hardy's 1940 translation and the 2015 translation of the rediscovered German original.

items.title: Darkness on the Edge of Town
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit reads this as Springsteen's purest statement of his own creed of hard work and risk — beautiful, simple language, every listener placing themselves on that hill. The album is also, in his framing, the moment Springsteen reaches lyrical greatness and never loses it.

items.title: DARPA
items.creator: United States Department of Defense
items.why: Ajay's only example of a government funder that works fantastically well. Worth knowing about because most government research funding (especially in India) is captured by cronies; DARPA is what is possible when state capacity exists for meritocratic risk-taking.

items.title: Darwin's Dangerous Idea
items.creator: Daniel Dennett
items.why: The book behind Ajay's opening line that evolutionary theory is a universal acid that strips away simple preconceptions and takes you a level deeper on the dynamics of the world.

items.title: Das Kapital
items.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
items.why: Read it to understand Marxism on its own terms (as Amit did at 18). The criticisms then become legible: zero-sum reasoning, prediction failures, reductionism on class, and incompatibility with human nature.

items.title: Dead Poets Society
items.creator: Peter Weir
items.why: Amit's first recommendation. He saw it at 17 or 18, was deeply inspired, and the ending still makes him well up. 'Carpe diem' as the pulse of a life of excellence and exposure.

items.title: Decathlon
items.why: After a lifetime of struggling to get the right equipment in India, Ajay finds it 'a breakthrough that Decathlon is here' — nice things, readily available, affordably priced.

items.title: DeepState Ukraine War Map
items.creator: DeepStateMap
items.why: Ajay walks through a static version of this map on the show; in the wild, a daily look reveals the slow reality of attritional warfare — meters per day, but every meter counted.

items.title: Defending the Undefendable
items.creator: Walter Block
items.why: Amit's reading recommendation of the day. He chose it because anyone listening to this episode could fairly call him a defender of sweatshops, prostitution, and gambling — and Block's book is the canonical exercise in defending the indefensible. You don't have to agree; you have to keep talking.

items.title: Der Edelstein
items.creator: Ulrich Boner
items.why: Shown to illustrate the point at which the printing press began to reshape what writing could be. Also the occasion of an inevitable Boner-themed wisecrack.

items.title: Determined
items.creator: Robert Sapolsky
items.why: Amit's second Sapolsky book recommendation; the natural follow-up to Behave for readers who want the philosophical implications.

items.title: Devdas
items.why: The classic Bollywood tragic arc — though Amit slyly notes that Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Devdas was, in his view, a tragedy of a film as much as a tragic film.

items.title: Devdutt Pattanaik and the Stories That Shape Us (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 404)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devdutt Pattanaik
items.why: The source of the Harappan-ahimsa-as-free-trade frame and Pattanaik's broader synthesis of mythology — recommended as background to this episode.

items.title: Development Projects Observed
items.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
items.why: Listed in the show notes as a foundational text for thinking carefully about implementation, side-effects and the gap between development plans and development reality.

items.title: Devils & Dust
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Ajay's exhibit for late-career mastery. Springsteen has said it wrote itself — once he had the idea, a lifetime of craft made the rest inexorable. Ajay compares the feeling on first hearing it to Beethoven saying, before the Ninth, 'now I know how to write music.'

items.title: Dharmesh on imperfectionism
items.creator: Dharmesh Shah
items.why: The closest distillation of Amit's mantra to his writing students: 'Perfection is the enemy of production.' Hit publish, accept the suckiness, and iterate forward.

items.title: Dhruv Rathee
items.creator: Dhruv Rathee
items.why: Cited (with quality caveats) as evidence that there is real demand for filtering and sense-making — work that mainstream media has abdicated and individual creators are picking up.

items.title: Did Frederick The Great Introduce The Potato To Germany?
items.creator: Matt Robinson
items.why: Companion piece to Ajay's telling of the Frederick-and-the-royal-gardens parable about how to make something desirable by pretending it's forbidden.

items.title: Did the Indian Capital Controls Work as a Tool of Macroeconomic Policy?
items.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Companion piece showing that the Indian state's capital-control machinery is largely ineffective — the political-economy rationale for the controls is far stronger than the macroeconomic one.

items.title: Diego Velazquez (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: Linked in the show description as part of Amit's invitation to keep researching after the episode — a reminder that the episode is a passion-share, not an art history lecture.

items.title: Dil Chahta Hai
items.creator: Farhan Akhtar
items.why: Three friends drive to Goa, things shift, they come back changed. Pure Voyage-and-Return in modern Bollywood.

items.title: Diluting the role of the IIT JEE
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: An earlier and shorter version of the case against JEE-as-everything; useful for tracing how the argument has evolved.

items.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge
items.creator: Aditya Chopra
items.why: The Eurail journey is the voyage; the slow train at the end is the return; Amrish Puri's letting-go is the rebirth. A clean, multi-archetype Bollywood text.

items.title: Discovering Faster Matrix Multiplication Algorithms With Reinforcement Learning
items.creator: Alhussein Fawzi and others (Nature, 2022)
items.why: The primary source for the 'first improvement in 50 years on Strassen' result — one of the two recent advances that had Ajay 'squealing with excitement' as evidence that machines are now doing genuinely novel scientific work in bounded domains.

items.title: Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night
items.creator: Dylan Thomas
items.why: Ajay invokes the 'rage rage against the passing of the night' line as the foil for his own stance — not raging, but quietly and curiously engaging with the world. The poem is the antithesis his 'everything is everything' equanimity is choosing against.

items.title: Do Prestigious Science Journals Attract Bad Science?
items.creator: Julia Belluz
items.why: The empirical companion to Ajay's claim that the higher the journal, the lower the quality. People hack the journal-publication system harder where the rewards are highest, and the data backs up the gut intuition.

items.title: Doing Applied Statistics Research in Julia
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Listed as a deeper pointer for viewers who want to follow up on the Julia and CRRao.jl work.

items.title: Domestic Violence and Intra-Household Resource Allocation in Rural India: An Exercise in Participatory Econometrics
items.creator: Vijayendra Rao
items.why: What mixing the two methods found: links between domestic violence and power within the family, female sterilisation, alcoholism and dowry demands. Amit also draws an incentives lesson from the story: no economics journal would take the mixed-methods version, so the work came out years later as two separate papers.

items.title: Don't Follow the Money
items.creator: Peter R. Neumann
items.why: Ajay's empirical anchor for the claim that the AML/CFT regime hasn't disrupted any meaningful terrorist plots — it has just fouled up the world's finance system while expanding state power.

items.title: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right (the Bob Dylan line on success and failure)
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: The neatest aphorism in the entire conversation about the dangers of success and the gifts of failure.

items.title: Down to Earth
items.creator: Sharad Joshi
items.why: Joshi was a great thinker, a great mass-politician, and a serious public intellectual who put real work into his columns. To understand Indian agriculture from the worm's-eye view of a farmer-leader who actually lived it, this is the resource.

items.title: Drew Houston on focus
items.creator: Drew Houston (clip)
items.why: Source of the Houston/Andy Grove story — the Dropbox founder's discovery, via Grove's book, that focus often means dropping product lines you've already paid for.

items.title: Dumb and Dumber
items.why: Even slapstick fits the comedy spine if you look for confusion, revelation, and reunion.

items.title: Dunkirk
items.creator: Christopher Nolan
items.why: Amit calls it 'one of the greatest war films I've ever seen.' Ajay independently invokes it as evidence Nolan can handle history he cares deeply about — which is part of why Ajay both wants and dreads what Nolan will do with Oppenheimer.

items.title: Dwarkesh Patel's question to Dario Amodei
items.creator: Dwarkesh Patel with Dario Amodei
items.why: Amit calls it a great question that he could not get a satisfying answer to anywhere — and offers it back to listeners as the most pointed challenge to current AI optimism.

items.title: Dylan O'Sullivan tweet quoting Matt Kahn — 'People can only meet you as deeply as they've met themselves.'
items.creator: Dylan O'Sullivan
items.why: Argues that the only path to understanding another person is to first understand yourself — the layers of self-knowledge are the layers of other-knowledge.

items.title: Dylan O'Sullivan tweet quoting Schopenhauer on the art of not reading
items.creator: Dylan O'Sullivan
items.why: Compressed by Ajay to a bumper-sticker — 'Don't follow anybody on Twitter.' A defence of curating inputs aggressively.

items.title: E-Yantra
items.creator: Kavi Arya and IIT Bombay
items.why: Ajay's anti-exam: a creative engineering challenge with no certificate at the end, only the pleasure of building. The kind of cohort he wants to see flowing into engineering schools.

items.title: Eamonn Butler's Primers (on Public Choice, Classical Liberalism, Hayek, Friedman)
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: When asked for an entry point to classical liberalism, Butler's primers are Amit's most reliable starting recommendation: short, lucid, and faithful to the source thinkers.

items.title: Earwitness to Place
items.creator: Bernie Krause (interviewed by Erin Robinsong)
items.why: The source for Krause's work on how environment shapes bird sound, and his Californian drought soundscape — the scientific anchor for the whole 'form shapes content' thesis applied to nature.

items.title: Eat a Peach
items.creator: The Allman Brothers Band
items.why: Amit's musical recommendation, smuggled in via the SEEPS pun. He singles out 'Little Martha' and 'Blue Sky' — both featuring Duane Allman, whose playing he calls 'great feel, great vibe, just incredible.'

items.title: Economic Freedom in Agriculture
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Sets out the four-mechanism framework — futures, storage, domestic trade, international trade — that organises this episode.

items.title: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: Ajay's recommendation as a meta-text on the difficulty of being a futurist. One of the smartest people in world history tried his very best — and a lot of it didn't work out. Read it as humility training before listening to Amit-and-Ajay's own forecasts for 2050.

items.title: Economic Sophisms
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's genius was distilling complex ideas into stories anyone could understand. Reductio ad absurdum done at a master level — once you've seen 'block out the sun to protect candlemakers' or 'ban the right hand to maximise productive effort,' you cannot un-see the absurdity in real protectionist arguments.

items.title: Economies of Scale, Economies of Scope
items.creator: Venkatesh Rao
items.why: Provides the textbook frame against which Sun-Google-Amazon's 'great leaps' stand out as anomalous.

items.title: Egregious Indian Protectionism Against Trade in Services
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Direct evidence for the episode's central economic claim: services are now 67% of world GDP and the GATT/WTO never opened them up. India's own protectionism in services is one example of why a TPP-style 'WTO 2.0' is needed.

items.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
items.creator: Hannah Arendt
items.why: Source of the phrase 'the banality of evil.' Amit invokes it as a cautionary tale: ordinary people can behave in the most evil ways, and neither religion nor rationality is a guarantee against that — humanity itself is like that.

items.title: El Amor de Mi Vida
items.creator: Warren Zevon
items.why: Amit reads the lines: 'I look outside, I know you're there / and you found a brand new life somewhere / I only wish it had been us / but I'm happy for your happiness.' Used as the truest test of love — wishing only that the other person be happy, even outside your life.

items.title: Eleanor Rigby
items.creator: The Beatles
items.why: Ajay's soundtrack for what happens with most government IT projects — the launch event, the inauguration, the empty ritual: nothing was actually saved.

items.title: Elon Musk on First-Principles Thinking
items.creator: Elon Musk
items.why: The case study for first-principles thinking: by going down to material costs, Musk cut battery cost from $600/kWh to $80/kWh — proving that 'experts say it can't be cheaper' was an artifact of accumulated lag, not physics.

items.title: Emacs Org Mode
items.why: Plays the same role Roam plays for Amit — nested entries, cross-linking, structured thinking — only locally and freely. Lacks Roam's collaboration, but for a solo workflow Ajay considers it a fully credible Swiss Army knife.

items.title: Emergent Ventures India
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Held up as a counter-example to bad gatekeeping — funding 'freaks, nutcases and Amit Varmas' on the explicit understanding that failure is a learning, not a debt to repay.

items.title: Emerging Markets Conference
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: Last year's conference had an entire session on recent developments in the U.S. administrative state — 'a field that is red hot with interesting developments and beautiful, interesting intellectual debates.'

items.title: Emil Sutovsky on the organisation of the event
items.creator: Emil Sutovsky
items.why: The CEO of FIDE's response to what he characterises as ransom-holding behaviour — Amit's evidence that Sutovsky behaved as a 'complete gentleman' through it.

items.title: Emma
items.creator: Jane Austen
items.why: Austen's most cleanly comic plot — and a useful reminder that genre-name and tone are not the same thing.

items.title: Enlightenment Now
items.creator: Steven Pinker
items.why: Source of the Boris and Igor parable about killing the goat — the cleanest illustration that 'fixing inequality' can mean making everyone equally poor.

items.title: Entry and Exit in Agriculture (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 1)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath and Karthik Shashidhar
items.why: Where Amit first encountered the argument that demanding every farmer simultaneously be a farmer and an entrepreneur is unfair — specialisation requires scale.

items.title: Envisioning an India-US Free Trade Agreement
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The episode's punchline. Ajay reports a 'fascinating consensus from the American side' that one of the few politically feasible US trade deals is a deep FTA with India. Trump's tariffs make it more salient, not less — Trump can claim victory; India can secure cheap goods.

items.title: Epic of Gilgamesh
items.why: One of humanity's earliest written stories — and already a 'Overcoming the Monster' template, showing how old this scaffolding is.

items.title: Episode 170 of A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
items.creator: Andrew Hickey
items.why: Recommended as the great podcast episode Amit had heard on the album, for anyone who wants the full story of how Astral Weeks was made.

items.title: Episode on Mary Wollstonecraft (Amit Varma)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The natural follow-on for anyone struck by Wollstonecraft's role in extending Lockean natural rights to women — Amit calls her one of his great heroes.

items.title: Episode with Arnold Kling on The Three Languages of Politics (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Arnold Kling
items.why: Kling discusses the three (now four) ideological tribes and how to argue across them; the interview accompanies the recommended book.

items.title: Episode with Jerry Rao on Indian conservatism (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jerry Rao
items.why: A 'very lively back and forth' — Amit pushed back hard, arguing that a Burkean conservatism (means matter, respect complexity) does not really exist in India. Worth listening to for the disagreement itself.

items.title: Episode with Rebecca Goldstein (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Rebecca Goldstein
items.why: Source of Amit's frame that early philosophers (Plato, Aristotle) were essentially scientists — the word 'philosopher' meant someone inquiring into everything — before the modern carving up into disciplines amputated their breadth.

items.title: Episodes with Akar Patel on Hindutva (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Akar Patel
items.why: Source of Patel's question that Amit puts to listeners: with most ideologies you can say what they are for; for Hindutva, you can only say what it is against. What is it for?

items.title: Epitaph on Sir Isaac Newton
items.creator: Alexander Pope
items.why: Quoted as the perfect crystallisation of the over-clean, sudden-genius mythology that Keynes's later reading of Newton's papers shattered. The couplet is the school-textbook Newton; Hessen and Keynes are the messy real one.

items.title: Eric Schmidt on five-year plans
items.creator: Eric Schmidt
items.why: Five-year plans fail at the level of an economy (no central planner has the information) but succeed at the level of a firm — they force strategic vision and surface where you'll need to pivot.

items.title: Eric Weinstein Won't Toe the Line (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 330)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Eric Weinstein
items.why: The episode where Amit posed the same question that ends this episode — given orders-of-magnitude more potential creators, why aren't we drowning in masterpieces? Weinstein vehemently disagreed with Amit's framing; the episode is the longer conversation.

items.title: Ernest Hemingway, The Art of Fiction No. 21
items.creator: George Plimpton
items.why: An additional source for Hemingway's account of his writing process and the 'one true sentence' approach to writer's block.

items.title: Essays
items.creator: Lydia Davis
items.why: The companion volume to the stories — Davis on her own craft and on the writers she loves. Read alongside the fiction to see how a working writer thinks about her tools.

items.title: Essays in Biography
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: Contains 'Newton, the Man' and other character studies. Ajay disagrees with almost everything Keynes did in economics, yet considers him one of the most beautiful and wonderful people who ever lived. 'Everybody should dream of writing like that.'

items.title: Essays in Persuasion
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: The companion volume — paired with Essays in Biography as masterclasses in writing and thinking. Ajay's broader point: you can disagree with a thinker's conclusions and still revere him as a craftsman.

items.title: Eurosport (cycling coverage)
items.why: Home to the great commentary team Amit lost when GCN Plus shut down — Dan Lloyd, Orla Chennaoui and Adam Blythe especially. Watching cycling without that commentary, he says, is missing half the experience.

items.title: eventstudies (R package)
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: Half-joking pitch to gentle readers: if you want to test whether a six in T20 actually shifts the bowler's psyche over the next few balls, an event study is exactly the right tool — and the code already exists.

items.title: Every Breath You Take
items.creator: The Police
items.why: Amit's song-of-the-day for an episode on financial surveillance. He quotes the lyric 'every vow you break, every claim you stake, I'll be watching you' and proposes the song should be emailed by every reader to every civil servant in their life — the Indian state being, in his framing, 'a creepy male stalker, and much worse.'

items.title: Everybody Lies
items.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
items.why: The seminal popular text on the idea that people are most truly themselves when searching anonymously online — turning the searchbar into a polygraph for the secret self. Source of the book's most-cited findings, from sexless marriages to gender-biased parenting Google queries.

items.title: Everything is Everything episode on constraints in computer technology
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay invokes the Apollo lunar lander built with 64KB of RAM — when constraints are extreme, the people who succeed develop deep insights that disposable, resource-rich modern engineers miss.

items.title: Export Versus FDI with Heterogeneous Firms
items.creator: Elhanan Helpman, Marc J. Melitz and Stephen R. Yeaple
items.why: The theoretical scaffolding for Ajay's claim that exports and FDI are not substitutes on a menu but complementary modes of internationalisation that emerge naturally from heterogeneity in firm productivity.

items.title: Exporting and Firm Performance: Evidence from India
items.creator: Apoorva Gupta, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Direct evidence for the episode's central claim — that exporting is not just a sales channel but a journey to higher productivity, with the data drawn from Indian firms.

items.title: ExpressVPN (or any good VPN)
items.why: Practical fix once GCN Plus disappeared. Amit's ad-libbed parental advisory: 'Young men watching this for porn — do not do that. It is sinful. Save your energy for studying economics and physics and aeronautical engineering.'

items.title: Ezra Klein interviewed by David Perell
items.creator: David Perell with Ezra Klein
items.why: Source of Amit's framing that the value of reading isn't getting a thousand-word summary you could otherwise look up; it's the 10-20 hour intimate grapple that trains your mind.

items.title: Facts Don't Matter, Stories Do
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: An independent arrival at the 'simplistic narrative' point of Muller's framework — Trump's appeal isn't about facts but about a coherent, simple story (jobs are leaving, immigrants are taking them) that gives people something to rail against. A useful companion piece showing the convergence of intuition and theory.

items.title: Fair Coins Tend to Land On The Same Side They Started
items.creator: Frantisek Bartos et al.
items.why: The empirical primary source for the 51%-same-side finding Ajay cites. A reminder that even the most boring deterministic objects hide structure inside what we call randomness.

items.title: False Alarm
items.creator: Bjorn Lomborg
items.why: Amit's central recommendation against the Ajay-style climate gloom. He frames the pitch in terms of incentives (NGOs need dystopia to fund themselves) and asks listeners to check the 1980s/1990s alarmist predictions against what actually happened. Lomborg's books are his data source.

items.title: Falsifiability (Wikipedia)
items.why: Ajay's organising principle for separating real knowledge from sloppy belief. He uses it to triage propositions into bins: hard knowledge, working hypotheses likely to become falsifiable, beliefs from social programming/peer pressure/political convenience, and pure fanciful nonsense (e.g., Erich von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods).

items.title: Famous Last Questions
items.creator: Sanjana Ramachandran
items.why: Source material for the lived experience of dating-app life, especially for women navigating the asymmetry.

items.title: Farmers, Technology and Freedom of Choice: A Tale of Two Satyagrahas
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The longer written version of the BT cotton satyagraha story he tells here, with the figures on adoption.

items.title: Fascism in Baroda
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Concrete instance of the speech-suppression dynamics this episode is generalising about.

items.title: Fast Car (Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert, 1988)
items.creator: Tracy Chapman
items.why: The performance that broke Fast Car wide open and Amit's all-time-favourite song. The story behind it is the seed metaphor of the episode — surface area of serendipity made visible in a single evening.

items.title: Fateful Choices
items.creator: Ian Kershaw
items.why: Especially timely amid the collapse of the Atlantic Alliance. Centres on how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side — until August 1941 about half the House of Representatives still didn't want to do it. Gives insights into America and into the present moment.

items.title: FATF Black and Grey Lists
items.creator: Financial Action Task Force
items.why: On Ajay's reading list as the institutional context for understanding the coercive architecture of FATF — countries either sign on to the AML regime or face the friction of being grey-listed.

items.title: Father and Son
items.creator: Cat Stevens
items.why: Ajay confesses he once wrote it off as cliched but, twenty years on, has come back to thinking it is a really great song — the same person voicing both sides of the generational argument. He pairs it with Independence Day and The Road as his triptych of father-son works.

items.title: Father Returning Home
items.creator: Dilip Chitre
items.why: Amit recites it in full as the episode's frame — the image of nomads through a narrow pass is the entry point to 300,000 years of human migration on the subcontinent.

items.title: Father, Son & Co: My Life at IBM and Beyond
items.creator: Thomas J. Watson Jr.
items.why: A pure family-business book — a design-one and design-two story, not a design-four story. Watson Jr. inherited a feudal company where employees sang the company anthem each morning, and rolled the dice on OS/360 — an inflation-adjusted gamble larger than the Manhattan Project. Ajay read it young and got great insights into the challenges of running a family firm.

items.title: Fear the Boom and Bust + Fight of the Century (Keynes vs. Hayek Rap Battles)
items.creator: John Papola, Russ Roberts (lyrics) and Emergent Order
items.why: Russ Roberts (host of EconTalk) wrote the lyrics. They are 'absolutely delightful' — proof that intellectual debate can be fun and accessible. (Bonus recommendation: Amit's Episode 182 of The Seen and the Unseen with Russ Roberts, on the art of conversation.)

items.title: Fierce Attachments
items.creator: Vivian Gornick
items.why: Brooks invokes Gornick to show how two people can understand each other completely and yet not at all — a portrait of human relationships that is the antidote to rushing to judgment about the messy interiors of others.

items.title: Fighting Against Censorship
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Background reading for the arguments developed in this episode.

items.title: Final Draft
items.why: Mentioned as the dedicated tool for screenplay form when Amit fantasises about a one-tool-does-everything workflow.

items.title: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission Report — Volume 1
items.creator: FSLRC, chaired by Justice B.N. Srikrishna
items.why: A crisp summary of 20 years of research on regulation and regulatory theory in India. Compact chapters explain the thinking on each issue and end with a box of drafting instructions handed to the law team. Ajay calls it the model for how reform documents should be written.

items.title: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission Report — Volume 2 (Indian Financial Code)
items.creator: FSLRC, chaired by Justice B.N. Srikrishna
items.why: About 140 sections of horizontal regulatory theory plus the financial-system-wide draft law. Ajay says without exaggeration that India has not had a better law-drafting team since independence — the cleanest, most modern law-drafting project in Indian history, a role model for how laws should be drafted.

items.title: Finding Love in Modern India (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 401)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Samrat Bansal and Sanjana Ramachandran
items.why: The fullest treatment of the chapter's central question: how Indian men and women actually experience dating apps differently.

items.title: Finding Nemo
items.why: Marlin's quest to find his son hits every five-act beat — call, journey, arrival, frustration, ordeal, goal.

items.title: Flying Spaghetti Monster (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Bobby Henderson
items.why: A model of the 'benign way of protesting religion' that Amit prefers — making the absurdity of dogma visible through tongue-in-cheek absurdism, demanding equal respect for an obviously fanciful 'religion' to expose the structure of all such claims.

items.title: Fogbank (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Wikipedia contributors
items.why: The publicly available account of how a top-secret know-how vanished even from a defence-grade record-keeping system, costing tens of millions to recover.

items.title: Follow-Up: A New Ending in Tale of Young Woman From Rural India
items.creator: Ellen Barry
items.why: The continuation of the human-drama story — what becomes of one young rural woman after she has stepped into the export-led modern economy.

items.title: For This Brave New World of Cricket, We Have IPL and England to Thank
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The praise piece for England and the IPL as the two engines that finally dragged cricket out of its three-decade ODI suboptimum and toward proper EV-based play.

items.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
items.creator: Ernest Hemingway
items.why: Ajay's counter-factual: imagine the same book in a purely urban setting and the oomph is gone. The mountains and forests are not background; they are the medium that makes the human drama matter.

items.title: Foreign Currency Borrowing by Indian Firms: Towards a New Policy Framework
items.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Nirvikar Singh
items.why: Directly relevant to the steel-mill example: Indian firms competing globally need access to cheaper foreign debt capital, and the current policy framework is unnecessarily restrictive.

items.title: Foreign Investors under Stress: Evidence from India
items.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Nirvikar Singh
items.why: A counter to the standard fear that foreign capital is 'hot money' that will flee in a crisis — the empirical record is more nuanced and the policy implications are different from the protectionist instinct.

items.title: Forests, Trees, and Intellectual Roots... (review of Seeing Like a State)
items.creator: Brad DeLong
items.why: Ajay missed the book in 1998 and missed DeLong's 1990s blog flag in his RSS feed; the review is still worth reading as one of the most substantive engagements with Scott's argument by an economist.

items.title: Forthcoming book on taxation
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit signals he is fully convinced this will be a major book. The whole reason Ajay is stepping back from EIE is to make room for this kind of long-form, durable contribution.

items.title: Fortress and Frontier in American Health Care
items.creator: Robert Graboyes
items.why: Won the Bastiat Prize in 2014. Introduced Amit to the fortress-and-frontier framework — heavy regulation creates walled industries that block innovation, while permissionless tech becomes the place where breakthroughs happen. Even when regulation seems to address asymmetric information, the lives lost by delay can outweigh the lives saved.

items.title: Foundation for Economic Development
items.creator: Rahul Ahluwalia
items.why: Ajay flags it directly in the show notes as worth following — Ahluwalia is one of the more lucid public voices on Indian economic reform.

items.title: Foundational Everything is Everything episodes on the state
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: If a listener wants the show's intellectual scaffolding on what the state is, what it can do, and what its failure modes look like, these episodes are the place to start before the rest of the catalogue clicks into place.

items.title: Four Thousand Weeks
items.creator: Oliver Burkeman
items.why: The arithmetic of mortality — roughly four thousand weeks per life — as a forcing function for action.
