Pairs with the Gurwinder Bhogal line about the future constantly shrinking, and with Amit's exercise: estimate optimistically how many more times you'll see your parents and notice it's a small number.

items.title: Francisco Goya (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: Same as above — Amit insists viewers Google these artists and look at the work themselves rather than rely on his summaries.

items.title: Freakonomics
items.creator: Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner
items.why: One of the popular economics books that teach the fundamentals without the weeds of regressions or general equilibrium: scarcity is real, and people respond to incentives. Once those first principles become part of your framework, everything else starts to make sense.

items.title: Free Banking in Britain: Theory, Experience, and Debate, 1800-1845
items.creator: Lawrence H. White
items.why: The empirical backbone for the case that competitive issuance of currency is not a thought experiment but a real, working system from history. The book that quietly laid groundwork for crypto.

items.title: Freedom at Midnight
items.creator: Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre
items.why: The book that inspired Ajay's never-written counter-book, Freedom After Midnight — the argument that 1947 delivered political freedom but withheld personal, social and economic freedom, leaving India's freedom struggle structurally incomplete.

items.title: Freedoms Delayed
items.creator: Timur Kuran
items.why: Where The Long Divergence shows how institutions produced economic backwardness, Freedoms Delayed argues the same institutions produced political backwardness. Read together they form one large account of how legal forms shape civilisational trajectories.

items.title: FreeStyle Libre Glucose Monitoring System
items.creator: Abbott Labs
items.why: Ajay's primary recommendation — and the tool at the heart of this episode — for running a two-to-three-month research project on yourself, once a year, to fix lifelong food habits. With a humble plea to Abbott to open the API so an open-source app can pipe readings into a Google Sheet. Practical wisdom: stick the patch in but wait a full 24 hours before initialising it, and do a couple of days of finger-prick calibration.

items.title: Frog and Toad on spring
items.creator: Arnold Lobel (via the Frog and Toad Bot)
items.why: A tonic for hard times: zoom out enough and the line trends up. Amit reads it as encouragement that even in dark moments and dark places, spring is on its way — though he and Ajay split on whether spring arrives by natural forces or because we make it arrive.

items.title: From bark to weed: The history of artemisinin
items.creator: Claude Faurant
items.why: The technical backstory to Tu Youyou's cold-extraction breakthrough and how the active sequence inside the molecule was later refined into modern derivatives.

items.title: From Cairo to Delhi With Max Rodenbeck (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 281)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Max Rodenbeck
items.why: Where Rodenbeck answered the 'Gangali' question with 'Cairo — but the Cairo of my childhood, which no longer exists.' Worth listening to for the most poignant version of the home-as-vanished-place idea.

items.title: From Domestic to Global Asset Pricing
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Theoretical underpinning for why financial globalisation lowers the cost of capital — Indian firms become priced against a global rather than a local risk-free rate.

items.title: Frédéric Bastiat's writings
items.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
items.why: Bastiat's nineteenth-century essays remain among the clearest demonstrations of unseen costs and unintended consequences. The original 'seen and the unseen' framing.

items.title: FSLRC Report and Draft Indian Financial Code
items.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
items.why: Ajay points to the FSLRC machinery as the one Indian context where a fully articulated investigation-prosecution-adjudication regime has been worked out — a worked example for how a regulator like SEBI could be redesigned with proper checks and balances.

items.title: Fun Home
items.creator: Alison Bechdel
items.why: Cited alongside Dykes To Watch Out For as proof that comics can compete with the best of literature. A masterpiece of the graphic-novel form.

items.title: Fund Schooling, Not Schools
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The chapter title of this episode and the cleanest formulation of the argument: the state may continue to spend, but the funding should follow the child, not the institution.

items.title: Furrows in a Field
items.creator: Sugata Srinivasaraju
items.why: The book Amit took several thousand words of notes on, stayed up all night for, and never mentioned in the resulting five-and-a-half-hour conversation. Cited here as the proof case that prep buys freedom.

items.title: Futures Markets in Agriculture (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 12)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Shashidhar
items.why: Demystifies futures markets as a basic tool for ordinary farmers, not arcane finance — the price discovered by speculators is a public good for everyone making sowing decisions.

items.title: Gambling on Development
items.creator: Stefan Dercon
items.why: Listed as a key contemporary read on the political economy of development success and failure — complementing the Pritchett–Easterly–Kelkar/Shah core.

items.title: Game Changer
items.creator: Matthew Sadler and Natasha Regan
items.why: Helps you rethink chess heuristics — particularly the relationship between material and initiative, play down the flanks, etc. — that AlphaZero showed were locally rather than globally true. Will make you a better chess player. Garry Kasparov's introductory essay on the evolution of computer chess is itself worth the price of admission.

items.title: Gandhi Before India
items.creator: Ramachandra Guha
items.why: The forming years are the formative ones. South Africa is where Satyagraha was actually invented — the one thing of which Gandhi had personal experience and was therefore right about.

items.title: Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World
items.creator: Ramachandra Guha
items.why: Pair it with the first volume for the full Guha treatment. Amit has done five episodes of The Seen and the Unseen with Guha, two specifically on Gandhi — the books are 'just superb.'

items.title: Garry Tan on acting small
items.creator: Garry Tan
items.why: Smallness is a luxury, not a handicap — it's the only stage where the CEO can answer every customer email personally. Don't perform bigness; use the access intimacy gives you.

items.title: Garry Tan on co-CEOs
items.creator: Garry Tan
items.why: Co-CEOs feel comfortable to the founders but slow every decision below them — every signoff requires two, and the firm crawls. Have one CEO, even with great co-founders.

items.title: Gekiga (Wikipedia entry)
items.why: If you want to understand what differentiates the dark, urban, adult manga of Tezuka's Ode to Kirihito and Tatsumi's collections from mainstream manga, this is a one-page primer on the form.

items.title: Genesis of Rgvedic Retroflexion
items.creator: Madhav Deshpande
items.why: Amit calls it a paper that 'pretty much blew everyone away' — definitive evidence that the Rig Veda's language was already shaped by what was here before.

items.title: Genetic Engineering (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 165)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shambhavi Naik
items.why: The serious conversation behind Ajay's chapter on gene editing. Naik covers not just CRISPR mechanics but the harder ethics of editing embryos, designer babies, and germline changes — the questions that arise once the technology actually works.

items.title: Geniuses and economic development
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Where Ajay works out the math behind the claim that India has the world's second- or third-largest plausible scientific and engineering workforce, even amid mainline failure.

items.title: Getting Things Done
items.creator: David Allen
items.why: Mentioned as the seminal text for the productivity-tools-and-techniques tradition, even as Amit and Ajay riff on its limits.

items.title: Ghost World
items.creator: Daniel Clowes
items.why: Listed alongside Fun Home and Blankets as comic-form masterpieces. Amit promises a future full episode with all his graphic-novel recommendations.

items.title: GOAT: Who Is the Greatest Economist of All Time?
items.creator: Tyler Cowen
items.why: An ideal starting point if you have not had exposure to Friedman, Hayek, Keynes, and the others. Cowen makes them legible as people, not just paradigms.

items.title: Goechala (Sikkim)
items.creator: Himalayan trek to Kanchenjunga viewpoint
items.why: Out of all the Himalayan treks Ajay has done, 'one of the best treks of my life.' From Goechala 1 you stand with Kanchenjunga in front of you.

items.title: Going from Strong as in Scary to Strong as in Capable
items.creator: Suyash Rai and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's worked-out version of the central distinction in the episode: the bad meaning of 'strong' is a state that can grab the most powerful person in the country and put them in jail; the good meaning is a state that can deliver a polio-vaccination programme on schedule. India admires the first and needs the second.

items.title: Gokhale: The Indian Moderates and the British Raj
items.creator: B.R. Nanda
items.why: Linked from the description, contextualising the Pune intellectual lineage — the Gokhale-Agarkar-Ferguson-College circle that gave the city its 200-year intellectual endowment.

items.title: Golmaal
items.why: Another canonical Bollywood comedy; identity confusion drives the plot.

items.title: Goodbye Sam, Hello Samantha
items.creator: Cliff Richard
items.why: Used as a half-joking metaphor for the individual agency the gig economy gives workers: today's Swiggy is tomorrow's Zomato is the next day's Urban Company.

items.title: Google Gemini (paid)
items.creator: Google
items.why: He treats LLMs as world-class language editors rather than AGI; he gives them a finished column and asks for ambiguous sentences and grammar errors. He converted to the paid tier the day Gemini gave him five master-editor-level suggestions on a Business Standard column.

items.title: Google Guys: The Playboy Interview
items.creator: Larry Page and Sergey Brin (interviewed in Playboy)
items.why: Concrete proof of how serious the magazine's long-form journalism was: an enormous, substantive interview with the most important tech founders of their generation, run in the same pages as the centrefold.

items.title: Google Scholar
items.creator: Google
items.why: His practical advice for non-specialists who feel disconcerted by papers: spend time there anyway. Even without the technical chops to grok the internals, you will absorb the rhythm — abstract, introduction, methodology, results, discussion — and over time you will be able to extract real value across an unusually large number of disciplines.

items.title: Google Trends
items.creator: Google
items.why: Amit's hands-on companion to Everybody Lies. The universally accessible version of search-data sociology — anyone can run it.

items.title: Google's AlphaZero Destroys Stockfish In 100-Game Match
items.creator: Mike Klein
items.why: The contemporaneous account of the moment when machine chess transcended human chess — the empirical underpinning for Peter Heine Nielsen's 'aliens playing chess' line.

items.title: Gorakhgad
items.creator: Day-hike route in Maharashtra
items.why: Cited as one of the phenomenal day hikes you can do in the Bombay region with just a backpack, two litres of water and five apples. A low-entry-barrier starting point.

items.title: GothamChess
items.creator: Levy Rozman
items.why: He makes you feel smarter when you watch his videos, because in that moment he genuinely helps you understand chess like an expert. The art is not just understanding — it's communicating in a way that fills the viewer with the same passion and the same joy of the magic on the board.

items.title: Grand Tamasha
items.creator: Milan Vaishnav
items.why: Amit's recommendation for understanding contemporary Indian politics from a fine thinker.

items.title: Grand Tour (cycling) (Wikipedia)
items.why: Background reading for the structure of the Grand Tour calendar that this episode constantly assumes.

items.title: Great leaders choose prosperity over pride
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The frame for 'no place for pride' in the dealing-with-Trump section. If flattery gets the job done, do the flattery; the only test is the Indian self-interest.

items.title: Great Soul: Mahatma Gandhi and His Struggle with India
items.creator: Joseph Lelyveld
items.why: A serious New Yorker writer's biography, banned in parts of India for implying a homosexual relationship between Gandhi and Kallenbach (their nicknames for each other were 'Upper House' and 'Lower House'). Amit read it side-by-side with Guha's first volume covering the same period.

items.title: Green Eggs and Ham
items.creator: Dr. Seuss
items.why: A canonical artefact of the central thesis of the episode — that an arbitrary, externally-imposed constraint can produce a beloved work that an unconstrained writer would not have produced.

items.title: Greg Isenberg on greatness
items.creator: Greg Isenberg
items.why: Five words that, Amit says, do the work of fifty thousand. Sets up the discussion of when staying in one's comfort zone is wisdom (deep mastery, adjacencies) and when it is cowardice (the leap one keeps not taking).

items.title: Groundhog Day
items.why: The full Booker comedy arc — characters trapped in unloving states, transformed by self-recognition and a change of heart.

items.title: Growing Up
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit's first-encounter memory of Springsteen as a kid was a live version of Growing Up — but specifically the long, almost half-hour spoken introduction Springsteen used to give before it. It is the canonical example of Springsteen's habit of refusing to be a covers band of himself, treating every live night as new material.

items.title: GST Across India, with Shruti Rajagopalan (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: A comprehensive deep dive on how the GST was actually playing out a year after rollout — paired with the Devangshu episode to track prediction against reality.

items.title: GST and the Indian Economy, with Devangshu Datta (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Devangshu Datta
items.why: Devangshu correctly predicted every implementation pathology before the GST went live. A canonical example of expert foresight on the failure modes of a conceptually sound reform.

items.title: Gukesh interviewed by Sagar Shah after the World Championship
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Source for the detail that Gukesh almost played Rg3 instead of seeing the winning trade — and confirms the team's deliberate plan to fatigue Ding.

items.title: Gukesh stating his ambition to Sagar Shah at age 11 (X post)
items.why: The viral moment Amit re-posted after the 2024 win — proof that Sagar was building the institution years before anyone realised.

items.title: Gurpriya Sidhu tweet — 'Be like a coach or a comrade in your professional relationships. Be like a gardener in your personal ones.'
items.creator: Gurpriya Sidhu
items.why: Used to draw the distinction between functional/transactional professional relationships and the open, accepting, gardener-style relationships of personal life.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal on our shrinking future
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: A second-by-second indictment of preparation as substitute for action. Pairs with Burkeman's four thousand weeks and with the parental-visits arithmetic.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal quoting Christ Williamson on hiding your true self
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Amit cites this idea (also attributed to Paul Graham) to bridge from search-data inauthenticity to the deeper cost of self-suppression.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal tweet on AI making us machine-like
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Used to argue not against AI but against treating AI as a crutch — let it be a tool that enhances thinking, not a substitute for it.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal tweet on complaining
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Becomes a launching point for Amit's near-mission-statement against negativity in his own life, and the brutal exit from toxic groups.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal tweet on tribal certainty
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: A diagnostic for tribalism. The moment you take the tribal line, you have confessed that you no longer care about the truth — you care about your team.

items.title: Gurwinder Bhogal's Substack
items.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
items.why: Recommended as the place to read Bhogal's longer-form synthesis when 280 characters isn't enough.

items.title: Gyan Prakash on the Emergency (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 103)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Gyan Prakash
items.why: Argues the Emergency was not aberrant — the centralisation was already in the constitution and the state's DNA, inheriting from the colonial state.

items.title: Halfway From Coal, Halfway to Diamond (Everything is Everything, episode 1)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Reference point — the episode where Kuran was first mentioned, which led him to DM Amit and ultimately to the long Seen-and-Unseen conversation feeding this episode.

items.title: Hamlet
items.creator: William Shakespeare
items.why: A tragedy of the noble protagonist who is lured into ignoble action and falls — the spine of Booker's tragedy chapter.

items.title: Hans Niemann interviewed in 2022 about his alleged cheating
items.creator: Hans Niemann
items.why: The other side of the Carlsen-Niemann story; lets you judge Niemann's own framing rather than only Carlsen's.

items.title: Harishchandragad
items.creator: Trek in the Western Sahyadris
items.why: 'World class' in Ajay's experience of hiking everywhere — though now overrun with boorish young men with alcohol. Memorable for him as a coolie on the first successful Konkan Kada climb.

items.title: Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: Recommended together with Runaway as the two collections to start with for anyone discovering Munro.

items.title: Havel: A Life
items.creator: Michael Žantovský
items.why: The definitive biography of one of the great accidental politicians — both for the texture of his early life as a thinker-dissident and for understanding how a playwright became a head of state.

items.title: Heaven's Gaits
items.creator: Adam Gopnik
items.why: Gopnik's line that humans are made for walking but are not very good at it — 'arches like querulous cabinet ministers' first complain and then resign. Also makes the point that walking-as-pastime depends on technologies — gaslight, the rule of law, the Walkman, sneakers — that have been arriving in stages.

items.title: Hikaru Nakamura on Gukesh's game against Wei Yi
items.creator: Hikaru Nakamura
items.why: Even Carlsen-circle commentators acknowledged the brilliance — Nakamura's video is the strongest praise in the genre.

items.title: Hikaru Nakamura's channel
items.creator: Hikaru Nakamura
items.why: Watching one of the world's best players play and explain simultaneously is fantastic and instructive. His COVID-era streaming revitalised his love for chess; he came back and played well in the next two candidates tournaments — a case study in how a side activity can rescue a top career.

items.title: Hind Swaraj
items.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
items.why: Many talk about it; few have read it. Worth reading precisely because it shows Gandhi was incoherent on most things (railways, lawyers, doctors, hospitals as 'institutions for propagating sin') yet right on the one big thing — nonviolent resistance. A demonstration of the courage to expose your own unfinished thinking publicly.

items.title: Hindi Cinema Through the Years (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 200)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: The episode in which Amit was supposed to read out a Dilip Chitre poem, started sobbing instead, and Rajagopalan had to read it for him — referenced as evidence that beauty itself, not only sadness, can break a man.

items.title: Homeopathic Faith
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A self-cited piece on why we should make fun of homeopathy. Used here as a model for being self-critical of one's own world; if you can mock pseudoscience outside, you should mock the hypocrisies of academia inside.

items.title: Horizon
items.creator: Barry Lopez
items.why: Surrounded by Bir's beauty, Amit thought of Lopez — one of the great travel writers, a 'philosopher of the world.' Every journey, Amit notes, becomes truly beautiful only when it is also a journey inside us, and Lopez is the master of that double movement.

items.title: Host-diet-gut microbiome interactions influence human energy balance
items.creator: Karen D. Corbin et al., Nature Communications, June 2023
items.why: The study Ajay leans on for the 200-calorie-a-day 'discount' from eating complex carbs — simple carbs are absorbed before they can reach the gut microbiome (which shrivels), while complex carbs feed the microbiome 8x more activity, and the microbes themselves consume some of the energy. A calorie is not a calorie.

items.title: Houseful
items.why: A modern example used to argue that laugh-out-loud comedy in Bollywood is alive and well, even if love and laughter have drifted apart in much of cinema.

items.title: Houseful Economics on Pragati
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The original platform for the kind of analysis on display in this episode (Newton on rational ignorance, Raees on bootleggers and Baptists). Amit asks listeners to vote on whether to bring it back as a recurring segment.

items.title: How 32-bit Float Recording Works on the Wireless PRO
items.creator: YouTube tutorial
items.why: For the curious: a deeper dive on how the audio tech that lets the show 'wave its arms about' actually works.

items.title: How Amazon grew an awkward side project into AWS
items.creator: Geoff Colvin
items.why: The detailed account behind Ajay's third great leap — how Amazon noticed idle peak-Christmas server capacity and turned it into a world-changing cloud business.

items.title: How Bing Crosby Made Silicon Valley Possible
items.creator: Ted Gioia
items.why: Evidence for the form thesis applied to vocals: pre-microphone, only opera could survive (you have to throw your voice — 'it ain't over till the fat lady sings'); the microphone enabled a new soft, sensual style of singing — Bing Crosby, Sinatra, the entire crooner aesthetic.

items.title: How Fiction Works
items.creator: James Wood
items.why: Amit promises it 'will transform the way you read a book' — voice, the influence of Flaubert, the evolution of the modern novel. Important for anyone who wants to learn to appreciate literature.

items.title: How Frameworks
items.creator: Sudhir Sarnobat and Rajendra Bhagwat
items.why: Not consultant talk or bookish talk — frameworks distilled from a lifetime of running businesses in Indian conditions. Useful even for non-business readers who love new lenses for thinking about life. Use code 'seenunseen' for a discount.

items.title: How Innovation Works: And Why It Flourishes in Freedom
items.creator: Matt Ridley
items.why: Amit's chosen counter to top-down innovation policy. Ridley argues innovation is a bottom-up process within society, fuelled by freedom and decentralised experimentation — a frame that supports Amit's skepticism about whether the state should be in this business at all.

items.title: How Laissez-Faire Made Sweden Rich
items.creator: Johan Norberg
items.why: Cited against the standard 'look at Scandinavia' rebuttal to free-market arguments. Sweden became rich on free markets first, and only then layered welfare on top — without ever giving up business freedom or ease of doing business.

items.title: How Life Imitates Chess
items.creator: Garry Kasparov
items.why: Kasparov is 'just a great mind' — a hero of both Amit and Ajay 'for more than just his chess' — and Amit hopes he succeeds in the larger game he's playing now (against Putin's regime). Worth reading for that mind alone.

items.title: How LLMs Will Impact Us
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The longer-form version of the LLM argument he makes in the episode: LLMs are powerful but limited statistical tools, useful for converting Q2 workers into Q3 work under a Q4 master, dangerous when treated as final arbiters.

items.title: How Much Does Free Education Cost?
items.creator: Centre for Civil Society
items.why: The Delhi counterpart to the Hyderabad work — same finding. Links the ground-level decisions of the urban poor to the larger argument for school vouchers.

items.title: How Much Wealth Do You Need to Retire? (Everything is Everything, episode 110)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The standard cross-link to the most recent EIE episode.

items.title: How Should One Read a Book?
items.creator: Virginia Woolf
items.why: Recommended as further reading on the theme of how to approach a book.

items.title: How Substantial Are Non-Substantive Hearings? (XKDR paper on Indian courts)
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: Ajay's defence against the old assumption (held by Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain in the 1990s) that the Bombay High Court is 'absolutely horrible, nothing will ever get done.' The paper shows the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably effective and improving — meaning the case for keeping a quasi-judicial function inside SEBI has weakened.

items.title: How The Desperate Norwegian Salmon Industry Created A Sushi Staple
items.creator: Jess Jiang
items.why: Source for the episode's opening parable that 'authentic' culture is often a foreign marketing fix from yesterday.

items.title: How the vaccine story will play out
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: A first-principles forecast written before the COVID vaccines existed; useful as a worked example of applying the public-policy toolkit to a real pandemic.

items.title: How the War Was Won: Air-Sea Power and Allied Victory in World War II
items.creator: Phillips Payson O'Brien
items.why: Even a lifelong student of the subject (Ajay) found it 'full of new knowledge and new insights.' The systems-destruction lens it builds maps directly onto how Ukraine is fighting today: degrade the enemy's logistics and command-and-control, not just take ground.

items.title: How This Nobel Has Redefined Literature
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Self-recommended as the seed of the show's central claim — that literature is not bound to the printed page, that it is words and storytelling, and that on those grounds Dylan, and Springsteen, qualify.

items.title: How to Correctly Draw the Perimeter for Government Software Systems (Big Ideas, Episode 20)
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The fuller version of Ajay's IRCTC point: the government should expose data via APIs and let private aggregators (ClearTrip, MakeMyTrip) build the user-facing layer, rather than building consumer products itself.

items.title: How To Know a Person
items.creator: David Brooks
items.why: Resonated deeply with what Amit has learned doing long-form podcasting — the power of long conversations, of learning to listen, of intentionality in friendship. Brooks himself came to it late in life: Oprah told him on his second appearance, six or seven years after the first, how much he had changed.

items.title: How to Miss By a Mile: An Alternative Look at Uber's Potential Market Size
items.creator: Bill Gurley
items.why: The pivot of the parable. Gurley's reframing showed why disruptors can never be sized using incumbent markets and prompted Damodaran's revaluation to ~$28 billion.

items.title: How to Read a Book
items.creator: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
items.why: The backbone of Amit's whole 'how to read non-fiction' section. Adler's four-step analytical reading and his concept of synoptical reading — building entry points into a subject across many books — are the sturdiest scaffolding the show offers.

items.title: How to Read and Why
items.creator: Harold Bloom
items.why: Source of the show's best reading rules: slow down for short stories (the writer leaves explanations for you to discern); memorize poems (first you belong to the poem, then it belongs to you); read Shakespeare, then watch, then read again.

items.title: How to Write a Paper (Everything is Everything, episode 62)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The companion to today's question of how to read a paper — Ajay refers back to it when telling listeners that even non-specialists can extract value from the literature once they know the rhythm.

items.title: How to Write Well
items.creator: Tim de Lisle
items.why: Tim's tenets are about clarity, and Amit uses some of his examples in his own writing course. The book is the source of the dictum that shaped young Amit: 'When in doubt, play your shots.'

items.title: How Will You Measure Your Life?
items.creator: Clayton Christensen
items.why: Direct extension of the inner-scorecard idea — Christensen's framework for evaluating a life by the things that won't show up on any external metric.

items.title: Huberman Lab episode on growth mindset
items.creator: Andrew Huberman
items.why: How Amit found his way into the Mueller-Dweck paper. Recommended as a clean entry point for anyone who wants to understand why effort-based feedback matters in their own and their kids' lives.

items.title: Huntsville, Alabama
items.why: Ajay's 'oddball' recommendation — visit it but more importantly study it. A live demonstration of how concentrating scientific talent in one place compounds, over generations, into a regional engineering powerhouse. The deep lesson about clusters and patience that runs through the episode.

items.title: Hussain Haidry, Hindustani Musalmaan (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 275)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Hussain Haidry
items.why: The episode that surfaced Hussain's reflection on the loneliness of being mobbed by the right wing — the seed of Amit's wider point about the chilling effect of mobs on discourse.

items.title: I'm Gonna Crawl
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: Ajay considers it 'one of the great things' Robert Plant, Jimmy Page, John Paul Jones, and Bonzo did. They were at the peak of their powers — and a poignant pick because Bonham died shortly after.

items.title: I'm on Fire
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit's example that Springsteen's universalising trick works even on subjects as un-metaphysical as lust. The repeated chorus refuses metaphor; the verse image of waking soaked in sweat with a freight train inside one's head does the rest.

items.title: I, Pencil — The Movie
items.why: The visual, animated rendering of Read's parable for those who learn better by watching than reading.

items.title: I, Robot: The Man Behind the Google Phone
items.creator: John Markoff
items.why: The reporting behind the late-evening, before-the-Macro-term-sheet story Ajay tells about how Android landed at Google.

items.title: Ideas of India
items.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Amit's favourite Indian podcast — Shruti does an incredible job of bringing diverse perspectives and rigorous analysis on India.

items.title: Identifying the Real SBO: A critique of the LinkedIn and Samsung Orders
items.creator: Chirag Motwani and Ananya Badaga
items.why: On Ajay's reading list as a worked example of how India's beneficial-ownership disclosure regime, downstream of FATF, has played out in problematic real cases.

items.title: ifrogs.org papers and xkdr.org firms-finance research
items.creator: IFRoGS and XKDR Forum
items.why: The empirical and theoretical bedrock of the Indian bankruptcy reform debate — for anyone who wants to actually understand the IBC rather than opine on it.

items.title: IIT Bombay Educational Outreach (CDEEP)
items.creator: D.B. Phatak and IIT Bombay
items.why: Ajay's exemplar of how to scale a great teacher to a country: one camera, one good lecturer, no rationing. Live proof that knowledge can be uncoupled from credentialism.

items.title: Illiberal Reformers
items.creator: Thomas Leonard
items.why: The uncomfortable origin story. Many early-20th-century minimum wage laws were explicitly designed by their authors to keep African-Americans, immigrants, and women out of the labour force. The privileged protecting themselves, dressed up as compassion.

items.title: Imagined Communities
items.creator: Benedict Anderson
items.why: Amit's favourite book on the subject and the spine of the episode. Source of the episode's central definition, the three paradoxes (modernity vs antiquity, universal vs particular, political force vs philosophical nebulousness), and the insistence that nations must be both 'limited' and 'sovereign' to make sense as a concept.

items.title: Implications of US Tariffs
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The detailed economic case that the destruction of existing global supply chains is 'tantamount to throwing bombs on present production facilities' — a direct reduction in the world's capital stock.

items.title: Impossible Germany
items.creator: Wilco
items.why: Mid-episode music recommendation — playful, unrelated to finance, and a fitting nod to the Impossible Trinity discussion that just preceded it.

items.title: Improving Governance Using Large IT Systems
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Source of the IRCTC-style argument that IT systems are valuable not for glamour but for converting high-discretion frontline interactions into low-discretion, transparent ones — and conversely, why a 'good IT system' celebrated for its own sake is precisely the trap.

items.title: In Defence of Tanmay Bhat
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: An earlier instance of the same principle Amit applied to the YouTuber in this episode — defend the speech rights of the disliked, the unfunny, and the tasteless.

items.title: In My Tribe
items.creator: Arnold Kling
items.why: Amit's complementary recommendation to the book — Kling continues to extend and refine the three-languages framework on the newsletter.

items.title: In search of inclusion
items.creator: Renuka Sane and Susan Thomas
items.why: Listed as further reading on extending pension coverage to the Indian workforce beyond the civil service.

items.title: In the Beginning... Was the Command Line
items.creator: Neal Stephenson
items.why: Not an engineering book — a novelist who 'gets the dream, gets the philosophy.' The instinctive, passionate telling of what makes the command line and Unix special.

items.title: India = Migration (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 128)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: Long-form version of Tumbe's argument that India's defining internal phenomenon is people moving — and most of all, women moving on marriage.

items.title: India Grows at Night
items.creator: Gurcharan Das
items.why: Amit invokes the title to capture his second point: the Indian state is so absent and so extractive for most citizens that asking whether it is 'legitimate' is almost a category error. We don't grant it legitimacy — we route around it.

items.title: India in the Nuclear Age (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 80)
items.creator: Amit Varma with General Prakash Menon
items.why: The counter-intuitive thesis nuclear weapons make conventional war more important, not less — directly supporting Ajay's 'principle one' that nukes do not obsolete conventional war.

items.title: India in the Persianate Age
items.creator: Richard Eaton
items.why: Source for the argument that Mughal India's high share of world GDP, and its eventual decline, may have come from how globalising port trade pulled power away from the imperial centre toward the coastal edges. A favourite of the Mughal historians on Amit's longer show.

items.title: India's Far From Free Markets
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Self-recommended companion piece on the unfinished business of India's economic reforms, the same theme that runs through Ajay's argument that 1991 didn't go far enough on state capacity.

items.title: India's Financial Globalisation
items.creator: Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik
items.why: Background for the 'Mr. Capital' argument — why foreign capital is structurally cheaper for Indian firms, and why interfering with capital-account flows is interfering with Indian firm productivity.

items.title: India's Founding Moment
items.creator: Madhav Khosla
items.why: Source of the framing that the Constitution was a 'pedagogical exercise' as much as a rulebook — written by elites who felt they had to teach a fractious country how to think, and which Amit views with a mix of sympathy and unease.

items.title: India's MSME Landscape — Some Useful Frameworks (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 419)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy
items.why: Ajay calls it one of the best Seen and the Unseen episodes he has experienced — expensive, difficult fieldwork brought into a single conversation, taking the listener inside the mind of how business actually runs in India and what is going wrong on the ground.

items.title: India's Tryst With Pandemics (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 205)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Chinmay Tumbe
items.why: The longer conversation in which Tumbe lays out why COVID was always going to evolve toward mildness — the same evolutionary logic that played out across previous pandemics.

items.title: India's Water Crisis (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 60)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vishwanath S (zenrainman)
items.why: Connects the dots between MSPs for water-intensive crops, free farm electricity, bore wells, and the depletion of the water table — a textbook chain of bad incentives.

items.title: India, Pakistan, Kashmir: We Won't Need To Fight A War If We Can Win The Peace
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: His own crystallisation of the Galula-Petraeus argument as it applies to India: if Kashmir is an integral part of India, Kashmiris are Indians, and the state's job is to serve them — not to occupy them.

items.title: India: Cookbook
items.creator: Pushpesh Pant
items.why: Source of the Vasco da Gama spice-cargo statistic (1,500 tons of pepper, 28 of ginger, 8 of cinnamon, 7 of cloves) and the case that Indian cuisine has always been a two-way exchange — they brought leavened bread, baking, noodles; we sent back curry, mango, chutney.

items.title: Indiahikes.com
items.why: Ajay has not used them as a services firm but rates their website highly: for almost any hike in India, often the best page — story, route, map — and you can jump from there to Google Earth.

items.title: Indian Bankruptcy Reforms: Where We Are and How To Move Forward
items.creator: Ajay Shah and others
items.why: Annual snapshots that let you trace how the IBC's promise was eroded year by year — a model of serious public-domain commentary on a reform in flight.

items.title: Indian Defence Strategy: Forces, Potential and Procurement Disasters
items.creator: Perun
items.why: Ajay urges viewers to watch the full video themselves. His own summary, he says, is just a stage-setter; the video is rigorous, data-rich, and worth the full hour.

items.title: Indian Economic Strategy in the New Globalisation
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: The single coherent argument behind this episode — what India should do in a world where 33% of global trade has gone rogue. The whole episode is a verbal walk through this paper.

items.title: Inside the CIA Mission to Haul Plutonium Up the Himalayas
items.creator: Robert Beckhusen
items.why: The American end of the story Ajay tells. The article walks through how the CIA recruited America's elite mountaineers one by one, sworn to silence in exchange for an all-expenses-paid Himalayan climb.

items.title: Insiders and Outsiders
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The post that crystallised for Amit why he no longer dismisses the engineers building inside government, even as he keeps griping at the state from outside. He notes that much of the clarity of that piece came through conversations with Ajay.

items.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Reforms in India
items.creator: Susan Thomas (editor)
items.why: The standing reference work on the IBC's design and early performance — the kind of book that anchors a knowledge community around a reform.

items.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Reforms in India: 10 Years After the IBC
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: A live attempt to reconstitute the bankruptcy research community in India — exactly the kind of knowledge-ecosystem activity Ajay argues the country needs more of.

items.title: Integration of the Indian States
items.creator: V.P. Menon
items.why: Listed in the show's resources alongside Basu's biography as a primary source for the nation-building story.

items.title: International Diversification Calculation Spreadsheet
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Lets you see for yourself how the equity premium and global diversification interact across long horizons — but presented with the explicit warning that no single spreadsheet can answer the retirement question.

items.title: Into the Wild
items.creator: Jon Krakauer
items.why: Tucked in alongside Into Thin Air. Different terrain, same author, same gift for the wilderness as a moral test.

items.title: Into Thin Air
items.creator: Jon Krakauer
items.why: The defining text on summit-fever decision-making. On the last day above the dead zone you have to ask, cold and rational, whether you can make it to the top and back; every accident on Everest is a wrong answer to that question.

items.title: Introduction to Modern Climate Change
items.creator: Andrew E. Dessler
items.why: Climate change is 'one of the great crises of the modern world right up there alongside populism' and you'll get the gist from this single book. Sensibly written, accessible to non-specialists.

items.title: Inventing Money
items.creator: Nicholas Dunbar
items.why: Ajay's view: the better of the two books on LTCM. Also covers the Black-Scholes model and the deeper finance theory that led to the disaster.

items.title: Inverted Anti-Suicide Logic (Bengali Theory)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: If you can kill yourself any time, including ten minutes from now, then the option is never closed — so you might as well do something now that makes you happier instead. Recommended only with the disclaimer that anyone with suicidal thoughts should also seek real help.

items.title: Inverting the Pyramid
items.creator: Jonathan Wilson
items.why: Amit's argument that watching sport tribally ('my team is winning') is shallow, but watching it as a chess game (which every sport is, underneath) is great intellectual fun. Wilson's book is the gateway for football.

items.title: Investment Risk in Indian Pension Sector and Role for Pension Guarantees
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The paper that grounds Ajay's warning about the UPS guarantee: a guaranteed pension is a put option on the portfolio, and put options can be very expensive. He invokes this work directly when asking whether the UPS guarantee is fiscally affordable.

items.title: Invisible Infrastructure (Everything is Everything, episode 82)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Amit predicts this phrase will appear in the title of a future Ajay book. The episode anchors the argument that beyond visible roads and ports, advanced economies run on invisible infrastructure — norms, contracts, dispute resolution — that India still needs to build.

items.title: IPCC Reports
items.creator: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
items.why: Ajay is 'normally very skeptical' about international-body reports (World Bank, IMF — bland, written by committee), but the IPCC's are awesome. Written by committees of scientists with proper processes for discussion and debate, they show state-of-the-art thinking AND portray the disagreements (clutch of models, range of scenarios). 'Just look at all the pictures' — the graphics will change the way you look at the world.

items.title: Is Google Making Us Stupid?
items.creator: Nicholas Carr
items.why: The seed argument behind Amit's claim that swipe-swipe leisure and book leisure are not interchangeable: the structure of your engagement physically rewires the brain, and the internet rewires it shallow.

items.title: Is Old Music Killing New Music?
items.creator: Ted Gioia
items.why: Amit thought his slow-down on new music was just personal aging — Gioia's data showed it's a structural phenomenon. Sets up the larger question of what has happened to the music industry since 'rock began when Dylan went electric and ended when Kurt Cobain [died].'

items.title: Is Your Impact Evaluation Asking Questions That Matter? A Four Part Smell Test
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Practical handbook for the long-road-to-change argument — a smell test for whether an impact evaluation is asking the question that matters or only the one that's tractable.

items.title: Is-Ought Problem
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: Linked as the philosophical guardrail for the entire episode: you cannot derive what ought to be from what is. Men being 'wired' for promiscuity does not make promiscuity right.

items.title: Jab We Met
items.creator: Imtiaz Ali
items.why: A train and a journey set off the change. A textbook Voyage-and-Return that is also a romance.

items.title: Jackson Katz on the passive voice in violence against women
items.creator: Jackson Katz
items.why: The clearest contemporary illustration of Havel's claim that language shapes reality — a passive voice silently rewrites a moral situation.

items.title: James C. Scott's principle: do things you can undo
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: Ajay quotes it as the cleanest one-line argument against the death penalty — Scott himself adds the heartbreaking footnote that this is one of the reasons he opposes capital punishment.

items.title: James Heckman / The Heckman Equation
items.creator: James Heckman
items.why: The cold ROI case for redirecting effort to ages 0 to 5. The right starting point for any parent, philanthropist, or policymaker who wants to know where their marginal rupee actually changes a life.

items.title: Jan Koum on charging for WhatsApp
items.creator: Jan Koum (clip)
items.why: Koum's reasoning: the dollar wasn't for revenue, it was a brake on growth — to keep the user base small enough that servers and customer service could keep up. A counterintuitive lesson on intentionally throttling your scale.

items.title: Jan-Krzysztof Duda interviewed by Sagar Shah
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: Duda himself confirms his contribution would have mattered more in a tiebreak than in classical — a useful corrective to neat narratives about why prep paid off.

items.title: Japanese Kit Kat Flavours — The Complete List
items.creator: Japan Candy Store
items.why: Showcase of what radical product localisation looks like — green tea, sake, wasabi, sakura. The aesthetic argument for adaptive product design across heterogeneous markets.

items.title: Jaws
items.creator: Steven Spielberg
items.why: Watch it once with Beowulf in mind: the call, the initial success, the confrontation, the final ordeal, the miraculous escape. Same five-act spine.

items.title: Jayaprakash Narayan Wants to Mend Our Democracy (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 334)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
items.why: The episode that first alerted Amit to the pensions crisis — JP Narayan told him this was the one issue keeping him up at night, and it set Amit on the path to making this episode.

items.title: Jeff Bezos on product and marketing
items.creator: Jeff Bezos
items.why: Build something good and word of mouth does the work. The reason a five-percent marketing optimum may exist but isn't worth optimising for if it costs you product bandwidth.

items.title: Jensen Huang on not wearing a watch
items.creator: Jensen Huang
items.why: 'Now is the most important time' — the watch is a constant prompt to be elsewhere; refusing to wear one is a small commitment to total presence.

items.title: Jensen Huang on work and suffering
items.creator: Jensen Huang
items.why: He doesn't feel joy every day toward his company — he feels love. The distinction between joy (a feeling) and love (a posture) is doing real work.

items.title: Jensen Huang's fish-pond metaphor
items.creator: Jensen Huang
items.why: An NVIDIA-scale demonstration that you don't have to fight for the pond — you can build a lake. Mission-bigger-than-yourself as a market-creation strategy.

items.title: Jerry Seinfeld on early naysayers
items.creator: Jerry Seinfeld (clip)
items.why: The clip behind Amit's Seinfeld pilot story. A working artefact for why customer focus groups misread genuine novelty.

items.title: Jhumpa Lahiri on Writing, Translation, and Crossing Between Cultures (Episode 17, Conversations With Tyler)
items.creator: Tyler Cowen with Jhumpa Lahiri
items.why: Amit's gateway to Agota Kristof — Lahiri cited Kristof as a model for her own late-in-life language acquisition. A conversation about literally crossing into a new language as an adult, the most intimate possible border-crossing.

items.title: Jim Goetz on pain points
items.creator: Jim Goetz (clip)
items.why: Cited as part of the cluster of founders who insist that real businesses begin with a pain point — a lived itch — not with a top-down search for a market hole.

items.title: Joan Didion (general)
items.why: Cited as the source of one of his favourite lines about writing: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down.' Didion is held up as a model of writing as self-discovery.

items.title: Joan Miro (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: Provided so listeners can read for themselves how Miro stripped down towards the essential and what his late minimalism really was.

items.title: Johan Norberg's work
items.creator: Johan Norberg
items.why: Norberg's key correction to the romanticised Indian view of Sweden: those countries became advanced economies through free markets and easy private entrepreneurship first, and only added a welfare state on top once the underlying invisible infrastructure was already in place.

items.title: John Collison on passion
items.creator: John Collison
items.why: An invitation to see infrastructure and institutions as accumulated stubbornness. Pairs with Ajay's Turkish proverb on the asymmetry of building and burning.

items.title: John Coltrane on Desire
items.creator: John Coltrane
items.why: Ammunition against the excuse that you can't pursue a craft because you lack the right tool. Shakespeare didn't say 'I don't have a laptop, I'm not gonna write.' Sincerity and passion are the prerequisites; gear is not.

items.title: Jonathan Haidt's work on social media and teenage girls
items.creator: Jonathan Haidt
items.why: Cited as the documented case for how the projected selves of others on social media have a particularly harmful impact on adolescent girls.

items.title: Jonathan Ive on saying no to things you love
items.creator: Jonathan Ive (interview)
items.why: Jobs's rule, as told to Ive: even something that keeps you up at night, that you wake up thinking about, must sometimes be said no to — because focus is decided in advance, not by enthusiasm.

items.title: Jugalbandi: The BJP Before Modi
items.creator: Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Recommended alongside Half-Lion as part of Sitapati's larger reading of post-Independence Indian political economy.

items.title: Jules et Jim
items.creator: Francois Truffaut
items.why: An archetypal modern tragedy with the same Macbeth/Lolita skeleton. Watch it once you know what to look for, and the structure pops out.

items.title: Julius Caesar
items.creator: William Shakespeare
items.why: Useful for testing the trope: the play is named for Caesar but the tragic arc belongs to Brutus. A reminder to look past the title to find the real protagonist of an archetype.

items.title: Jungle Lore
items.creator: Jim Corbett
items.why: The third in Ajay's recommended Corbett trilogy — together they document the arc from sport hunter to compassionate hunter of man-eaters to staunch conservationist.

items.title: Jungleland
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Ajay's case study for how a long song earns its length by changing modes. Where Stairway to Heaven starts with an alaap and builds, Jungleland inverts the form — wall of sound, guitar solo, the saxophone passage Springsteen calls the world's greatest, then a quiet coda that does the alaap at the end. Ajay also uses it to demonstrate his 'every live version in chronological order' practice; the 1976 and 2012 versions, he says, are different songs sung by a different man.

items.title: Just
items.creator: Radiohead
items.why: A different Radiohead song than the self-pity-on-loop hit. The video is itself a masterpiece worth watching. (Show notes will link it.)

items.title: Karthik Muralidharan Examines the Indian State (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 290)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: One of the long-form conversations where Karthik laid out the data on India's state size, scale, and governance challenges.

items.title: Katadyn gravity-fed water filter (BeFree 6L)
items.why: Ajay's standard kit on his hikes — fill, hang, gravity does the rest, perfect clean water at the output. A big gain that many in India aren't yet using.

items.title: Kavitha Rao and Our Lady Doctors (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 235)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Kavitha Rao
items.why: The companion conversation to 'Lady Doctors' — the long form discussion of these pioneering women's lives.

items.title: Keeping India Safe (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 219)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sushant Singh
items.why: Companion deep-dive on Indian defence and national security from The Seen and the Unseen — listed in the show notes as further reading.

items.title: Kefirwala kefir grain
items.why: Ajay's source for high-quality kefir starter. Part of his broader plea that fermentation — sourdough, kefir — is a Pareto-superior way to eat, even if India's 36C climate fights the 20C optimum.

items.title: Kevin Hale on marketing
items.creator: Kevin Hale
items.why: The line that anchors Amit's chapter on product over marketing — and his own personal philosophy with The Seen and the Unseen.

items.title: Kevin Systrom on a bias for action
items.creator: Kevin Systrom (clip)
items.why: Systrom: don't run a six-month private beta — put your product in the world, find the hundred who love it, and let real users teach you what's broken.

items.title: Kitaben Bahut Si
items.creator: Anu Malik (composer), Zafar Gorakhpuri (lyricist), from the film Baazigar
items.why: Amit reads its lyrics as a thesis against credentialism: bookish knowledge is irrelevant, real knowledge is local. It frames the whole episode's argument that national firms must learn to honour local knowledge.

items.title: Knowledge Lost and Knowledge Regained (Everything is Everything, episode 63)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay invokes it directly: once a country is cut off from international trade, knowledge, and expertise, its ability to participate is fundamentally contaminated. The USSR experience showed that 'self-reliance' under sanctions does not catch up — it falls further behind.

items.title: Kohrra
items.creator: Sudip Sharma
items.why: Cited as evidence of brilliant Indian storytelling and as a casting source — Ajay would cast Suvinder Vicky from Kohrra to play Montek. Vicky's range of restraint and authority is the right register for the character.

items.title: Kothaligad
items.creator: Day-hike route in Maharashtra
items.why: Another of Ajay's named day-hike picks for first-timers in the Maharashtra region.

items.title: Lady Doctors
items.creator: Kavitha Rao
items.why: Where Amit first encountered Haimabati Sen. Every subject in the book had to be remarkable simply to enter medicine in the 19th century — but Haimabati's child-widowhood-to-doctor arc stands out even there.

items.title: Lancelot Pinto tweet on respecting patients
items.creator: Lancelot Pinto
items.why: The good-doctor attitude in one line: an informed patient is an ally, not a threat. It leads into Ajay's worry that most Indian doctors never read the literature, and his hope that AI, fed a patient's full history, can beat most doctors.

items.title: Lant Pritchett's key works (papers, blog posts and podcast episodes)
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: Amit calls his work eye-opening and absolutely brilliant — built on hardcore real-world data, not intentions. Two papers in particular underwrite the episode: that ~99% of cross-country variation in poverty rates is explained by median income, and that economic growth is both necessary and sufficient for development.

items.title: Lanterne Rouge Cycling Podcast
items.creator: Patrick Broe and Benji Naesen
items.why: Pairs naturally with Horner — different lens, deeper detail. Their Tour de France preview is a model of how to set up a multi-week sporting event for a viewer.

items.title: Las Meninas
items.creator: Diego Velazquez
items.why: Amit's central exhibit for late mastery in this episode — a painting whose complete technical command is so absorbed it disappears, leaving only the layered, meta, light-and-depth play that no 25-year-old Velazquez could have produced.

items.title: Lawrence Freedman on Substack
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: The closest thing to a continuous masterclass in strategic analysis being written today — Amit thanks God for it.

items.title: Lay Lady Lay
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: Ajay deploys the song to defeat Amit's claim that Dylan can't sing — there are some songs only Dylan can sing, and the nasal twang on 'Lay, lady, lay, lay across my big brass bed' is uncoverable. (He also has a story of playing it for Ayush Patnaik, who didn't believe it was Dylan.)

items.title: Layla
items.creator: Derek and the Dominoes
items.why: Amit insists on the original studio version: 'be sure to find the right version, it is not the lame Eric Clapton unplugged version' — Duane Allman's slide work is what makes the song a masterpiece. (Amit later softens — the unplugged version 'is very good' — but the original is the real thing.)

items.title: Learning to Eat Soup with a Knife: Counterinsurgency Lessons from Malaya and Vietnam
items.creator: John Nagl
items.why: The institutional-learning question — why some militaries absorb lessons and others don't. Pairs naturally with Galula and Kaplan: Galula tells you what to do, Nagl tells you why your organisation will probably refuse to do it.

items.title: Led Zeppelin
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: A playful but earnest recommendation: invest in great music. Compounds in joy what equity compounds in money.

items.title: Lenin's Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire
items.creator: David Remnick
items.why: A great narrative about how a society struggles with itself in dealing with an authoritarian state, and how the possibilities for progress are damaged for a very long time. Doubly interesting today because we know what Remnick didn't — that Russia was about to slide back to hell under Putin. As Gordon Brown said, the rule of law is a difficult project for the first 500 years.

items.title: Let It Be
items.creator: The Replacements
items.why: The home of 'Answering Machine' — and a chance for Amit to make his cheerful, contrarian case for The Replacements over the Beatles on the question of who owns that album title.

items.title: Letters to Chief Ministers
items.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
items.why: A working demonstration that writing is a way of thinking. Modern Indian politicians of any party do nothing of the sort, and that is itself a great loss.

items.title: Letters to Olga
items.creator: Václav Havel
items.why: Source of the line that ends conversations in this house: 'If I am to be punished, let it be for who I am. If I am to be free, let it be as myself.'

items.title: Life and Labour of the People in London
items.creator: Charles Booth
items.why: Cited approvingly via Biju Rao as the kind of 'dying breed' of magisterial multi-method inquiry the modern academy no longer rewards — proof that the disciplinary silos are an accident of 20th-century institutional incentives, not a feature of how reality is best studied.

items.title: Life in the Fast Lane
items.creator: Eagles
items.why: Amit quotes the lines: 'They knew all the right people, they took all the right pills, they threw outrageous parties, they paid heavenly bills.' Used as a warning against the cosmetic, pharmacological, social-mimicry life — a life lived through props.

items.title: Life Lessons (segment of New York Stories)
items.creator: Martin Scorsese
items.why: A masterpiece Amit first saw as a kid when his father was administrative director of the Film Institute of Pune. It is the source of the phrase that named Amit and Ajay's course Life Lessons, and where Amit first heard 'A Whiter Shade of Pale' — over a slow-motion shot of a cigarette falling and bouncing before a foot crushes it. A piece of editing magic he still remembers 25 years later.

items.title: Life's Grandeur: The Spread of Excellence From Plato to Darwin
items.creator: Stephen Jay Gould
items.why: Cited for its analysis of how baseball's tinkering with rules — a rare domain where 'central planning' actually works because complexity is bounded — illustrates how constraints redefine a sport.

items.title: Lifespan: Why We Age — and Why We Don't Have To
items.creator: David Sinclair
items.why: Recommended in tandem with Roshan Abbas as the corrective to the assumption that long life means decades of dementia. Sinclair argues for compressed morbidity — vitality stretched, decline shortened. Without this premise, Ajay's 'extended lifespan = extended possibility' frame collapses.

items.title: LifeStraw bottle
items.why: Output cleaner than any tap water in India. Self-sufficient hydration in places where carrying enough clean water is impossible.

items.title: Like a Rolling Stone: Bob Dylan at the Crossroads
items.creator: Greil Marcus
items.why: Amit cites Marcus as a model of what serious music criticism can do. Marcus's review of Born to Run famously described Backstreets as so stately it could be the prelude to a rock-and-roll Iliad; Amit says Marcus put into words what he had always felt but couldn't name.

items.title: Lincoln
items.creator: Steven Spielberg
items.why: Ajay calls it an eye-opener — proof that political reform is not about explosions or set-piece battles but about the patient legal struggle to pass a single amendment through Congress, persuading one mind at a time. A masterclass in the long game of democratic change.

items.title: Lines on Maps Are Toxic! (Everything is Everything, episode 51)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Worth listening to for the case that the world is becoming less geographically destined — that internet-mediated communities of choice are slowly displacing communities of circumstance.

items.title: Listen, The Internet Has SPACE
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Connects to the lost 200,000 words on Jane Jacobs in The Power Broker. Today, an author could simply put the remainder online; the constraint that destroyed that text no longer exists.

items.title: Live Chess Ratings (2700chess.com)
items.why: The reference Amit uses for Arjun's rise past 2800 (peak 2809) and the live world rankings that decide who gets super-tournament invitations.

items.title: Lolita
items.creator: Vladimir Nabokov
items.why: Humbert's affair as the dreamlike phase that curdles into the nightmare — a key piece of evidence for Booker's claim that wildly different works share one underlying structure.

items.title: Long As I Can See the Light
items.creator: Chris Cornell
items.why: The cover Amit promises to send Ajay during recording — 'a great song, and I'll send you a great cover of the song.' A glimpse of Amit's musical evangelism on the side.

items.title: Looking beyond the label 'algorithmic trading'
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The longer version of his 'sack the peasants' / 'live above the API' argument — humans should compose symphonies, computers should be the diligent clerks executing the trades humans have designed.

items.title: Lord of the Flies
items.creator: William Golding
items.why: Amit's revised diagnosis of the modern social-media dystopia: he spent his life worried about 1984 (state-imposed misery) and stumbled, almost without noticing, into Lord of the Flies (peer-imposed misery). You don't even need a state to make people miserable.

items.title: Lost a Shock Absorber
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's argument on what is lost when the central bank's shock-absorber function is impaired — relevant to the engine-room mechanics of monetary policy described in the episode.

items.title: Louie
items.creator: Louis C.K.
items.why: Source of the 'bang bang' bit — eating a complete meal at one restaurant, walking out, and immediately eating another complete meal of a different cuisine at the next. Amit's COVID-era biryani-plus-pizza days qualify.

items.title: Ludwig von Mises — A Primer
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: An accessible doorway into Austrian economics for readers who do not want to start with Human Action.

items.title: Luke Burgis Sees the Deer at His Window (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 337)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Luke Burgis
items.why: The episode where the thin-desire/thick-desire frame was developed, drawing on Burgis's reading of Girard.

items.title: Lunapark
items.creator: Luna
items.why: Recommended as the natural next step after On Fire — Dean Wareham's later band, in the same lineage.

items.title: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
items.creator: Rob Henderson
items.why: The seminal short piece that gives the show its title — read it for the original framing in Henderson's own words.

items.title: LYN tweet — 'Too broke to smoke crack, gotta get up and make it happen.'
items.creator: LYN
items.why: If you want something badly enough — addictively enough — you will find a way. The same energy as a dope head wanting crack, channelled into a creative life.

items.title: M Govinda Rao on the post-tariff response
items.creator: M Govinda Rao
items.why: Personal recommendation — Ajay calls him out specifically as 'my ex-boss' worth reading on this.

items.title: Macbeth
items.creator: William Shakespeare
items.why: An archetypal tragedy. Reading it alongside Lolita and Jules et Jim is how Booker himself derived the pattern.

items.title: Machines of Loving Grace
items.creator: Dario Amodei
items.why: Ajay says he is not a crazy boosters of technological paradises, but he finds Amodei sensible and thoughtful and the essay 'makes you think.' Recommended as a serious meditation on what will happen as AI advances.

items.title: Madame George (cover)
items.creator: Marianne Faithfull
items.why: Amit calls it a 'glorious ethereal cover' — one of the two covers he pairs with the original.

items.title: Madame George (cover)
items.creator: Luka Bloom
items.why: Amit found this cover during his January hospital stay and has been evangelising it since — a more recent discovery to set against the long-known Faithfull version.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen on getting his way
items.creator: Take Take Take
items.why: The second leg of the jeansgate saga, including Carlsen's 'no grown-ups in FIDE' line and his dismissals of Anand and Sutovsky.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen on Jeansgate
items.creator: Take Take Take
items.why: The primary source where Carlsen calls out FIDE, dismisses Anand and Sutovsky, and invokes Dvorkovich — the basis of Amit's power-corrupts argument.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen Ranks the Candidates Players
items.creator: Magnus Carlsen
items.why: Referenced as the controversy-before-the-tournament backdrop. Carlsen's ranking turned out wrong on Gukesh, but Amit notes Carlsen 'got it right' on the average — what he missed was that Gukesh was high-variance with a high ceiling.

items.title: Magnus Carlsen's interview on Take Take Take about Freestyle Chess
items.creator: Take Take Take
items.why: Source for Carlsen's claim that classical preparation has become drudgery and his pivot to a freestyle world tour.

items.title: Main Aai Hoon U.P. Bihar Lootne
items.creator: Anu Malik / Sameer (lyricist), from the film Shool
items.why: Amit's playful pivot song after Ajay's argument for hyperlocal markets — a step towards thinking UP-Bihar rather than national, even if not yet hyperlocal.

items.title: Make Me a Canteen for My Soul (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 304)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sameer Seth and Yash Bhanage
items.why: Source of the moving Bombay Canteen project where Indians mailed in their grandmothers' recipes and the restaurant cooked them as a one-day menu — a model for participatory cultural preservation.

items.title: Making Policy Fun with Khyati Pathak and Friends (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 374)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Khyati Pathak, Anupam Manur and Pranay Kotasthane
items.why: Released just before this episode, and the source of the Bangalore-water-pricing example and the broader conversation about counterintuitive uses of the price system that make up the episode's final chapter.

items.title: Making Regulation in India Work Better
items.creator: K.P. Krishnan
items.why: The senior civil servant who launched the FSLRC project from inside the Department of Economic Affairs explains the practitioner's view of why the regulatory state went wrong and how to fix it.

items.title: Making Sense
items.creator: Sam Harris
items.why: Amit recommends it specifically as a study of the art of conversation — its flow and rhythm shaped his sense of how interviews can be conducted.

items.title: Making the way for nuclear energy in India
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: The fullest written form of the five-pillar argument the episode summarises. Anyone wanting to act on the policy ideas — import freedom, direct sale to private buyers, CISF-style security, IAEA compliance, civil nuclear liability reform — should read this directly.

items.title: MAMI 2018 Live Tweet Thread
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Linked in the show notes as a reading list of the year's films, written in real time — a way for listeners to use Amit's surface area as their own.

items.title: MAMI 2019 Live Tweet Thread
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Companion to the 2018 thread; the show notes link both.

items.title: MAMI Film Festival
items.creator: Mumbai Academy of Moving Image
items.why: Amit's annual vacation: four films a day for ten days. He frames it as a deliberate investment in his own surface area — by being in Mumbai near the venues, he is luckier in cinema than he would be anywhere else.

items.title: Man's Search for Meaning
items.creator: Viktor Frankl
items.why: Source of the point that for concentration-camp inmates, holding onto literature — actually or just by remembering and discussing it — was a wellspring of solace. Reading tells us we are not alone, and that this too shall pass.

items.title: Man-Eaters of Kumaon
items.creator: Jim Corbett
items.why: Ajay grew up around Corbett's books; they are the gateway drug to a lifetime of mountains and forests. 'Everybody will enjoy them.'

items.title: Manifold Destiny
items.creator: Sylvia Nasar and David Gruber
items.why: Background and depth on the Grigori Perelman story Ajay tells, and on why Perelman walked away from journals and the million-dollar Clay prize.

items.title: Marc Andreessen on early naysayers
items.creator: Marc Andreessen (clip)
items.why: Andreessen's reminder that the telephone was once thought to be a tool for telegraph operators, the internet was a curiosity, and the car was a rich man's toy. Useful armour against the well-meaning skeptic.

items.title: Margaret Atwood, Ursula Le Guin, Ted Chiang, Ken Liu
items.creator: Various
items.why: Amit's general blanket recommendation for serious science fiction — because the genre 'grapples with the biggest questions of the time and the questions that today's philosophers haven't begun to answer, but tomorrow's philosophers must.'

items.title: Marginal Revolution
items.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: A live counter-example to the claim that academic writing must be turgid. Amit cites Cowen and Tabarrok as economists who write academic ideas in clear prose; if you are an academic looking for a model, this is one.

items.title: Marginal Revolution / Marginal Revolution University / Emergent Ventures
items.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: An academic-disruptor model in three parts. Few academics have the courage to think aloud every day, in public; fewer still build a free university and reinvent how research capital is allocated. 'It's just beautiful.'

items.title: Marginal Revolution University
items.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
items.why: A miracle of free public education on prices, opportunity cost, and harder concepts — beautifully clear because Cowen and Tabarrok actually understand both the economics and how to teach it. Amit also calls Marginal Revolution the best blog in the world for the past fifteen years.

items.title: Marginlands: Indian Landscapes on the Brink
items.creator: Arati Kumar-Rao
items.why: Contains the desert-navigation-by-bird-flight passage Amit cites — a window into geographies organised by lived relationship rather than the state.

items.title: Mark Strand
items.creator: Mark Strand
items.why: Amit's other proposed replacement for the romantic poets in school curricula — a contemporary the kids could actually fall in love with.

items.title: Mark Zuckerberg on Peter Thiel's advice
items.creator: Startup Archive
items.why: Zuckerberg's account that Thiel told him 'in a world that is changing rapidly, the biggest risk you can take is not changing.' Amit's central anchor for why side gigs and reinvention matter in an AI-era economy.

items.title: Mary Oliver
items.creator: Mary Oliver
items.why: Amit's swap-out for the romantic poets: 'We should be teaching Mary Oliver and Mark Strand instead.' His view is that Shelley/Byron/Keats are over-romanticised, not actually that good, and that they kill young people's love of poetry.

items.title: Massacre in Korea
items.creator: Pablo Picasso
items.why: Amit's pushback against critical disdain — he reads it as a direct descendant of Goya's Third of May and as a masterpiece. Picasso's quote about good artists borrowing and great artists stealing is the frame: stealing here means making something fully your own.

items.title: Maya C. Popa tweet quoting William Faulkner — 'You cannot swim for new horizons unless you have courage to lose sight of the shore.'
items.creator: Maya C. Popa
items.why: Anchors the episode's argument for courage — that doing something new requires letting go of the conventional shore. Maya's Twitter feed is recommended as a whole.

items.title: Mayabono Biharini (from BEDROOM by Somlata)
items.creator: Somlata
items.why: Cited as the kind of 'Rabindro-rap' the Tagore estate's IP-policing has tried to prevent — proof that the work is alive and wants to keep evolving.

items.title: Mera Joota Hai Japani
items.creator: Shailendra (lyrics), Shankar-Jaikishan (music), from Raj Kapoor's Shree 420
items.why: Amit cues it as the anthem of globalization's cultural reality — that hybridity is the real condition of identity, and that monolithic 'pure' nationalism collides with how people actually live.

items.title: Messy: How to Be Creative and Resilient in a Tidy-Minded World
items.creator: Tim Harford
items.why: The case against over-curation. Harford documents how mess and constraint and unfamiliarity force creativity, while comfort and routine produce autopilot mediocrity. Sets the philosophical counterweight to an over-zealous decluttering instinct.

items.title: Michael Pettis interviewed by Forward Guidance
items.creator: Forward Guidance with Michael Pettis
items.why: Ajay calls Pettis 'one of the world's good experts on China' — the conversation is 'absolutely eye-opening' on the local context of Chinese macroeconomics and the global protectionist response China is now triggering.

items.title: Michael's response to Dwarkesh
items.creator: Michael (@mmay3r)
items.why: Michael's frame: to an LLM, a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error, because anything outside its training distribution looks like hallucination. Amit treats this as a partial but suggestive answer.

items.title: Mihir S Sharma on the post-tariff response
items.creator: Mihir S Sharma
items.why: Closes the list of Indian writers thinking carefully about how India should respond to the new global order.

items.title: Mike Dawes interviewed by Rick Beato
items.creator: Rick Beato with Mike Dawes
items.why: Source of the point that Angus Young's three-or-four-chord 'wall of sound' is perfectly suited to ACDC's arena form — a useful corrective to snobbery about technical complexity.

items.title: Mike Moritz on Bill Gates's car radio
items.creator: Mike Moritz
items.why: The story that anchors the obsession chapter — Gates removed the radio so he could think about Microsoft on the drive.

items.title: Milestone
items.creator: Ivan Ayr
items.why: Where Suvinder Vicky was first noticed — Danish Husain mentioned it on Amit's podcast. A subtle, powerful study of an ordinary life that establishes Vicky as the right kind of actor for a story about quiet reformers.

items.title: Miller's Pyramid
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: From Amit's archive of poker-and-life writings collected for this episode.

items.title: Milton Friedman: A Concise Guide to the Ideas and Influence of the Free-Market Economist
items.creator: Eamonn Butler
items.why: Friedman is the bridge between academic economics and public life; Butler's primer is the cleanest short path into him.

items.title: Missing in Action
items.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Raghu S. Jaitley
items.why: Referenced in passing as part of the 'state, society, market' framing Amit pushes back on — a useful book even where one disagrees, because it crystallises the dominant frame in Indian public-policy thinking.

items.title: Modern Principles of Microeconomics
items.creator: Alex Tabarrok and Tyler Cowen
items.why: Source of the line 'a price is a signal wrapped in an incentive' — which Amit calls a perfect compression of Hayek's 'Use of Knowledge.'

items.title: Modern Times
items.creator: Charlie Chaplin
items.why: Ajay invokes it as the popular mental image of manufacturing — vast factories with twenty thousand or fifty thousand obedient workers on an assembly line — that lives in everyone's head when they hear 'economic development.'

items.title: Mohak Mangal
items.creator: Mohak Mangal
items.why: Cited as a young creator who works hard to perform the filtering and sense-making function mainstream media should perform — an example of the new shape, even if the institutional question remains unsolved.

items.title: Mohit Satyanand's newsletter
items.creator: Mohit Satyanand
