items.why: Three years in, and not a single missed Sunday — the demonstration that bloody-minded weekly writing is itself the path to becoming a better writer.

items.title: Monetary Policy is Easy, Financial Regulation is Hard
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The original short statement of the central worked example of the episode — that two superficially similar central-bank activities sit at opposite ends of the difficulty spectrum once decomposed by the four metrics.

items.title: Moondance
items.creator: Van Morrison
items.why: Every song is great. Where Astral Weeks is the masterpiece-by-accident, Moondance is the masterpiece-by-intention — Van Morrison fully in control of his band, doing R&B classics in the traditional way.

items.title: More Ammo: Improving Resilience Against Extreme Surges in Demand
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: The concrete reform proposal behind his 'defence economics' principle: a single contract that obligates the producer to deliver 100 tubes/year in peacetime and gives the government the option (not the obligation) to scale to 300 — building surge capacity into peacetime procurement rather than scrambling when war comes.

items.title: Morgan Housel tweet quoting Montesquieu
items.creator: Morgan Housel
items.why: Used to discuss the corrosive effects of comparison-driven happiness, especially after social media made everyone's curated highlight reels visible to everyone else's real selves.

items.title: Morgan Housel's writing on money
items.creator: Morgan Housel
items.why: Amit suggests Ajay should read Housel — referenced in passing as an author worth reading.

items.title: Mosquitoes As Big As A Bus
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The piece behind the line about Versova mosquitoes; an example of hyper-local Indian knowledge that no abroad researcher would ever produce.

items.title: Motivations for Capital Controls and Their Effectiveness
items.creator: Radhika Pandey, Gurnain K. Pasricha, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
items.why: Speaks to the policy thread of the episode: India's anti-internationalisation reflexes (RBI, ED, capital controls) hurt firms more than they help, and the empirical case for the controls is much weaker than the political enthusiasm for them.

items.title: Munna Bhai MBBS
items.creator: Rajkumar Hirani
items.why: A gangster transformed by exposure to medicine, kindness, and 'jadu ki jhappi' — a recognisable rebirth narrative.

items.title: Murali Neelakantan's tweet
items.creator: Murali Neelakantan
items.why: The proximate trigger for revisiting Lant Pritchett's argument in this episode — Neelakantan's 'maybe it's a two-way relationship' was the conventional wisdom that the show then dismantles.

items.title: Murder in Mahim
items.creator: Jerry Pinto
items.why: The setup for Amit's prediction: a few years from now you'll be able to ask an AI to write nine more books in this series and they'll be so good Pinto himself will go 'wow' and not know the difference. A specific, named test case for AI-generated fiction at the level of a real master.

items.title: Murli Neelakantan Looks at the World (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 329)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Murli Neelakantan
items.why: The conversation that surfaced the contrast between the Western and Indian dharma of a lawyer — perjury as career-ender vs. perjury as expected service to the client.

items.title: Mutual Funds With Feet of Clay
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: A worked example of a securities-market positive feedback loop: a one-day surge in redemptions, an illiquid market, a price hit, NAVs fall, more redemptions. Worth reading as a concrete model of how a market becomes the trigger for its own crisis.

items.title: My Hero, Oppenheimer (Everything is Everything, episode 5)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Background for the Gottingen story: the same misfit who tried to poison his physics teacher became Oppenheimer once placed inside a cluster of giants.

items.title: My Life and Struggle
items.creator: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
items.why: Both for its account of the man behind the movement and for its window into a period when 'your best minds, your finest intellectuals, were not in universities, they were in jails.' His descriptions of fellow prisoners like Baba Kharak Singh are formative reading.

items.title: My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring YouTubers
items.creator: Ali Abdaal
items.why: Source of the 'two videos a week for two years; don't look at the numbers' rule. Validation kills creators; iteration makes them — and the only way to survive iteration is to stop measuring.

items.title: Nannari Root
items.why: Ajay's concrete recommendation: buy the root, grind it into powder, put it in your tea. A direct way to act on the philosophy that biodiversity in what we ingest hedges against modern science's incomplete understanding of micronutrients.

items.title: Narrative and Numbers: The Value of Stories in Business
items.creator: Aswath Damodaran
items.why: Source of the Uber-valuation parable. The story you tell about a company — taxi service vs. replacement of car ownership — moves the valuation by orders of magnitude. A vital read for understanding what firms are really about.

items.title: Narrative Economics
items.creator: Robert J. Shiller
items.why: Cited as one example of the second lesson — take words seriously, not just numbers — and as an indication that economics is slowly opening up to the kind of mixed-methods approach Biju Rao argues for.

items.title: Nashville
items.creator: Robert Altman
items.why: One of Amit's favourite films of all time. He uses it as the structural touchstone against which Short Cuts inevitably suffered.

items.title: National Development Delivers: And How! And How?
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: The paper that introduces the 'national development versus kinky development' distinction Amit relies on heavily in the second half of the episode.

items.title: Naturalistic Fallacy
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: The converse of the is-ought trap — defining 'natural' as 'good' and using it to denigrate, e.g., homosexuality. Essential reading before drawing any moral conclusions from evolutionary findings.

items.title: Naval Ravikant on co-founder qualities
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: High intelligence, high energy, high integrity — and integrity is the most important by far. Without it, intelligence and energy work against you, not for you.

items.title: Naval Ravikant on networking
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: 'Do something great and your network will instantly emerge' — networking is personal marketing; doing the work is the only durable signal.

items.title: Naval Ravikant on working like a lion
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: Lions sleep 18 hours then sprint. Humans, evolved as hunter-gatherers, are wired the same way — sustained 9-to-5 focus is unnatural; bursts of furious work followed by recovery is the ancestral pattern.

items.title: Naval Ravikant — accept the whole package
items.creator: Naval Ravikant
items.why: An antidote to envy. Once you ask the whole-package question, you usually find there's no one you'd actually trade places with.

items.title: Naval Ravikant: 'The future will be almost all startups'
items.creator: Naval Ravikant (clip)
items.why: Naval's claim that ten years out, most companies will be small startups — four-to-ten-person firms scaling to a billion dollars — used to support the show's thesis that the era of 'company man' careers is ending.

items.title: Never Mind the Bullocks, Here's the Lamborghini
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: An extension of the front-loading argument as the new orthodoxy started to take hold.

items.title: Never normalise anything; keep questioning
items.why: Inflation targeting is a rare elegant piece of legislation but it is always under threat. The price of preserving good policy is constant vigilance — refusing to take any settled good for granted.

items.title: New Work on District Courts in Kerala
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Concrete evidence that India is finally getting serious process improvements in the lower judiciary — the precondition for the contract-enforcement that complex manufacturing requires.

items.title: Newton, the Man
items.creator: John Maynard Keynes
items.why: The original source for the 'Newton was the last of the magicians, not the first of the men of reason' frame — and the document that destroyed the sanitised schoolbook image of Newton. Beautifully written, freely available as a PDF.

items.title: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeshwari Sengupta on de-facto convertibility
items.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeshwari Sengupta
items.why: Empirical proof that the 'closed' Indian capital account is a fiction maintained by lawyers and accountants — the rich get out, the poor are choked, and the system functions as an employment guarantee for compliance professionals.

items.title: Nightfall
items.creator: Isaac Asimov
items.why: Amit refuses to say more — saying any more would be a spoiler. A fitting close to an episode about civilisations that lose what they once knew.

items.title: NighttimeLights.jl
items.creator: xKDR Forum
items.why: Made fully public so any researcher anywhere can apply the same techniques to any country, change parameters, and reproduce or extend the work. An embodiment of the 'spirit of inquiry' Amit praises in the episode.

items.title: Nina Teicholz on The Joe Rogan Experience
items.creator: Joe Rogan with Nina Teicholz
items.why: An accessible long-form gateway to her case against the saturated-fat orthodoxy.

items.title: No Surprises
items.creator: Radiohead
items.why: Ajay loves both the original and the Regina Spektor cover with equal force — one of those 'schizophrenic' double loyalties he can't resolve.

items.title: No Surprises (cover)
items.creator: Regina Spektor
items.why: Ajay's preferred cover. Recommended alongside the original as both sitting at the top of his playlist for this song.

items.title: Nonstop Dan on Air India
items.creator: Nonstop Dan
items.why: The case study Amit uses for what happens when 'pretend to know' culture meets safety-critical service — the crew lied about the meal being vegan with cheese clearly visible.

items.title: Not Dark Yet
items.creator: Bob Dylan
items.why: Amit reads the famous lyric ('Sometimes my burden is more than I can bear / It's not dark yet, but it's getting there') as the emotional summary of the entire late-mastery thesis: the awareness of finitude as fuel, not anaesthetic.

items.title: Not Waving but Drowning
items.creator: Stevie Smith
items.why: Amit reads it in full as the emotional close of his swimming-pool fable. A standing reminder that the people who look fine often aren't, and that the gestures of distress and of greeting can be physically identical from the shore.

items.title: Nothing Is Indian! Everything Is Indian! (Everything is Everything, episode 12)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Source of the argument that everything we consider quintessentially Indian — clothes, food, languages — actually came from somewhere else and is a melding of influences. No culture is sui generis.

items.title: Notion
items.why: Amit calls it a great productivity tool that he has not yet adopted, mentioned for readers who want a more structured workspace than Roam's loosely-organised knowledge graph.

items.title: Nowhere Near
items.creator: Yo La Tengo
items.why: He calls it one of the great love songs.

items.title: Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers
items.creator: Richard Hamming
items.why: The Bell Labs ethos in textbook form. Hamming, who first told management that more than half of Bell Labs' work would be computation, also produced the great line: 'the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.'

items.title: Observations on International Labor Standards and Trade
items.creator: Alan B. Krueger
items.why: A second academic source on the same threshold-of-prosperity argument — that prohibition divorced from material conditions does damage.

items.title: Obsidian
items.why: Markdown storage means the entire Unix toolchain works on your notes — grep, sed, awk, whatever you like — so your second brain isn't trapped inside one company's app. A practical halfway house between Roam's polish and Emacs's depth.

items.title: Odati
items.creator: Bombay-based mountaineering services firm
items.why: Ajay has gone with them on many of his projects and likes their work a lot.

items.title: Ode to Kirihito
items.creator: Osamu Tezuka
items.why: A monumental, dark masterpiece of visual storytelling about the human condition and moral decay under circumstantial change. Plot-summary cannot capture its power. Tezuka, in his late period, was so taken by Tatsumi's young Gekiga movement that he himself adopted the form to write this.

items.title: Oedipus Rex
items.creator: Sophocles
items.why: If you want to see where the tragic five-act structure comes from, go to Sophocles.

items.title: Offshore wind in Tamil Nadu: from potential to reality
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly, Charmi Mehta, Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
items.why: The full economic and policy case for what Ajay calls India's 'North Sea' — the 14-lakh-crore offshore wind bounty that hinges on Tamil Nadu fixing its electricity policy and India fixing its Sri Lanka relationship.

items.title: On Diversification by Firms
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Background on the standard frames — economies of scale and economies of scope — which the 'great leaps' of Sun, Google and Amazon explicitly transcend.

items.title: On Fire
items.creator: Galaxie 500
items.why: Amit calls it a brilliant album and says you've got to listen to it. It also closes a loop he couldn't have closed in 1990s India when alternative-rock back-catalogues were unfindable.

items.title: On Inequality
items.creator: Harry Frankfurt
items.why: Source of the 'doctrine of sufficiency': don't level for equality, define what is enough to live on and try to get everyone above that line. A philosopher's version of the policy intuition Amit and Ajay defend.

items.title: On PLI: Many roads lead to a sound GST
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: The full argument behind 'fix the indirect tax system instead of running ad-hoc PLI subsidies for Apple.'

items.title: On the Mechanics of Economic Development
items.creator: Robert E. Lucas
items.why: Source of one of the episode's animating quotes: 'Once you start thinking about [development], it's hard to think about anything else,' because the 10x per-capita gap between India and the US is a moral and intellectual problem of the first order.

items.title: On the Natural History of Destruction
items.creator: W.G. Sebald
items.why: A 'masterpiece' that fuses photographs and prose. Amit also takes it as an inspiration for what a modern multimedia solo essay-vlog could look like.

items.title: On the Rise of FinTechs: Credit Scoring Using Digital Footprints
items.creator: Tobias Berg, Valentin Burg, Ana Gombovic and Manju Puri
items.why: The German-data study quoted in the episode — that iPhone users default less than Android users, that typos in email addresses predict default, that 2 a.m. shoppers are riskier. The empirical foundation for digital-exhaust credit scoring.

items.title: On Tyranny
items.creator: Timothy Snyder
items.why: The essential primer on the small everyday acts that preserve or surrender freedom.

items.title: On Tyranny: Graphic Edition
items.creator: Timothy Snyder and Nora Krug
items.why: Ajay's tongue-in-cheek recommendation for the 'WhatsApp uncle' in your life who, like Gaston in Beauty and the Beast, complains there are no pictures. A serious gift wrapped in a friendly gibe.

items.title: Once in a Lifetime
items.creator: Talking Heads
items.why: A personal hinge point: post-1991 India opened, MTV arrived, and a single song could rearrange a young Indian's musical universe. The artefact of the Reformers' work, made tangible.

items.title: One Bad Law Goes, but Women Remain Second-Class Citizens
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Triggered by the recollection that Padma Desai and Jagdish Bhagwati were warned 'living in sin' was a crime under the IPC. Amit's column dismantled the adultery law as one that treated women as a husband's property — a frame still alive in other parts of the IPC.

items.title: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
items.creator: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
items.why: Cited as 'answer one' to the question 'does socialism work?' — the satellite image of North Korea vs South Korea at night being 'answer two.' Both are devastating in their compression.

items.title: Only the Paranoid Survive
items.creator: Andy Grove
items.why: The book that made Drew Houston pivot Dropbox to focus on file sharing alone, dropping the rest. A working manual for recognising when 'doing many things' has become incompatible with winning the one thing that matters.

items.title: OpenStreetMap (OSM)
items.why: The true digital public good — non-rival, non-excludable, public domain, built by volunteers worldwide, including Indian OSM mapping parties that ride around with GPS phones marking points of interest. The example to point to whenever someone misuses the phrase 'digital public good.'

items.title: Oppenheimer
items.creator: Christopher Nolan
items.why: Amit hadn't yet seen it but framed Nolan as an 'author at scale' — bringing the sensibility of an artistic, intimate-drama filmmaker to massive cinematic experiences. Nolan switched studios from Warner Brothers to Universal because Warner planned a same-day HBO Max release and Nolan is a stickler for the big-screen experience.

items.title: Oppenheimer, Nullified and Vindicated
items.creator: Kai Bird
items.why: The reference for the rehabilitation story Ajay tells. Required reading on how, decades after the fact, citizen-led archival work and FOI access can force a state to admit error in writing.

items.title: Opportunity, Choice and the IPL
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: He cites it with pride for getting almost everything right ex ante — IPL would revolutionise Indian cricket, seep into test cricket, expand the ecosystem despite the BCCI being a monopsony.

items.title: Orienting
items.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
items.why: A 'spectacularly good writer' on Japanese culture — a fine companion volume to the post-war Japan story for readers who want texture beyond economics.

items.title: OSI: The Internet That Wasn't
items.creator: Andrew Russell
items.why: The single best historical case study Ajay invokes for the entire episode — top-down telecom-monopoly standard versus DARPA-funded, hobbyist-extended, robust-under-failure protocol. The internet revolution exists because TCP/IP beat the government standard.

items.title: Our FSI Problem (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 11)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
items.why: Source of Tabarrok's striking line that 'in Bombay you reclaim the sea — you need to reclaim the sky' — extending Amit's argument that India is full of artificially dead capital.

items.title: Outliers
items.creator: Malcolm Gladwell
items.why: Source of the 'birthday effect' research showing elite athletes cluster in the first months of the year because of age-group cut-offs. A vivid illustration of how small initial advantages compound through feedback loops.

items.title: Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevity
items.creator: Peter Attia
items.why: Attia is the practical companion to Sinclair: less the science of why we age and more the daily protocol for how to age well.

items.title: P.G. Wodehouse
items.why: Wodehouse is rarely taken as 'serious' literature, but his Jeeves-and-Wooster machinery is comedy in the technical Booker sense — confusions, revelations, reunions, in some of the most polished prose in English.

items.title: Pablo Picasso (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Wikipedia
items.why: Provided so the audience can trace Picasso's full chronological arc themselves — the protocubism, analytic and synthetic cubism phases, neoclassical return, surrealism dabbling, and late period.

items.title: Padosan
items.why: An older-Bollywood demonstration of the same confusion-resolution-reunion machinery.

items.title: Pallavi Aiyar Has Seen the World (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 351)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pallavi Aiyar
items.why: The audio companion to Orienting — Aiyar on her years in China, Indonesia, Japan and what it does to a mind to keep moving.

items.title: Pandit's Mind
items.creator: Time magazine (1951)
items.why: Source of the famous lines that Beatrice and Sidney Webb were 'in a truer sense Nehru's creators than Vishnu and Shiva,' and that Nehru carried 'the aristocratic Brahmin's contempt for the Banya caste' on top of his socialist's contempt for capitalism.

items.title: Paper Thin Hotel
items.creator: Greg Dulli
items.why: Triggered by Ajay's Suzanne pick — Amit wanted to add another Cohen cover and reaches for what he calls 'an absolute masterpiece.'

items.title: Parade's End
items.creator: Ford Madox Ford
items.why: Source of Ajay's read-aloud passage on why long companionship is necessary to ever finish a real conversation — the romantic counterweight to the chapter's data on app-driven disposability.

items.title: Paradise Lost
items.creator: John Milton
items.why: The germ of Frankenstein's moral question — the creature confronting its creator — is already in Milton. A reminder that no work is truly sui generis: even the inventor of a genre is rewriting the books she grew up with.

items.title: Parkinson's Law
items.creator: C. Northcote Parkinson
items.why: Amit's favourite public-choice-disguised-as-comedy book. Captures bureaucratic incentives perfectly: 'work expands to fill the time available,' officials multiply subordinates rather than rivals, budgets always grow, status quo bias is structural. Funny and devastating.

items.title: Party
items.creator: Govind Nihalani
items.why: A small parable of how the early Netflix mail-order model genuinely solved a cultural-preservation problem that the Indian film industry could not solve for one of its own great directors.

items.title: Passports Were a Temporary War Measure
items.creator: Speranta Dumitru
items.why: Source of the breathtaking historical fact: before 1914 there were no passports anywhere in the world. The freedom to migrate was treated as an inalienable human right; Versailles tried to restore it; Soviet Russia killed the idea; the EU is the only meaningful modern restoration.

items.title: Pather Panchali
items.creator: Satyajit Ray
items.why: Cited alongside The Lives of Others and Court as one of the greatest debut films ever made — invoked as a benchmark of how high The Lives of Others sits in Amit's pantheon.

items.title: Patrick Collison on beauty
items.creator: Patrick Collison
items.why: Beauty isn't a luxury feature; it's a value driver. Pairs with Steve Jobs' aesthetic at Apple — you can't always quantify it, but it makes the maker smile and the user choose you.

items.title: Patrick Collison on choosing co-founders
items.creator: Patrick Collison
items.why: Closeness is a feature, not a bug. The risk people fear (mixing friendship and work) is dwarfed by the alternative — sharing the most consuming experience of your life with a stranger.

items.title: Patrick Collison on Stripe's mission
items.creator: Patrick Collison
items.why: The vision-bigger-than-the-product example — and the one that translated tactically into killing PayPal's seven-day integration.

items.title: Paul
items.creator: Big Thief
items.why: Amit, the self-confessed 'old fogey' whose music is 'all ancient,' is amazed to find a song made as recently as 2016 that he absolutely loves. The recommendation is a small, charming proof that the anti-uncle posture extends even to musical taste.

items.title: Paul Graham on being loved by a few rather than liked by many
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Amit treats this as one of the most important lessons EIE confirmed. Depth of engagement — readers who buy your books, take your courses, leave thoughtful comments, recognise you at airports — beats undifferentiated reach. Aiming to be liked by many is, in Amit's words, 'a path to mediocrity.'

items.title: Paul Graham on compressing your working life
items.creator: Paul Graham (clip)
items.why: The frame: instead of working at low intensity for forty years, work at high intensity for four. The middle-ages trading voyage as the model for a modern startup.

items.title: Paul Graham on hiring
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Pick ten random people to row a boat and you get a mediocre boat; pick the best ten and the boat flies. The asymmetric returns to A-list hiring.

items.title: Paul Graham on talent
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Used by Amit as a refutation of xenophobia and the closed-team mentality. The math is unforgiving: if you want the best, most of them are not from your country, and that is true everywhere.

items.title: Paul Graham says, Just Learn
items.creator: Paul Graham
items.why: Graham's instruction: don't begin by hunting markets — begin by learning a domain deeply. Projects emerge from expertise; almost every great company started as a hobby project of someone who already loved the field.

items.title: Pedestrianism
items.creator: Matthew Algeo
items.why: The case study for the movement-business-racket arc. A man who loved walking turned walking into a sport, and the sport ate the love until the sport itself died.

items.title: Penelope Fitzgerald's body of work
items.creator: Penelope Fitzgerald
items.why: Amit's broader recommendation — not just one book but the late-bloomer arc itself, as a model for what a creative life starting at 60 can look like.

items.title: Perplexity (Pro)
items.creator: Perplexity
items.why: He says virtually all the angiography, angioplasty and stent knowledge in this episode came not from search engines or Wikipedia but from Perplexity Pro — and emphasises that LLMs are great at prompting you toward the right next questions, not just answering.

items.title: Perseverance and Adaptation: Ukraine's Counteroffensive at Three Months
items.creator: Michael Kofman and Rob Lee (War on the Rocks)
items.why: Detailed, on-the-ground reporting on what is actually working and what is not — the kind of granular work that keeps you out of the propaganda swamp on either side.

items.title: Persuasion
items.creator: Yascha Mounk
items.why: Cited as a working example of independent creator-led journalism on Substack — a model for what may replace mainstream media in the sense-making function.

items.title: Perun (YouTube channel)
items.creator: Perun
items.why: The whole episode is built off Perun's video on Indian defence. He is the model of expertise without credentials, depth without dumbing-down, and a sense-maker for both Ukraine and Indian defence.

items.title: Peter Leko and Judit Polgar on Gukesh's heart rate
items.creator: Peter Leko and Judit Polgar
items.why: A vivid illustration of physiological composure as a marker of elite competitive performance — Leko's joke that he doesn't even drop to 62 when he's doing nothing.

items.title: Peter Pan
items.creator: J.M. Barrie
items.why: Children leave for Neverland and come home different — pure archetype.

items.title: Peter Thiel on working on problems that wouldn't get solved without you
items.creator: Peter Thiel (clip)
items.why: Thiel's triage rule: do work that wouldn't happen without you. Amit reads this not as Promethean hubris but as a practical filter — your uniqueness, however small, is the only reason your project deserves your finite hours.

items.title: Peter Thiel says trends are overrated
items.creator: Peter Thiel (clip)
items.why: Thiel's heuristic: the more buzzwords (big data, blockchain, AI/ML), the more likely the pitch is hollow. A genuinely new idea usually doesn't have a buzzword to fit it into.

items.title: Peyman Milanfar tweet quoting Max Weber — 'I am not a donkey, I do not have a field.'
items.creator: Peyman Milanfar
items.why: The case against academic siloing — invoked against the kind of researcher who spends ten years studying wheat production in Arizona in 1853 without seeing the bigger picture.

items.title: Peyman Milanfar tweet — 'If you're a researcher in tech and you're not reading anything older than five years, your work will be forgotten in five years.'
items.creator: Peyman Milanfar
items.why: The tweet that opens the discussion of why even obsolete past work is worth studying — to understand how thinking in a field evolved, and to learn from people who designed under harder constraints.

items.title: Pick up a musical instrument
items.why: If you have even 2% of the willpower to do it, do. It changes your life. When concentration and meditation are hard to find by other means, an instrument can be one of the things that gives them to you.

items.title: Pico Iyer tweet quoting Rousseau
items.creator: Pico Iyer
items.why: A clean closer to the episode's curation theme — and a teasing barb at Ajay, who had been on his phone for half an hour beforehand taking calls about markets.

items.title: Pilgrim's Progress
items.creator: John Bunyan
items.why: A Christian allegory built entirely on the Quest spine — call, journey, arrival, frustration, ordeal, goal.

items.title: PISA
items.creator: OECD
items.why: Anyone reading education seriously needs a working sense of PISA — what it measures, who scores well (Finland, South Korea, Japan, Shanghai), and what India's brief, suppressed exposure to it actually showed.

items.title: Planners vs. Searchers in Foreign Aid
items.creator: William Easterly
items.why: Source of the planner-searcher distinction at the heart of this episode. Planners think they know the answers, treat poverty as engineering, impose top-down solutions. Searchers admit ignorance, see poverty as a tangle, use trial-and-error and feedback. Markets and democracies are searchers.

items.title: Planning Democracy
items.creator: Nikhil Menon
items.why: The source of much of the Mahalanobis material in this episode — the jute survey vindication, the diary-and-attendance authoritarianism, the Bharat Sadhu Samaj, Chintaman Deshmukh. Essential for understanding the Nehruvian planning era from the inside.

items.title: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
items.creator: Edited by Alice K. Turner
items.why: A treasured volume of Amit's, and the evidence behind his claim that Playboy genuinely was a major venue for the best short fiction of the late twentieth century — 'people did read it for the stories.'

items.title: Polina Pompliano quoting Brené Brown on normalcy
items.creator: Brené Brown (via Polina Pompliano)
items.why: The clearest articulation Amit has seen of why ordinary moments deserve attention while we still have them. Lands harder for him post-heart-attack.

items.title: Political Order and Political Decay
items.creator: Francis Fukuyama
items.why: The companion volume on how mature states decay — vital for understanding why getting institutional design right is a permanent project, not a one-time triumph.

items.title: Politics (limerick)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: 'A neta who loves currency notes / Told me what his line of work denotes / It is kind of funny / We steal people's money / And use some of it to buy their votes.' The whole democracy-as-rent-extraction thesis in five lines.

items.title: Polls Get Elections Wrong. So Use Google
items.creator: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz
items.why: A vivid demonstration that word order in search queries beat televised polling. The kind of finding only an algorithm would surface, and once surfaced, never quite leaves you.

items.title: Possible, Plausible and Probable: Big Markets and Networking Effects
items.creator: Aswath Damodaran
items.why: An exemplary public display of intellectual humility — Damodaran acknowledging Gurley was right and rebuilding his Uber valuation from the new narrative.

items.title: Postwar
items.creator: Tony Judt
items.why: The masterwork on what reconstruction of Europe actually looked like — the human and institutional capital that came back, and the ethnic cleansing 'horrible nightmare' that ran from 1945 to 1948.

items.title: Power and Discourse in Policy Diffusion: Anti-Money Laundering in Developing States
items.creator: J.C. Sharman
items.why: On Ajay's list as the scholarly account of how 'global best practice' AML was forced on countries lacking the institutional substrate that makes it tolerable elsewhere — the Lant Pritchett critique applied empirically.

items.title: Pranay Kotasthane's post on Plasma and organ sales
items.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
items.why: An example, alongside parking and water, of where the price system is suppressed by squeamishness and where allowing markets would dramatically improve outcomes — including saving lives.

items.title: Prem Throws Your Heart to the Ground
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Sets up the wider thesis of the episode: most of us live in a routine, urban, thing-dependent mode and somewhere we lose something. The estrangement is from the world we ourselves built.

items.title: Pretty Woman
items.why: A textbook Cinderella structure for the contemporary audience.

items.title: Price controls for vaccines?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Concrete application of the general result that price controls cause shortages and hurt the poor most. A companion read to the show's argument against state coercion in vaccine pricing.

items.title: Price Theory
items.creator: Milton Friedman
items.why: Ajay's beautiful book from his childhood. Sometimes the old masters got it right and we should just go back. The clearest exposition of how prices actually work.

items.title: Pride and Prejudice
items.creator: Jane Austen
items.why: A perfect Booker comedy — misunderstandings, slow clearing of fog, marriage as reunion — without a single belly laugh.

items.title: Pritika Hingorani Wants to Fix Our Cities (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 361)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Pritika Hingorani
items.why: Background reading for the episode's claim that the 'urban dreamers and town planners of India' should redirect attention from Bangalore and Bombay to smaller towns — Hingorani is one of the people Ajay names as the right kind of expertise to draw on.

items.title: Privacy 3.0
items.creator: Rahul Matthan
items.why: The companion text to the Matthan TSATU episode — Amit's reference for the historical claim that privacy is a recent technological achievement, not a default state, and that the 'rich interior life' it enables is the bedrock of human progress.

items.title: Private Education Is Good for the Poor
items.creator: James Tooley and Pauline Dixon
items.why: Provides the data behind the surprising claim: even families on incomes under Rs 5,000 a month often pay for a private school over a free government one. The 'revealed preference' that ought to settle the public-vs-private debate.

items.title: Probal DasGupta Goes to the Himalayas With Books in His Bag (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Probal DasGupta
items.why: Amit's deep dive with the military historian, source of the General Sagat Singh story at Nathu La and Cho La and the discussion of when local commanders should and should not disobey orders.

items.title: Project Oasis Report
items.creator: Surendra Dave (chair), with Ajay Shah and others
items.why: The foundational document of Indian pension reform — where the design philosophy of low-cost index funds, defined contributions, and individual-owned accounts was first articulated.

items.title: Promenade
items.creator: U2
items.why: Ajay's second pick from the same album — paired with Bad as 'two songs that are absolutely great.'

items.title: Public Policy courses at Takshashila
items.creator: Takshashila Institution
items.why: Implicitly endorsed via Shubham Dhiman's story — he is the Takshashila-trained young Himachali whose curiosity sparked the episode. The path the episode imagines for Bir runs through people like him.

items.title: Publish and Perish
items.creator: Agnes Callard
items.why: Amit calls Callard the best kind of public intellectual, always engaging on Twitter. The essay maps tenure-track economics onto why young academics are forced into deadening prose, and is the piece he gives his writing students stuck in academia.

items.title: Punish Rioters, Not Writers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Crystallises the core principle Amit returns to in this episode: punish the unlawful act, not the speech that supposedly preceded it.

items.title: Quizzing is Not Just a Trivial Pursuit
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The home of the Warhol quiz question Amit poses on the show — and his case for quiz questions you can derive rather than only recall.

items.title: Racing in the Street
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Ajay flags this as a model of structural surprise. It looks like a young-man-and-cars song; halfway through, the camera pulls back into a psychological portrait of a deeply sad woman, and the song you thought you were hearing turns out to be hers.

items.title: Raiders of the Lost Ark
items.creator: Steven Spielberg
items.why: Indiana Jones searching for the Ark — the Quest in pulp form.

items.title: Rajeswari Sengupta on the post-tariff response
items.creator: Rajeswari Sengupta
items.why: Friend-and-collaborator recommendation — part of the small group Ajay names as defining the current discourse.

items.title: Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman
items.creator: Aziz Mirza
items.why: Amit borrows the title as a metaphor for Indian firms wanting to graduate into being global firms — Raju ko gentleman banna hai. The film's title is the chapter heading for the section on Indian outbound FDI.

items.title: Ramki and the Ocean of Stories (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 415)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ramki
items.why: Source of the Wenders / Perfect Days conversation Amit references — both of them agreeing the film could only have been made by an older director.

items.title: Ranbir Kapoor's dialogue from Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year
items.creator: Shimit Amin (Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year)
items.why: Listed in the description as a Bollywood reference threaded through Amit's argument about firms, salespersons and what really matters in business.

items.title: Ranjit Hoskote Is Dancing in Chains (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 363)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ranjit Hoskote
items.why: Source of the phrase 'dancing in chains' — we are all constrained, and the art of life is dancing the best we can within those chains. Used to reframe Hemen's tiny New York apartment as a constraint that produces choreography rather than as a deprivation.

items.title: Rashomon
items.creator: Akira Kurosawa
items.why: Used as illustration of the Anais Nin point — the multiple credible versions of one event are not lies; they are how perception actually works.

items.title: Raspberry Pi 4
items.why: Best bang for the buck for getting hands-on with Unix. Boot Linux, tinker, build art installations (as Nomsita and Vaishnav have done), control plant watering, measure outdoor temperature — the whole thing comes to life at a low entry point.

items.title: Ratangad
items.creator: Trek in the Western Sahyadris
items.why: One of the most beautiful places Ajay has ever been — 'I have never seen anything as beautiful' as Ratangad and Harishchandragad. Genuine adventure with real route-finding, unlike the corseted standard Himalayan routes.

items.title: Raw Umber
items.creator: Sara Rai
items.why: Recommended alongside her podcast episode as evidence of what attentive observation, formed in a low-stimulation childhood, becomes on the page.

items.title: Read books for ideas, read papers for techniques
items.creator: Edward Glaeser
items.why: Ajay's organising frame for the whole 'how should we read?' question — papers have driven themselves toward narrow rigour ('rigour mortis'), and big ideas now live in books, blogs, podcasts, and YouTube; you need both halves of the diet.

items.title: Reading Like a Writer
items.creator: Francine Prose
items.why: Teaches you to notice why the author chose this word and not another, this sentence rhythm and not another. Reading like a writer enriches the experience even if you never write.

items.title: Reading Lolita in Tehran
items.creator: Azar Nafisi
items.why: Cited not just for itself but for Nafisi's living point — that classical liberal values are spoken most clearly by those who have lost them. People in comfortable democracies have forgotten the vocabulary the dissenters in Iran still need every day.

items.title: Rebel Sultans
items.creator: Manu Pillai
items.why: Recommended for the syncretic story — Mughal emperors with Hindu generals, Hindu rebels with Turkish mercenaries, the Deccan as the case study of Islamic-Hindu coexistence.

items.title: Rebooting Indian Education (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 350)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
items.why: Implicitly referenced by the strong claims about humanities departments and the over-medicalisation of attention; Amit's broader work on what education in India actually needs.

items.title: Red Dead Redemption 2
items.creator: Rockstar Games
items.why: A slow, character-driven game with a thick story, accurate history, and dialogue that landed enough to make Vaishnav cry at the end. He frames it as a moral exercise — running from law and society alongside twenty companions, deciding for yourself what is right or wrong in that world, then carrying the question back into your own.

items.title: Reflections on Gandhi
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Amit reads aloud the passage on saints being judged guilty until proved innocent, on Gandhi's vanity, and on the shrewd 'near-saint' inside the saint. A demonstration that Orwell's clarity is not a tic of style but a way of seeing.

items.title: Reforming Development Economics (Ideas of India)
items.creator: Lant Pritchett with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: The constructive sequel to the 'where did it go wrong' conversation — together they form a complete reading of Pritchett's reform agenda.

items.title: Reforms of Prosecution in the Indian Criminal Justice System
items.creator: Smriti Parsheera
items.why: Ajay's recommendation for anyone who wants to go deeper into the broken state of the Indian public prosecutor's office — the institution that has 'withered away' over the years and needs to be revived.

items.title: Regulation: A Primer
items.creator: Susan Dudley and Jerry Brito
items.why: The first and last chapters are relevant to the general theory of regulation. Most of the book is about how regulation works in America, but it covers a useful sample of the territory mapped in the episode.

items.title: Republic
items.creator: Plato
items.why: Ajay points out that Plato was already clear-eyed about democracy — 'this is not gonna work too well' — long before mass media, radio, television, and social media made the simplistic-narratives problem much worse.

items.title: Resisting State Injustice (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 120)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Jason Brennan
items.why: Where the policeman-and-beggar question was first put to Amit, and where Michael Huemer's work on authority came up. Amit recommends it as the longer treatment of everything that's compressed into his closing monologue.

items.title: Resources vs Constraints: Why T20 Teams Need to Attack More
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Crisply lays out the wickets-as-resource, balls-as-constraint inversion that flips T20 strategy and is still misunderstood by most teams and most commentators.

items.title: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
items.creator: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
items.why: Amit insisted Ajay recommend his own paper so he wouldn't cop out. Amit calls it awesome — clear, rigorous, written in plain English unlike most academic papers. It lays out the make-vs-buy decision for state R&D, why contracting out generates spillovers, and a concrete twenty-year transition path for organisations like ISRO.

items.title: Rethinking NEET, and medical education
items.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
items.why: The companion piece showing the eligibility-plus-lottery and free-the-colleges arguments adapted to NEET, which has the worst supply-demand mismatch in Indian higher education.

items.title: Rethinking Regulation in India
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay's own talk that systematises the masterclass given in this episode — separation of powers, rule of law, surgical delegation, checks and balances — with the slides as a companion document.

items.title: Rhyme and Reason
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Self-referenced as evidence Amit was 'perhaps the only professional limerick writer in the world' — a small, charming taste of the limerick habit at Sunday-newspaper scale.

items.title: Rick Beato's YouTube channel
items.creator: Rick Beato
items.why: Amit enjoys his work a lot — high-quality content for anyone who wants to understand the technical and creative architecture of songs. Source of the Mike Dawes / Angus Young conversation cited earlier.

items.title: Rising to the China Challenge
items.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade and Ajay Shah
items.why: Ajay flags this as the venue for the deeper argument that India cannot confront China alone — the GDP and population ratios are similar to Ukraine vs Russia, and only deep partnerships make the math work.

items.title: Rob Henderson's tweet on dark-triad men and the dating-app defect-defect equilibrium
items.creator: Rob Henderson
items.why: The single most-quoted text in Chapter 3 — Amit reads it out in full as the core explanation of why dating-app dynamics generate so much bitterness on every side.

items.title: Robert Sapolsky's Biology Lectures
items.creator: Robert Sapolsky
items.why: Amit's headline pick: he says he had never been interested in biology in his life until these lectures opened his mind. The point is that the world's best teaching is now available for free anywhere; the credentialing layer is the only thing being rationed.

items.title: Rockstar
items.creator: Imtiaz Ali
items.why: An Indian instance of the archetype — and proof that the form crosses cinematic traditions almost untouched.

items.title: Rocky
items.creator: Sylvester Stallone
items.why: Both the film and the story behind the film exemplify the archetype — the hero not just rises in fiction, but the writer himself rose by refusing the safe deal.

items.title: Rolling Thunder Revue
items.creator: Martin Scorsese
items.why: Captures the spirit Amit and Ajay try to articulate in words — the ambition to actually get to something and to do it with the people you love. Music as one of the greatest gifts we have been given.

items.title: Rollo Tomassi quoting Ronnie Coleman on the hard yards
items.creator: Ronnie Coleman (via Rollo Tomassi)
items.why: A blunt diagnostic for thin desire vs. thick desire. The aspiration without the willingness to lift the weight is a tell that the desire was never actually one's own.

items.title: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead
items.creator: Tom Stoppard
items.why: Another model for writing two seemingly minor figures into the moral centre of a story — useful template for Bota and Garja's interior life.

items.title: Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans
items.creator: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott
items.why: The foundational text of the rational expectations revolution: optimization by the policymaker assumes credulous, static citizens, but real citizens watch and adapt. The paper forces serious treatment of credibility, commitment, and handcuffs as commitment devices — and Ajay literally re-read it at 7am preparing for this episode and got 'drunk with happiness.'

items.title: Rumblefish
items.creator: Francis Ford Coppola
items.why: An underrated Coppola masterpiece — and, Amit notes, 'everything you talk about good corporate culture, it was right there in that film.' Tied to the personal memory of Shamim Desai's film-appreciation talk at Channel V.

items.title: Runaway
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: Munro sets her stories in one province of Canada but captures the human condition with such depth that she is beloved everywhere — proof that good fiction is universal. A deliberate counterweight to an episode about states and policy.

items.title: RUSI's commentary on Ukraine
items.creator: Royal United Services Institute
items.why: If you want to follow the war beyond armchair speculation, this is one of the highest-quality continuously-updated sources in the world.

items.title: Saaya & The Rituals Of Tamil Muslim Milk Tea
items.creator: Maazin Buhari
items.why: The article that completed Ajay's triangulation: after smelling-his-way-to-the-aha-moment that nanari and amrutmul were the same plant, this piece showed him there was a whole Tamil-Muslim culinary tradition built around the root. Source for the 'novel take on masala chai' recipe.

items.title: Sagar and Amruta meeting Gukesh in Singapore
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: The image that anchors Amit's chapter on community organisers: that Gukesh recognises Amruta as part of the foundation he stands on.

items.title: Sagar Shah at the under-11 workshop all those years ago
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: The full video of the long-game in motion — a future world champion sitting on the floor among peers learning from a man who 'just had no shame in speaking to the smallest kid.'

items.title: Sagar Shah's interview with Ashwin Subramanian
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: A claim of Indian priority in a small but real innovation — and a window into how unsung tinkerers seed practices that later get attached to celebrities.

items.title: Sahil Bloom on making it
items.creator: Sahil Bloom
items.why: An antidote to complacency at the top. Apple stops shipping iPhones for a few years and stops being Apple. The 'making it' fallacy is dangerous because the fight gets harder, not easier, with success.

items.title: Sahil Bloom tweet on planning vs preparation
items.creator: Sahil Bloom
items.why: Anchors the planning-vs-preparation distinction — invoked alongside Tyson's 'everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth' and the planning-is-everything line.

items.title: Sajjid Z Chinoy on the road ahead
items.creator: Sajjid Z Chinoy
items.why: Part of the 'communal sense of knowledge' building in India around the Trump-tariff response — Ajay names Chinoy as one of the cool people thinking about this.

items.title: Salil Tripathi and the Gujaratis (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 409)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Salil Tripathi
items.why: Source of the 'Then I shall tell him he is wrong' anecdote that anchors this episode's portrait of Havel's authenticity.

items.title: Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat
items.creator: Samin Nosrat
items.why: A second mid-episode recommendation. The same first-principles move Amit makes in his prawn improvisation: master the four primitives and you can cook anything, organically and with the flow.

items.title: Sam Altman on being a generalist
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: The hinge of Amit's first chapter: at the moment a project becomes a company, narrow expertise stops being enough — you have to step back and look at the whole world.

items.title: Sam Altman on burnout
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: Momentum is energising. Burnout comes from worrying, procrastinating, and overthinking — not from output itself. Counter to the 'work hard = burn out' folk theory.

items.title: Sam Altman on focus
items.creator: Sam Altman (clip)
items.why: The exact quote Amit reads: 'Focus is a force multiplier on work … it is much more important to work on the right thing than it is to work many hours.' The defining text on saying no.

items.title: Sam Altman on hiring
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: Values first, aptitude second, skill third. CVs reveal skills, interviews reveal aptitude, but values determine whether the hire ever thinks like a co-founder.

items.title: Sam Altman on long-term thinking
items.creator: Sam Altman
items.why: The most concise statement of long-termism as competitive advantage: in a world obsessed with the next quarter, vision over a decade is unguarded territory.

items.title: San Fransicko
items.creator: Michael Shellenberger
items.why: Modern proof that the rent-control mistake hasn't been learned. Among many factors, well-intentioned price controls helped make one of America's wealthiest cities unaffordable to the people the controls were meant to help.

items.title: Sarbpreet Singh Finds His Sikhism (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 407)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Sarbpreet Singh
items.why: Amit mentions it while crediting Sarbpreet, whose book he calls 'magnificent': the place to hear the historian behind the story at length.

items.title: Sarkari Khatiya Private Karo
items.creator: Govinda
items.why: Used as a comic chapter break — a reminder that the hosts treat economic seriousness and Bollywood absurdity as equally legitimate registers of language.

items.title: Scrivener
items.why: Paired with Final Draft as one of the dedicated form-specific writing tools Amit has tried and admired.

items.title: Secret Garden
items.creator: Bruce Springsteen
items.why: Amit's exhibit for Springsteen 'going a level deeper than you expect' — what looks like a song about seduction reveals itself as a song about the unreachable interior of another person. The recess, he says, is what no one else can ever finally enter.

items.title: Seeing Dead Fruit Flies Is Bad For The Health Of Fruit Flies
items.creator: Christi Gendron
items.why: Ajay's closing data point: moral injury from witnessing death goes all the way down to flies. The implication is enormous — if even fruit flies grieve, the case for lab-grown meat is not just sentimental but ethically and biologically grounded.

items.title: Seizing the Enigma
items.creator: David Kahn
items.why: The book whose first two pages so transfixed Ajay at Strand Bookstall that he gave up his commute home and read it through to 9 PM in an Irani cafe. A demonstration of the gripping-from-page-one power of great non-fiction.

items.title: Self-Portrait
items.creator: A.K. Ramanujan
items.why: Amit closes the episode with it. He hears the poem as Ramanujan's miniature on the same theme that Springsteen, Cat Stevens and McCarthy circle in their own ways — the father carried inside the son, signature already in the corner of the frame.

items.title: Self-Portrait Facing Death
items.creator: Pablo Picasso
items.why: Amit's case for late Picasso even when the critics jeered. He reads it as masterful, raw, and fearless — the kind of work an art critic 'who learned something from some academic fool' was unequipped to recognise.

items.title: Sense and Sensibility
items.creator: Jane Austen
items.why: Same architecture as Pride and Prejudice — confusion, clearance, union — and proof comedy is structure, not laughter.

items.title: Serenity Prayer — 'God, give me the strength to change the things I can, the serenity to accept the things I can't, and the wisdom to know the difference.'
items.creator: Reinhold Niebuhr (Christian sources)
items.why: Ajay's framing for treating the world as a fixed field on which only your levers, resources, and agency matter. Everything else is conversation.

items.title: Seven Pillars of Wisdom
items.creator: T. E. Lawrence
items.why: Source of the line that has come to define how counterinsurgency feels in practice — that doing it conventionally is 'like eating soup with a knife.' Awkward, slow, and shaped wrong for the work.

items.title: Sexual Behavior in the Human Female
items.creator: Alfred Kinsey and others
items.why: The book that shattered the Victorian-era assumption that women did not experience sexual desire or pleasure — and got Kinsey defunded by the Rockefeller Foundation for the trouble.

items.title: Sexual Behavior in the Human Male
items.creator: Alfred Kinsey and others
items.why: Foundational for the modern empirical study of human sexuality — busted the myth that homosexual experience was a fringe deviance and forced society to confront the gap between professed and actual behaviour.

items.title: Shahab Bakhtiari co-tweet on geographical reading
items.creator: Shahab Bakhtiari
items.why: Used to argue for interdisciplinarity not as opportunism (finding gaps at the boundaries) but as depth — narrow papers on superconductivity get read only by superconductivity people; depth comes from breadth.

items.title: Shallow
items.creator: Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper
items.why: Cited as further evidence that the modern era is producing worthy songs even if they don't reach an audience whose taste froze in the 1990s.

items.title: Shane Parrish's books
items.creator: Shane Parrish
items.why: High-quality syntheses of mental models for thinking and decision-making. A solid library if you want to build out your toolkit.

items.title: Shane Parrish's tweet on working from home
items.creator: Shane Parrish
items.why: 'Those who show up at work at the office will end up being the bosses of those who show up at work at home.' Cited not as a brief for bureaucratic presenteeism but as a reminder that creative interaction — the water cooler, the post-office beer — is where real work happens.

items.title: Short Cuts
items.creator: Robert Altman
items.why: Structurally reminded Amit of Altman's earlier Nashville. He admits he was 'a little disappointed' — anchoring effect, given that the source material was Carver and the comparison was Nashville — but the experiment is still worth seeing.

items.title: Shruti Jahagirdar
items.why: Customised the protocol for Amit's body, goals and lifestyle. Specialises in keto for vegetarians (rare expertise). Source of the insight that multivitamins are useless — like a five-star buffet that meets no daily requirement; better to identify deficiencies and dose B12, E, C separately.

items.title: Shruti Jahagirdar is the Sporty One (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 289)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Jahagirdar
items.why: Background on Amit's nutritionist and physical trainer — a window into her thinking before consulting her.

items.title: Shruti Rajagopalan Remembers the Angle of the Light (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 410)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Cited as a vehicle for celebrating Shruti as a model gatekeeper — willing to fund 14- and 15-year-old mavericks at Emergent Ventures India without monthly or yearly targets.

items.title: Sign of the Times
items.creator: Harry Styles
items.why: An invitation not to dismiss new artists out of hand — Harry Styles, listened to with attention, is 'bloody good.'

items.title: Signull's newsletter
items.creator: Signull
items.why: Rare sustained quality. Amit doesn't know the writer's identity but considers each post genuinely thought-provoking — the kind of independent voice that justifies paid subscription.

items.title: Simon Sinek on Nike's mission
items.creator: Simon Sinek
items.why: Mission-as-empathy in action: Nike isn't selling shoes, it's standing under the lamppost cheering on the runner who refused to stop.

items.title: Simulating Pension Income Scenarios with penCalc
items.creator: Renuka Sane and William Price
items.why: A worked example of the kind of pensions modeling India's discourse needs more of — listed in the episode's resources.

items.title: Sinocism
items.creator: Bill Bishop
items.why: Amit's go-to example of the new economics of niche. Bishop is not a mainstream byline; mainstream outlets might never commission him; his subject is too specialised. And yet on Substack he is a superstar making a fortune — proof that being loved by a few in a deep niche beats being liked by many.

items.title: Sirf Ek Naam Sunayi Deta Hai
items.creator: Shimit Amin (Chak De! India)
items.why: Amit uses the 'I'm a captain of a state team / and I'm the coach of the Indian national women's team' exchange as a Bollywood metaphor for the national-firm transition — local satrap subsumed into a national structure with central command.

items.title: Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age
items.creator: Duncan Watts
items.why: A 'mid-episode recommendation.' Used here to push the idealised model: if transmission loss were zero, six degrees would mean Jimi Hendrix only needs to play guitar for one person before stepping back into the bathroom — Vladimir Putin would already know.

items.title: Sleepify
items.creator: Vulfpeck
items.why: The most playful demonstration in the episode of how creators arbitrage the constraints of a new form — a 30-second-payout rule becomes the basis of an entire album as conceptual prank.

items.title: Sleeping Beauty
items.why: A literal awakening — the simplest skeletal version of the rebirth plot.

items.title: Sleepless Series (Beggars in Spain)
items.creator: Nancy Kress
items.why: A thought experiment about engineered humans and societal stratification, recommended in the context of sleep as a fundamental biological function. (Ajay calls it 'The Sleepwalkers' in the recording; the series is correctly Sleepless / Beggars in Spain.)

items.title: Slouching Towards Utopia
items.creator: Brad DeLong
items.why: Ajay's pick for understanding the post-1989 economic-policy consensus — the one that has now fragmented under Trump, Putin, Xi, and the rise of right-wing authoritarianism. To know what we are losing, read what we had.

items.title: Slow Productivity
items.creator: Cal Newport
items.why: An antidote to startup-culture sprint-fetishism. Newport argues you don't have to run a perpetual marathon sprint — you can live a quiet life and let ideas marinate, and creativity emerges from that slower rhythm. Pairs with Amit's distinction between needing the din of the world for new dots and needing the stillness (terav, sukun) for those dots to be assembled into a picture.

items.title: Smoke and Mirrors
items.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
items.why: Source of the bicycle-to-two-cars vignette and the haunting passage about old men in Mao suits walking caged songbirds along expressways. A first-person record of how Chinese people fluidly absorbed enormous rupture, with little visible trauma — the texture of mass adaptation under authoritarianism.

items.title: Snatching decline from the jaws of growth
items.creator: KP Krishnan
items.why: The clever proposal Ajay endorses: start labour-law deregulation in IT and IT-enabled services, where the workers are clearly competent adults who don't need state paternalism, and expand outward as the experiment proves itself.

items.title: Snow White
items.why: Another fairy-tale rebirth: from death-sleep to new life.

items.title: Social Conformity Despite Individual Preferences for Distinctiveness
items.creator: Paul Smaldino and Joshua Epstein
items.why: The paper's title is the diagnosis. Young rebels enter university convinced they are independent thinkers, then conform to the toxic fashion of the day. Pair with Paul Graham's 'aggressively conventional-minded' to see why.

items.title: Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis
items.creator: Ludwig von Mises
items.why: The book that converted the young Hayek from democratic socialism and Marxism into a classical liberal — and therefore the proximate cause of all of Hayek's later contributions.

items.title: Soham Das on the post-tariff response
items.creator: Soham Das
items.why: Cited as part of the wider Indian intellectual response that this episode is in dialogue with.

items.title: Solitude
items.why: Not a book or app but a practice: think about how you are approaching a thing, and observe yourself approaching it 'just like a cat approaches a prey.' The point is the meta-observation, not just the time alone.

items.title: Solving the intermittency of renewables
items.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
items.why: The deeper technical argument behind the episode's core claim — that the price system, paired with storage as its own market, dissolves the intermittency problem of solar and wind.

items.title: Son of Bosey
items.creator: Anand Ramachandran
items.why: A side-recommendation tucked inside the 'blade' joke — Amit calls Anand Ramachandran possibly the funniest man in Indian history, and Son of Bosey is his comic home base.

items.title: Son of the Family
items.creator: Danish Radio (circa 1997)
items.why: The other landmark Amit cites for 'show don't tell' in audio. The inflections of voice and the specific memories produce a full picture of a person no abstract narration could deliver — heartbreaking, immersive, and the standard for what audio can do.

items.title: Song of Myself, 51
items.creator: Walt Whitman
items.why: Source of Amit's permission to contradict himself within a single episode: 'Do I contradict myself? Very well, then I contradict myself; I am large, I contain multitudes.' The whole argument structure of the episode (just do it / just be it / just do it) leans on it.

items.title: Sonictown — Business World 2000 archive
items.why: The only surviving public trace of his pre-iTunes, pre-MySpace business idea in Bombay — included so listeners can see the exact pitch he made before the Nasdaq crash.

items.title: Sonnet 18 (Akala)
items.creator: Akala
items.why: Amit's punchline against IP-policing of dead artists: nobody wraps Shakespeare in cotton wool, and Shakespeare is better for it. Pink Floyd, David Gilmour, Akala — culture is people taking each other's stuff and dancing with it.

items.title: South vs North
items.creator: Nilakantan RS
items.why: Source of the headline statistics in this episode — Kerala life expectancy 75 vs UP 64, Kerala IMR 7 vs Madhya Pradesh 48 — and the framing that India contains genuinely different countries by outcome.

items.title: Stalemate, Zugzwang and a long Middle Game
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: The intellectual scaffolding for the chess metaphor (Capablanca / Karpov / Carlson positional play) that Amit and Ajay riff on through the episode.

items.title: Star Wars
items.creator: George Lucas
items.why: A clean instance of the archetype: small protagonist, looming Empire/Death Star, near-defeat, miraculous escape.

items.title: Statistical Basis for Predicting Technological Progress
items.creator: Bela Nagy, J Doyne Farmer, Quan M Bui and Jessika E Trancik
items.why: The decisive empirical answer to which framework best explains technological progress: Wright's Law (aggregate lifetime volume) is the strongest predictor, beating both Moore (time) and Goddard (annual scale). A foundational reading for anyone who wants to think rigorously about innovation curves.

items.title: Steve Jobs hates consultants
items.creator: Steve Jobs (clip)
items.why: Jobs' rule: hire the best people, not consultants. Skin in the game beats credentialed outside advice.

items.title: Steve Jobs on hiring
items.creator: Steve Jobs
items.why: A-list people want to work with other A-list people — first-five hiring is how you trigger that flywheel or kill it.

items.title: Stocks for the Long Run
items.creator: Jeremy Siegel
items.why: Builds the fundamental intuition for the equity premium across centuries — the empirical bedrock for everything Ajay argues in the episode. Read and internalise.

items.title: Strategy: A History
items.creator: Lawrence Freedman
items.why: Amit's all-time recommendation for a single book that gives you the full intellectual sweep of strategy as a discipline.

items.title: Sturgeon's Law
items.why: Cited as the standard reply to the complaint that creator-economy content is mostly bad. Of course it is; ninety percent of everything always was. The point is that today anyone can be in the ten percent without asking permission.

items.title: Supernova in the East
items.creator: Dan Carlin
items.why: Where Amit first encountered the story of Hiroo Onoda — the soldier who defended a Philippine island for 29 years after the war ended.

items.title: Surface Area of Luck
items.creator: Jason Roberts
items.why: The phrase that frames the entire episode. Roberts gives a near-mathematical definition: your chance of being lucky equals the action you take towards your passion multiplied by the number of people you effectively communicate that passion to. Linked from the show notes via Model Thinkers.

items.title: Survivorship Bias (Wikipedia)
items.why: The fallacy Ajay flags mid-episode: any list of 'three great firms that took audacious leaps' is at risk of cherry-picking the survivors and ignoring the many that tried similar leaps and failed.

items.title: Suzanne
items.creator: Leonard Cohen
items.why: Ajay calls it 'one of the great songs to know' — a really, really deep song that anyone serious about songwriting should sit with.

items.title: Swachh Bharat (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 82)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: The deeper exploration of the toilets-without-drainage example — and how the missing invisible infrastructure of sewage and social norms made the campaign exacerbate the caste problem it was supposed to dignify away.

items.title: Sweetness and Power
items.creator: Sidney Mintz
items.why: Provides the cultural and historical grounding — including the line that 'highly refined sucrose produces peculiar physiological effects,' and the tradition of sugar's first taste being an 'astonishment, a kind of intoxication.'

items.title: Taking the Hands
items.creator: Robert Bly
items.why: The poem opens the conceit of the episode — that something small (hands, a printed sheet, a map) can contain a vast universe. The compression of meaning into a tiny object is the same magic as a map.

items.title: Talking Heads
items.creator: Talking Heads
items.why: Amit's own pathway into Byrne's work and the meta-thinking of How Music Works.

items.title: Talking to an Empty Room
items.creator: Sharad Joshi
items.why: The title breaks Amit's heart — Joshi had great ideas the country desperately needed, and he was speaking them into a chamber that didn't care. A reminder of how much policy-quality knowledge gets wasted in Indian public life.

items.title: Tangerine
items.creator: Led Zeppelin
items.why: Ajay challenges listeners to first read the lyrics on the page and ask what kind of song you would make from those lines — because that is what happened to him many years ago, and the actual song is surprising and brilliant. 'It'll just make you think about songs.'

items.title: Taxes Should Be Used for Governance, Not Politics
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Operationalises the 'every act of government is violence' frame: if the violence is justified for protecting rights, it is much harder to justify for statues and frivolous schemes.

items.title: Technology, Taxation, and Corruption: Evidence from the Introduction of Electronic Tax Filing
items.creator: Oyebola Okunogbe and Victor Pouliquen
items.why: A cautionary example, not an endorsement. The paper credits e-filing with its results, but Ajay argues e-filing is always part of a complex reform, shaped by '500 subtle details' of law, public administration, invisible infrastructure, culture and norms. Crediting the intervention alone is the reductionist mistake he warns economists against.

items.title: Television Price Controls (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 27)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ashok Malik
items.why: The episode where Malik explains exactly why Indian TV news is so screamy: government-mandated subscription price caps left advertising as the only revenue, which makes the race-to-the-bottom inevitable. The 'shouty news' problem is a regulation problem in disguise.

items.title: Terror as a Bargaining Instrument: A Case Study of Dowry Violence in Rural India
items.creator: Francis Bloch and Vijayendra Rao
items.why: The finding Amit highlights: domestic violence was often a rational choice, a way to forcibly extract money from the wife's family, which made economists rethink how they model household and transfer behaviour. As Rao puts it, 'without the fieldwork, we would never have thought of studying domestic violence.'

items.title: Testaments Betrayed
items.creator: Milan Kundera
items.why: Source of the man-in-the-fog parable that closes the episode — you walk forward step by step, making your road; from a distance an observer sees the road but not the fog. Amit's signature image for the bias for action.

items.title: The 5 Types of Wealth
items.creator: Sahil Bloom
items.why: Mentioned by Amit as sitting in his Kindle queue at the time of recording, expected to be read by telecast.

items.title: The age of the partial outsider
items.creator: Janan Ganesh
items.why: The phrase that frames Amit's whole approach: someone with enough proximity to understand a field and enough distance not to be enslaved by its conventions. A useful self-diagnosis tool for any reader.

items.title: The Alchemy of Finance
items.creator: George Soros
items.why: Source of the concept of reflexivity — the idea that the narratives we impose on a system change how the system behaves. Amit applies it to caste here, but it originated as a theory of finance.

items.title: The Amitava Kumar episodes (The Seen and the Unseen)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Amitava Kumar
items.why: The companion listening for Amit's exhortation to journal — Kumar's blue book, yellow book and now green book journal both writing and drawing.

items.title: The ancient fabric that no one knows how to make
items.creator: Zaria Gorvett
items.why: The story Amit followed down the rabbit hole — covers the 18th-century scandal, the 1200-thread thread-counts, and the modern reverse-engineering project.

items.title: The Annihilation of Caste
items.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
items.why: A foundational critique of any reductive theory (Marxism, in particular) that explains everything by class while ignoring caste. Free to read online as part of Ambedkar's 60+ volumes of collected writings.

items.title: The Answer Is 42
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: From Amit's archive of poker-and-life writings collected for this episode.

items.title: The Anxious Generation
items.creator: Jonathan Haidt
items.why: Ajay's evidence base for the claim that social media has done massive damage to society, especially to people under 25.

items.title: The Art of Narrative Nonfiction (+ JBS Haldane) (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 183)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Samanth Subramanian
items.why: The episode that surfaced the 'I don't want to wear socks' anecdote and other Haldane stories Amit draws on here.

items.title: The Art of Reading (Everything is Everything, episode 120)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: A favourite of both hosts because it surfaced their private passion for books — why and how to read better. Amit cites it as proof that the show worked best when it ranged into personal territory, not just public-policy territory.

items.title: The Atheism Episode (Everything is Everything, episode 83)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: The hosts' joint case for atheism, and the framing that taking the fundamental tragedy of mortality seriously paradoxically frees you to laugh at the smaller absurdities.

items.title: The Balancing Act
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: From Amit's archive of poker-and-life writings collected for this episode — likely on balanced ranges in poker.

items.title: The Ballad of John Axon
items.creator: Charles Parker, Ewan MacColl, Peggy Seeger
items.why: A foundational landmark in audio storytelling and a model of 'show, don't tell.' The producers gathered village interviews and ambient sound never originally meant to air, then had the master stroke of using all of it — letting the people who knew Axon paint his portrait through their own voices instead of any narrator describing him.

items.title: The Bastiat Prize
items.why: Self-referenced because Amit won it twice. He uses it as the live counter-example to Ajay's case against prizes: a non-elite, ideologically-specific prize that meaningfully helped a lonely writer continue his work.

items.title: The Bear Came Over the Mountain
items.creator: Alice Munro
items.why: Possibly Amit's favourite short story of all time. 'Just magnificent.' A specific entry point into Munro for anyone unsure where to begin.

items.title: The Beautiful Tree
items.creator: James Tooley
items.why: Documents how budget private schools spring up wherever the state has failed, and how the poor — given any choice at all — vote with their feet to pay for them rather than take a free government school. The empirical answer to the 'private is for the rich' caricature.

items.title: The Big Fat Surprise
items.creator: Nina Teicholz
items.why: Demolishes the saturated-fat-causes-heart-disease consensus and traces the dogma back to Ancel Keys's Seven Countries Study and the lobbying that protected it. Essential to understanding why the conventional dietary wisdom you grew up with is wrong.

items.title: The BIGGEST Day of My Career — Chris Horner On His Vuelta a España Win
items.creator: Chris Horner
items.why: The clearest first-person account of how a 41-year-old beat the world's best — strategy, calorie management, and team tactics narrated by the rider himself.

items.title: The BJP Before Modi (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 202)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
items.why: Source of the line Amit quotes from Sitapati: 'Never let perfection be the enemy of production.' A whole hour of writing-process discussion compressed into one practical aphorism.

items.title: The Black Paintings
items.creator: Francisco Goya
items.why: Amit's emotional centre of the episode — the singular case of an old master making radically modern work for no audience, decades before the moderns arrived. The room at the Prado is the recommendation.

items.title: The Book of Laughter and Forgetting
items.creator: Milan Kundera
items.why: A meditation that pairs naturally with the episode's argument that the marriage of love and humour, once so natural in Shakespeare, has become rarer in contemporary work.

items.title: The Book of Love
items.creator: Magnetic Fields
items.why: Used to draw the analogy that the book of love remains as mysterious today as it was six hundred years ago, while our spatial map of the world has been utterly transformed by Google Maps and GPS. Different domains modernise at radically different speeds.

items.title: The Book That Incited a Worldwide Fear of Overpopulation
items.creator: Charles Mann
items.why: Source of the chilling detail Amit reads aloud: birth-control pills literally pitched out of helicopters over Philippine villages; health workers' salaries determined by the number of IUDs they inserted. Sets the global context for what Sanjay Gandhi did in India.

items.title: The Bridge: The Life and Rise of Barack Obama
items.creator: David Remnick
items.why: Mentioned as another Remnick gem, and the source of Amit's poker-trivia favourite — that Obama played poker in the late 1990s not for the game or the money but because it was the best way to socialise and network with Democratic insiders in a relaxed, convivial setting.

items.title: The Bureau of Industry and Security sanctions list
items.creator: U.S. Department of Commerce
