items.why: The episode where Shruti pointed out the fundamental mismatch in Indian cities — power and accountability aren't linked. The people residents have power over can't act; the people who can act aren't accountable to residents.

items.title: Utilitarianism (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
items.why: Listed as one of the secular moral frameworks. Amit's main critique is the Hayekian knowledge problem — the world is too complex to know the consequences of any action, so utilitarian calculation is hard to operationalise.

items.title: V-Dem
items.creator: Varieties of Democracy Institute
items.why: Ajay notes V-Dem is in many ways a better measure than Freedom House but more work to use; mentioned as the more rigorous alternative for serious students of democratic backsliding.

items.title: Vaishnav Vyas's football Substack
items.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
items.why: Amit and Vaishnav talk football constantly while shooting; the recommendation is offered as a window into a way of loving sport that is about playing philosophy ('what is Guardiola doing now?') rather than tribal allegiance to a national or club flag.

items.title: Vasanth Dhar's writing
items.creator: Vasanth Dhar
items.why: Personal-tone writing on subjects Vasanth knows well, and the just-completed book that grew out of that newsletter discipline.

items.title: Vinayak Calling Vinayak (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 385)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Vinayak Chaturvedi
items.why: The deep dive on Savarkar — including the two-Savarkars frame (before and after the Andamans) that Amit alludes to here.

items.title: Vinod Khosla on investors
items.creator: Vinod Khosla (clip)
items.why: Khosla's claim that 70% of VCs add negative value. The principle: without skin in the game and lived founder experience, textbook gyan from a credentialed outsider can actively harm a company.

items.title: Vinod Khosla on vision and tactics
items.creator: Vinod Khosla
items.why: How long-term thinking and daily reality coexist: the vision is the why; tactics adjust hourly when reality bites back.

items.title: Virtue Ethics (Wikipedia)
items.creator: Aristotle
items.why: The third secular moral school cited. Has appeal for Amit because it identifies ways of behaving that 'make everybody better off' and lead to human prosperity — derived from observation of humans, not revelation.

items.title: Visakan Veerasamy tweet quoting Nietzsche — 'He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.'
items.creator: Visakan Veerasamy
items.why: Springboard for the discussion of purpose as superpower — practical aspects are solvable; the fire is what keeps you going.

items.title: Vishnu Prasanna interviewed by Sagar Shah
items.creator: Sagar Shah
items.why: First-hand account of the experiment that may explain Gukesh's exceptional calculation skills and his weaker positional/blitz profile.

items.title: Vishwanathan Anand piece for ESPN
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The piece anticipates the Sultan-Khan parallel — Indian players rising through intuition rather than osmosis.

items.title: Vitalik Buterin's writings
items.creator: Vitalik Buterin
items.why: Vitalik is at the global frontier of rethinking identity, and Ajay frames him not as 'some random crypto guy' but as a deep thinker on politics and political philosophy — 'the card-carrying engineer that turned into a card-carrying political philosopher.'

items.title: Vivian Gornick on Amazon
items.creator: Vivian Gornick
items.why: Amit credits his conversation with Bhattacharya for introducing him to Gornick as 'a great memoirist' worth reading.

items.title: Vlad Tenev's product philosophy
items.creator: Vlad Tenev
items.why: 'One screen, one button, one action' as a literal design constraint — and a generalised rule against the kitchen-sink temptation.

items.title: VP Menon: The Unsung Architect of Modern India
items.creator: Narayani Basu
items.why: Amit calls it a 'marvellous book' and credits it explicitly for all the details of Menon's early life that drive his pitch.

items.title: Waiting for Godot
items.creator: Samuel Beckett
items.why: Two characters waiting for nothing, riffing on each other, embody the kind of tragicomic alienation Amit wants for his Khalsa-bridge film.

items.title: Waking Life
items.creator: Richard Linklater
items.why: Linklater, for Vaishnav, has captured the essence of life on film — the work has taught him how to look at people, how people look at us, and how to develop self-awareness about who he is.

items.title: Want Free Trade? May I Introduce You to the Tariff
items.creator: Robert Lighthizer
items.why: Ajay calls it 'the best article I read' from the American Right on tariffs. Multiple people sent it to him asking how he would respond, which forced him to think carefully. Contains the cleanest articulation of how non-tariff barriers, hidden subsidies, currency manipulation, and predatory tax systems have hollowed out the WTO framework — even where you reject Lighthizer's prescriptions, he frames the diagnosis sharply.

items.title: Warren Buffett on inner scorecards
items.creator: Warren Buffett
items.why: The closing principle of the episode: build a life and a company guided by what you privately know to be right, not what is publicly applauded.

items.title: Warrior Lovers
items.creator: Catherine Salmon and Donald Symons
items.why: Source of the central juxtaposition in this episode: the 'pornotopia' of male fantasy versus the 'romantotopia' of female fantasy — and the argument that the romance novel is, structurally, a chronicle of female mate choice.

items.title: Watching the Wheels (Chris Cornell version)
items.creator: Chris Cornell
items.why: Amit's favourite version of the song. He texted Gaurav Chintamani after hearing Ishaan's first cut to ask whether Ishaan was performing the Cornell version — but Ishaan had heard both and made his own.

items.title: Watershed 1967: India's Forgotten Victory Over China
items.creator: Probal Dasgupta
items.why: The basis for the episode's stories about Sagat Singh, the Shuddh-Hindi loudspeaker propaganda, and the 1965 US war-game prediction of Pakistan's proxy invasion. Amit just recorded a Seen and the Unseen episode with Dasgupta on this.

items.title: Ways of Seeing
items.creator: John Berger
items.why: Amit's deeper-dive recommendation for readers who want to go past art history and into how vision and ideology shape what we see in pictures.

items.title: We Are All Amits From Africa (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 343)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Krish Ashok and Naren Shenoy
items.why: Source of the Upma-as-WWII-compromise story and the broader argument that caste endogamy multiplied India's micro-cuisines.

items.title: We Must Save Our Farmers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Self-recommended along with his other agriculture writing as an entry point into the policy diagnosis.

items.title: Weapons of the Weak
items.creator: James C. Scott
items.why: The companion piece to Against the Grain. If states emerged to tax and conscript, large numbers of people throughout history just wanted the state to leave them alone — and they had ingenious quiet methods of doing so. Ajay sees 'more than a shadow' of this disposition in much of Indian society today.

items.title: What Cricket Can Learn From Economics
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Spells out the economic logic behind front-loading. Every dot ball is a foregone alternative; in T20 the constraint is balls, not wickets; therefore aggression is the rational default.

items.title: What Economics Can Learn (Everything is Everything, episode 75)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Used to extend the Weber point — that even within an academic discipline, sub-silos prevent the bigger picture from emerging.

items.title: What Happened to Global Food Prices?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Shows how the international market is the great buffer against domestic shortages — and why India's habit of banning imports and exports at whim destroys the very stabilisation it claims to seek.

items.title: What I, as a development economist, have been actively 'for'
items.creator: Lant Pritchett
items.why: The constructive companion to his many critiques — what is to be done, in his own words. Linked in the show notes as a key Pritchett primer.

items.title: What is Hindutva
items.creator: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar
items.why: Cited not as endorsement but as primary source. Amit calls it 'a theory of violence in search of a history' (per Shruti Kapila) — masterful in achieving its end of othering Muslims and Christians while assimilating Jains and Buddhists. Read it to understand what nationalism in India actually rests on.

items.title: What Is the New Chinese Currency Regime?
items.creator: Ajay Shah, Achim Zeileis and Ila Patnaik
items.why: Cited not for its content but as Ajay's exhibit for distance-based collaboration done well. It is the proof, in his life, that internet-scale rapport can produce real intellectual work, provided the contracting problem is solved first.

items.title: What Should India Do? (Everything is Everything, episode 114)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Referenced for the principle invoked in this episode — that strategic action requires deep understanding of your adversaries (Hitler did not understand America; this episode's MAGA-isolationist America is similarly poorly understood).

items.title: What You Can Learn from Family Business
items.creator: Nicolas Kachaner, George Stalk Jr., and Alain Bloch
items.why: Counters the Indian elite's reflexive disdain for family firms by showing they are frugal in good and bad times, keep the bar high for capex, carry little debt, acquire fewer and smaller companies, are surprisingly diversified and international, and retain talent better. In good times professional firms do better; in bad times family firms do less badly.

items.title: What's Consolation for an Atheist?
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Confronts the one role of religion — consolation in bereavement — that Amit acknowledges he cannot fully replace, while refusing to embrace a comforting fiction. His honest conclusion: 'I can't help being an atheist. I'm not going to start believing in a fiction because I need to console myself.'

items.title: What's Wrong With the Indian Media? (Everything is Everything, episode 113)
items.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
items.why: Sets up the discussion of the information space as a domestic-reform priority — trusted information is more valuable, not less, in a noisy world.

items.title: When All Else Fails: The Ethics of Resistance to State Injustice
items.creator: Jason Brennan
items.why: Amit's recommendation for the day. The book contains the policeman-and-beggar thought experiment that Amit uses to crack open how silently we grant the state moral authority. It will leave you thinking about legitimacy, authority and morality at the same time.

items.title: When and where do great feats of architecture come about?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: His argument: imposing structures are usually a totalitarian regime's way of making peasants bow. First-principles architecture, by contrast, evolves from local materials, weather, and craftsmanship — and is the right model for food culture too.

items.title: When Crime Pays
items.creator: Milan Vaishnav
items.why: A must-read on the role of criminal candidates in Indian politics.

items.title: When Genius Failed
items.creator: Roger Lowenstein
items.why: A cautionary tale about derivatives, leverage, and the limits of even the best academic models when faced with the real world. A reminder of what can go wrong even when the brains involved are at the very top.

items.title: When Harry Met Sally
items.creator: Rob Reiner
items.why: The film whose central premise — 'men and women can't be friends because the sex part always gets in the way' — names the index The Economist proposed for the Facebook cross-gender friendship dataset (the WHMSI / WIMSY index).

items.title: When McKinsey Comes to Town
items.creator: Walt Bogdanich and Michael Forsythe
items.why: Ajay recommends 'cautiously' — he finds the book a bit mean and one-sided — but it offers genuine insight into what goes wrong when consulting-firm logic is dragged into the complex problems of public policy.

items.title: When the Chips Are Down
items.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
items.why: Demystifies the semiconductor wars and what's really going on in the chip industry — pairs naturally with Chris Miller's Chip War for understanding the stakes of the current US-China tech competition.

items.title: When We Were Robots in Egypt
items.creator: Jo Walton
items.why: Linked in the show notes as the 'beautiful poem' the hosts wanted to share — a literary counter to science-fiction alarmism about machines taking over.

items.title: Where Did Development Economics Go Wrong? (Ideas of India)
items.creator: Lant Pritchett with Shruti Rajagopalan
items.why: Companion long-form interview that goes deeper into the institutional and incentive distortions behind development economics' decline.

items.title: Where Did the Bombay Club Go Wrong?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Counterpoint to the rosy view that Indian industry was always pro-liberalisation. The Bombay Club showed how local capitalists can choose 'rule a small protected pond' over 'compete in a big global market' — the wrong choice that better entrepreneurial confidence would have rejected.

items.title: Where Your Taxes Go (India Uncut series)
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A running gag that doubles as a moral inventory. Each entry is a worked example of coerced money being spent on something whose justification under 'protecting individual rights' is, at best, strained.

items.title: Wherever I Lay My Hat (That's My Home)
items.creator: Paul Young
items.why: Linked alongside the Marvin Gaye version because the Paul/Paul Young/Marvin Gaye chain is what Amit's free-association makes of the song title. Both versions sit in the show notes as the closing musical thread of the episode.

items.title: White Magic Adventure Travel
items.creator: Delhi-based mountaineering services firm
items.why: Their fixed-calendar model means you can show up alone — no need to do the community project of gathering your own people. The flight will take off either way.

items.title: Who's Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
items.creator: Adam Mastroianni
items.why: Provides the three-step pattern for outlaw ideas: '1. A weirdo outsider proposes some new idea. 2. Experts and authorities ignore or suppress it because it seems stupid. This can go on for a long time. 3. Eventually, the new idea wins out because it is a good idea.' And it argues the modern system is so disincentive-loaded that step 1 barely happens any more.

items.title: Why Abhijit Banerjee Had to Go Abroad to Achieve Glory
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Sets up the central argument of the episode: Banerjee's Presidency College and JNU years mattered, but it was Harvard, the cluster, that was decisive. The piece introduces Kremer's O-Ring theory as the underlying mechanism.

items.title: Why AI Will Save the World
items.creator: Marc Andreessen
items.why: Amit's anti-doom recommendation: 'a beautiful essay he addresses all of these questions in great detail' — the long-form counter to the 'AI is going to wipe out humanity' framing.

items.title: Why are firms short-sighted?
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Background for his claim that high cost of capital in an underdeveloped financial system makes Indian firms structurally short-sighted — and that this is precisely what governments must not be.

items.title: Why Children Labour
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: The longer version of the Bangladesh and Nepal stories — what happened to the children who were laid off when Western activists succeeded.

items.title: Why Does the Pandemic Seem to Be Hitting Some Countries Harder Than Others?
items.creator: Siddhartha Mukherjee
items.why: The article that occasioned Ajay's encounter with the New Yorker's fact-checking machine — and the reason he can speak first-hand about what real editorial process looks like.

items.title: Why Gig Work Matters
items.creator: Maitreesh Ghatak and Ajay Shah
items.why: The source of the 'gig work as urban NREGS' argument: gig work is self-targeting (only people down on their luck will pick up Swiggy deliveries) and self-adjusting (supply and demand find the price), but unlike NREGS it is not self-liquidating, and that is fine — it should be there permanently.

items.title: Why I Loved and Left Poker
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Tells you why Amit left poker — and may, he warns, tell you why you shouldn't start playing. The practical companion to the cautionary final chapter of his presentation.

items.title: Why I Write
items.creator: George Orwell
items.why: Linked in the show notes alongside Orwell's other essays; a companion piece for any reader who wants to understand the writer's relationship to their craft.

items.title: Why India Needs School Vouchers
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: His original case for vouchers — give the per-pupil money to parents and let them pick the school. Includes the detail about Delhi requiring some 42 licences to open a private school.

items.title: Why Is Solving India's Inflation Crisis Important? (2012)
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: An early formulation of the arguments developed in this episode, written during the 2007-onwards inflation crisis that ultimately won the case for institutional reform.

items.title: Why Is There A Commotion?
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: A companion piece to the victimless-crimes argument, focused on why public moral panics keep producing bad law.

items.title: Why Nationalism
items.creator: Yael Tamir
items.why: Amit reviewed it (he will link the review). He doesn't accept Tamir's case but found the book serious enough to be worth engaging with — and ends his review by reclaiming the term 'anti-national' for those who divide us.

items.title: Why Nations Fail
items.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson
items.why: The institutional-economics canon for understanding why some countries make it to advanced-economy status and most don't.

items.title: Why Read the Classics?
items.creator: Italo Calvino
items.why: Recommended as one of the 'meta-books on reading' the episode has gathered.

items.title: Why the Future Doesn't Need Us
items.creator: Bill Joy
items.why: Ajay invokes it as the cautionary frame: editing DNA is harder than editing computer code, and we know how badly software fails. Approach with respect — neither ban nor blank cheque.

items.title: Why the RBI Communication to Government on the Failure to Meet Inflation Target Must Be Placed in the Public Domain
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: Argues for the public release of the RBI's mea-culpa letter when it misses its inflation target — the same humiliation/peer-respect mechanism used in New Zealand. Make missing the target painful, public and structural; that's how a handcuff works.

items.title: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
items.creator: Christopher Blattman
items.why: Ajay's central recommendation. Blattman opens up violence as an object of economic analysis — both citizen-citizen and state-citizen violence — and treats taming it as essential to development. Ajay is delighted that an economist has finally taken this seriously.

items.title: Wild Strawberries
items.creator: Ingmar Bergman
items.why: Amit's recommended best gateway into Bergman, who can otherwise feel inaccessible. A magnificent film about old age and growing old gracefully.

items.title: William Niskanen's books
items.creator: William A. Niskanen
items.why: The serious treatment of what Parkinson satirised: officials systematically maximise their bureau's budget and turf, with ripple effects across all of policy.

items.title: William Spaniel (Game Theory 101)
items.creator: William Spaniel
items.why: He combines first-draft-of-history (videos in real time) with slower considered books — exactly the dual register Ajay argues this age demands.

items.title: Wiring the World
items.creator: Emily Thompson
items.why: The factual backdrop of Amit's 'Silence of the Heart' film pitch — Thompson tracks how ERP grew, how the French burned a theatre down to repel the evangelists, and how the Indian film industry eventually told them to get lost.

items.title: Womaning in India With Mahima Vashisht (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 293)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Mahima Vashisht
items.why: The other Roam demo: when source material doesn't come with chapters, build a 'themes' layer (controlling female sexuality, Raja Beta syndrome, world designed by men, interior lives) and re-index everything against your own classification.

items.title: Women at Work (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 132)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Namita Bhandare
items.why: Background reading for the puzzle Ajay raises: why FLFP went up and then dipped, partly because rising household income made it 'shameful' for the wife to keep working.

items.title: Words
items.creator: Bee Gees
items.why: A light cultural anchor for the episode's serious point: getting the technical meaning of words like 'populism' right is itself a foundation for clear thinking.

items.title: Working paper on global carbon coordination
items.creator: Ajay Shah
items.why: An optimist's case that with the requisite carbon taxation and the energy revolution already in progress (solar, wind, nuclear, storage), the climate problem is far more tractable than the alarmist framing suggests.

items.title: World Energy Outlook 2023
items.creator: International Energy Agency
items.why: Ajay's recommendation for the episode. He acknowledges nobody reads reports, but says this one is unputdownable. The world of energy is pure drama right now and the report's data, graphs, and stories will repay the time. Make an exception.

items.title: Worldly Philosopher: The Odyssey of Albert O. Hirschman
items.creator: Jeremy Adelman
items.why: Ajay's strongest recommendation of the episode. Even where Hirschman's specific 'linkages' argument was overtaken by globalisation, the man himself led 'the world's best life' — economist, political philosopher, thinker — and his biography is the kind of life one reads to learn how to live. Ajay puts him in the same category of love as James C. Scott.

items.title: XKDR Working Papers
items.creator: XKDR Forum
items.why: Recommended in the same spirit as the Leap blog — his answer when teaching/speaking invitations come: 'I point people to these things; please use them.'

items.title: Young Rural Women in India Chase Big-City Dreams
items.creator: Ellen Barry
items.why: Ajay sees the emergence of firms and exports as 'the heart and soul of the Indian story,' but the data alone misses the human drama. Barry's article zooms in on the personal transformation — agency, choices, escape from village constraints — that even entry-level export jobs deliver to women.

items.title: Your Maid Funds Unani
items.creator: Amit Varma
items.why: Demolishes the popular myth that 'only 3% of Indians pay taxes.' If the state spends violence-extracted money on, say, Unani medicine, it is your maid who is funding it. The moral cost of state spending is borne all the way down the income ladder.

items.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
items.creator: Robert M. Pirsig
items.why: Source of the line, 'The Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there.' What you experience on the trail depends on what you carry in your head.

items.title: Zombie Firms and Creative Destruction (The Seen and the Unseen, episode 118)
items.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
items.why: The deep dive on the same diagnosis Ajay revisits here — what zombie firms do to a healthy economy.
